name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: After Iowan’s death, assisted living company fires regional administrator
text:
Lawton Senior Living, an assisted living center in Woodbury County. (Photo via Google Earth)  An assisted-living company recently fired one of its top administrators after a resident death in Iowa resulted in a care facility being cited for numerous violations and its license being downgraded to conditional status.
State records indicate Natasha Kanealy, 39, began working for Jaybird Senior Living, also known as JSL Workforce Solutions, in July 2017, most recently as the company’s full-time regional director of clinical operations.
In 2025, the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing inspectors visited one of the company’s facilities, the Parker Place Retirement Community, which is an assisted living center in Parkersburg. DIAL ordered Parker Place to stop accepting new patients, while also placing the facility’s license on conditional status. Parker Place was one of the businesses over which Kanealy had oversight responsibilities, according to state workforce records.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In August 2026, DIAL inspectors investigated another of the company’s businesses, Lawton Senior Living, an assisted living center in Woodbury County, and issued a report citing the facility for 31 regulatory violations.
Inspectors said the Lawton home’s “management company failed to provide adequate oversight and operational direction to maintain a safe, healthy environment and ensure consistent service delivery to tenants at Lawton Senior Living.” The inspectors described what they called “systemic breakdowns” in operations, resulting in unsanitary living conditions, a lack of completed background checks on staff, a failure to respond to “significant” medical events, and also noted “chronic staffing shortages” that had left the home’s memory care unit understaffed.
Caregiver of resident who died was 16 years old  
The inspectors reported that an 88-year-old female resident of the home was taken to a hospital emergency room by ambulance on April 6, 2026, and was diagnosed with multiple wounds, including bruises and skin tears on her arms, legs and face, as well as multiple fractured ribs and a broken hip. The woman died two weeks later, with medical records showing evidence of blunt force trauma with head and neck contusions.
A subsequent investigation indicated that a 16-year-old universal worker at the home had been working alone in the dementia-care unit with woman and nine other residents, during an evening shift when the woman’s injuries were most likely sustained. The teenager allegedly told inspectors he saw the woman fall to the floor and that although she was not making sounds or speaking after the incident, he had put her to bed without informing a nurse or documenting the alleged fall.
According to the DIAL inspectors, some of the staff later concluded the injuries most likely were caused not by a fall but by an employee of the home. Inspectors say the state medical examiner said he could not determine the cause of death but that the injuries to the woman’s left side suggested they were not the result of her falling on her right side as had been reported.
According to state inspection reports, the 16-year-old employee was fired the day the injured woman was taken to the hospital. The youth allegedly told inspectors he had completed all his training at the home on a computer, was given no hands-on training, and had not worked with a nurse on his skills. He also alleged he had been given no specific training on emergency situations, the individual residents, or the residents’ care plans.
In addition, inspectors reported, records showed the youth and two other employees had administered medications to residents without having completed the required, DIAL-approved course on medication management.
As a 16-year-old employee, inspectors reported, the youth was not “old enough to pass medication,” regardless of training. In Iowa, individuals as young as 16 can work in health-care settings such as assisted living centers and can also become certified nursing assistants.
According to state records, one employee of the Lawton home told inspectors the 16-year-old universal worker had been tasked with training him to work in the memory care unit, but that the teenager then told him he didn’t like training his co-workers and did not like people.
Previous deaths at Jaybird-managed homes
State inspectors said they reviewed 15 employee files and found that in five of the 15 cases, the home had not completed the mandatory background checks on those individuals before putting them to work in the home.
After citing Lawton Senior Living for 31 regulatory violations, DIAL fined the facility $13,500. Because Jaybird Senior Living didn’t appeal the fine, DIAL then reduced the penalty 35% to $8,775.
State workforce records indicate that on Aug. 17, 2026, Jaybird Senior Living fired Kanealy for allegedly failing to meet the “essential leadership, clinical oversight, regulatory compliance, and accountability responsibilities” of the job. Kanealy then applied for unemployment benefits, which led to a Sept. 29, 2026, hearing before Administrative Law Judge Daniel Zeno.
In a recent decision, Zeno ruled that Kanealy was entitled to collect unemployment benefits, finding that she had “attempted to perform the job to the best of her ability.” Kanealy’s inability to meet her employer’s work expectations did not establish the sort of job-related misconduct that would disqualify her from collecting benefits, Zeno stated in his ruling.
“The employer did what was in its best interest and ended Ms. Kanealy’s employment, but the employer has not established disqualifying, job-related misconduct,” Zeno ruled.
Jaybird Senior Living is headquartered in Cedar Rapids and manages 17 care facilities in Iowa, as well as 28 facilities in 10 other states. Jaybird manages Bondurant’s Courtyard Estates at Hawthorne Crossing, the assisted living facility where 77-year-old Lynne Stewart froze to death in January 2022. Jaybird is also the former manager of Keelson Harbour Senior Living, an assisted living center in Spirit Lake where 95-year-old Elaine Creasey froze to death in December 2021.
No criminal charges were filed in the Keelson Harbour death, but in the Courtyard Estates case, a caregiver was charged with second-degree murder before prosecutors agreed to a plea deal that resulted in the murder charge being downgraded to misdemeanor dependent adult abuse.
Jaybird is a for-profit company headed by CEO Kevin Russell, a former lawyer and investment banker from Rancho Santa Fe, California.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Kanealy, Russell or the two Jaybird executives who testified at Kanealy’s unemployment hearing.

title: Vermont colleges should recruit closer to home
text:
Dear Editor,
If Vermont schools hadn’t overlooked the current pool of stateside kids looking for a quality Vermont college, enrollment at those places wouldn’t have collapsed as it has. Until college administrators get smart, they’ll have a parade of international students using Vermont as an entryway to America and not for higher learning. 

READ MORE

Why weren’t students from northern New England, where I lived for 42 years, and other stateside locations tapped for Vermont’s schools? Why does it seem that Vermont was chasing the elusive — frankly, nonexistent — international students well-versed in English who wanted to stay in Vermont after graduation? In my opinion, that pool doesn’t exist. 
Meanwhile, Vermont offers fewer and fewer choices for colleges. 
Betty LaChausseeBoca Raton, Fla.

title: After upsets in 2024, parties focus on key races for balance of power in Vermont Senate
text:
Democratic incumbent Sen. Ruth Hardy, left, speaks during an Addison County Senate candidates forum in Addison on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Seated next to her are Republican challenger Andrew Klein, Republican incumbent Sen. Steve Heffernan, and Democratic challenger Hannah Sessions. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
On election night in November 2024, a red wave crashed over the Vermont Senate. 
In a single evening, the GOP shattered Democratic supermajorities in both legislative chambers and nearly doubled conservative membership in the Senate to gain Republicans’ highest share of power there since 2000.
“Certainly the biggest thing to rectify,” Vermont Democratic Party Chair Lachlan Francis said wryly of his party’s strategy this fall, “is winning.”
Weeks ahead of Election Day, leaders across the political spectrum are watching a number of competitive Senate races closely. While Democrats seek to make up ground in Montpelier as the national party gains momentum in midterm polling, Republicans want to build on their newfound legislative clout to flip control of the chamber for the first time in decades.
For former Sen. Chris Bray, an Addison County Democrat who served nearly two decades in the Statehouse and was among those voted out on Nov. 5, 2024, the outcome wasn’t entirely surprising. As “shock and dismay” rolled in from his legislative colleagues through texts, calls and emails, Bray said in an interview last week, he reflected on a deep uneasiness he’d felt over much of the six-month campaign.
The former Senate Natural Resources and Energy Committee chair recalled warning colleagues during a June 2024 veto session that “people are upset and angry” over property tax spikes in particular. Conservative messaging around the Legislature’s role in that problem, Bray argued, was “unfair and inaccurate” and took advantage of a poorly understood issue for the electorate.
Ultimately, the political fallout was intense, with Republican Gov. Phil Scott conducting an “orchestra” of affordability-focused messaging, according to state GOP Chair Paul Dame.
Nationwide, Republicans managed to flip roughly 50 state legislative seats that evening. Twenty-six were in Vermont, according to a post-election report written in part by Francis.
Alongside Bray, then-Sen. Mark MacDonald, D-Orange, whom voters had sent to the Legislature for three cumulative decades, lost decisively to GOP challenger Larry Hart. Republican Pat Brennan flipped the Grand Isle County seat long held by the late center-left veteran Dick Mazza. And three more seats turned red, adding now-Senate Minority Leader Scott Beck to the chamber representing Caledonia County, as well as Sen. Chris Mattos and former Sen. Sam Douglass on behalf of the Chittenden North district and Orleans district, respectively.
Beck said in an interview recently that his party’s wins in 2024, which brought GOP Senate membership to 13 out of 30, placed outright control of the chamber “much more within reach.” And if Republicans are making a pitch to control the legislative agenda in the Senate for the first time since 1996, he said, it’s more important than ever for voters to understand the caucus’s priorities.
Beck has been a central architect of Senate Republicans’ Vermont Promise campaign this year, which lays out a slate of goals ranging from property tax reforms to repealing the state’s “Raise the Age” law that routes young adults charged with most offenses through juvenile delinquency proceedings instead of criminal court. 
For Dame, part of the effect of Vermont Promise is to separate his party from national Republicans, who face what he called a negative environment. 
“I think it sets up that contrast,” Dame said, adding that the policy slate concentrates on the issues over which state legislators have the most direct control. 
Beck, for his part, said national GOP policies did not figure into the campaign’s creation. He and his colleagues simply sought to lay out their plans for controlling Vermonters’ costs, among other goals, he said. Beck faces a challenge in the general election from Democrat David Roth.
The anti-incumbent sentiment that Democrats experienced in 2024 may be a factor again this November, according to Sen. Kesha Ram Hinsdale, D-Chittenden Southeast, who serves as Senate majority leader. But this time, she said, Republican lawmakers and the governor in particular have had considerably more policy influence to answer for in the last two years.
“I don’t think any political party can rest on their laurels and say, ‘Those are our red voters, or our blue voters,’” she said in an interview.
For Francis, the Trump administration’s influence in recent years — including broad cuts to social services, fuel price increases during the Iran war and a continuing trade conflict with Canada — are sure to have a local electoral impact in November. State lawmakers, he said, can make a difference to Vermonters’ pocketbooks one way or another, regardless of their ability to intervene in national or international affairs.
“Everywhere you go, people are seeing the ripple effects of federal policy, and it’s affecting negatively their community,” he said. “I think there’s no doubt that’s going to motivate people of like mind with Democrat candidates to get out and vote.”
When national Republicans gained momentum across the country in 2024, Ram Hinsdale said, some Vermont conservatives were “happy to ride that wave.” Now, she said, “They have to take a side.”
Ram Hinsdale faces a challenge this fall from Republicans Bruce Roy, Javen Sears and Rohan St. Marthe in the three-seat Chittenden Southeast district.
‘The greatest vulnerability and the greatest opportunity’
Addison County is the state’s only Senate district with both Democratic and Republican representation. 
Strategists agreed that the race for the district’s two seats may be the most closely watched contest of the cycle. Republican Sen. Steve Heffernan, who overcame Bray two years ago, and Democratic Sen. Ruth Hardy face two well-funded challenges from political newcomers Hannah Sessions and Andrew Klein.

Democratic challenger Hannah Sessions chats with a prospective voter at the end of an Addison County Senate candidates forum in Addison on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Republican challenger Andrew Klein, right, chats with another voter behind her. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

“It’s sort of like the greatest vulnerability and the greatest opportunity at the same time,” said Dame of his party’s newfound half-grip on the Addison district.
For East Middlebury’s Hardy, 2024 represented a particular moment of political anger over property taxes and several other issues.
Although those concerns have not dissipated, “I don’t think it means that there’s a shift overall in Addison County,” she said in an interview, adding that issues like childcare and education reform have been her focus during her Senate tenure. “This year, I’m feeling a different feel, you know? I think people are scared about what’s happening at the federal level. They’re worried about losing their rights.”
Sessions, a Democrat who owns a goat dairy farm and cheese operation in Leicester, agreed. 
“The big picture is one that we can’t ignore,” she said, pointing to new tariffs’ effects on local economies and to the end of expanded federal healthcare subsidies.
Donald Trump’s election in 2016 was part of what pushed her toward political work in the first place, Sessions added. A “rural-urban divide” by Vermont’s definitions that she saw emerging around land use and agriculture has also been a factor.
“Being a farmer that’s a Democrat, I thought that I could be useful in, you know, approaching some of these really sensitive topics,” Sessions said in a recent interview.
Klein, who spent years in finance and real estate before moving to Vermont and serving as a lieutenant with the Middlebury Fire Department and technical rescue team, enters the race as a self-described “Rockefeller Republican.” In the past, the New Haven resident has essentially been a fiscally conservative Democrat while living in New York and Connecticut, he said in an interview — and none of his beliefs has changed.
“I’d never make it through the primary as a Democrat,” Klein said, adding “it’s not like I shoehorned myself in there — I actually am a Vermont centrist Republican.”
And within the dynamics of the county, he feels his goals — which include pushing for financial efficiency on services like education while acknowledging the state’s fundamental need for more tax revenue — fit the bill, particularly given the electoral shifts in 2024 that allowed Heffernan to overcome Bray by fewer than 700 votes.
Heffernan, a Bristol resident, said in an interview that he believed the 2024 election illustrated the importance of political balance in the Legislature. A long-term supermajority on either side that can disregard the governor, he said, is not a recipe for success.
Pocketbook issues such as property taxes, coupled with what Heffernan called inadequate outcomes from public services like education, likely swayed people two years ago, he said. The national political context, he added, has little relevance to his role as a state lawmaker. His priorities in Montpelier have included education reform and supporting the farm economy, he said.
The Senate challengers in Addison County have mounted two of the best-financed campaigns in the state: Klein’s contributions now total over $65,000, including $12,000 from the state Republican Party. Heffernan has raised over $81,000, second among state Senate races this cycle only to Nikhil Goyal’s record-breaking war chest in Chittenden County. Sessions has raised $77,000, and Hardy has registered $51,000.
“It is crazy what either party is having to spend for a Senate race in Addison County,” Heffernan said. “That being said, that’s the nature of the beast.”
All roads
Essentially any path to a Republican Senate majority would need to run through Bennington County, according to Dame. Francis likewise cited the district as a primary area where Democrats need to play defense.
November 2024 saw Democrats keep a relatively narrow hold on the two-seat district, which has long been a blue stronghold represented by the likes of the late Sen. Dick Sears. The Democratic nominees — then-House Rep. Seth Bongartz and Deputy State’s Attorney Rob Plunkett — won in a crowded field, with a Republican in third place falling short by fewer than 600 votes.

READ MORE

Three independents who also entered the race garnered nearly 9,000 votes among them. Two of the independents were former Democratic House representatives.
The third, Lawrence “Spike” Whitmire, of Shaftsbury, has reemerged this fall as one of the GOP’s nominees — along with Josh Williams, of Arlington — challenging Bongartz and Plunkett. He’s always been fiscally conservative, Whitmire said in an interview Monday — and in a year where his district could make all the difference in the Senate, joining the Republicans is a more practical path to victory. 
His chief priority in the Statehouse, he said, would be fiscal responsibility. Williams likewise outlined himself as a moderate, intent on controlling education spending. 
Plunkett, who disputed the characterization of his campaign as “defense,” expressed confidence in the Democratic ticket’s chances. Sears’ death before the 2024 Senate primary was one of a number of factors that made that cycle a unique year for the county, said the Bennington resident.
“Bennington, sort of as a whole, is more purple than many counties,” Plunkett said. “But I think we are still a strong Democratic county.”
Both Republicans referenced the Vermont Promise agenda as a part of their policy platforms. For Beck, that was part of the campaign’s purpose: He has offered to meet with every Republican candidate to talk through the plan, he said, and to offer it as a partial basis for their campaigns.
Despite close attention from party leadership, the Bennington challengers are worried about money. Whitmire has raised just under $13,000, and Williams sits on $18,000 — of which he himself recently contributed $10,000. 
Although Democratic incumbents have raised comparable amounts, Williams said he’s at a clear disadvantage, primarily due to a lack of name recognition.
“I don’t have funding to get out a postcard,” he said earlier this month. “I’m definitely concerned.”
Whitmire believes his would-be constituents are simply too hard-pressed financially to furnish him with more campaign funding. But he’s striving to make up the difference through events and door-knocking, he said.

Republican incumbent Sen. Steve Heffernan, center, debates Democratic challenger Hannah Sessions, right, during an Addison County Senate candidates forum in Addison on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Republican candidate Andrew Klein is on the left. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

“The big-dollar donations just — just aren’t out there,” Whitmire said. “They’re being absorbed by (the) cost of living.”
However, Williams and Whitmire may have received some extra help, though both told VTDigger it came entirely without their involvement.
Francis said Bennington has been a primary site of advertising paid for by political action committees. In particular, a set of mailers from the Manchester-based Common Sense PAC attacking Plunkett and Bongartz over their records on education reform and public safety has recently been the subject of formal disclosure complaints.
“One of the big takeaways from 2024 was that our side got significantly outspent in paid media and expenditures,” Francis said, adding that the state party is trying to better shore up key candidates this year. Last week, the Vermont Democratic Party spent roughly $70,000 on advertising to weigh in against GOP Senate nominees.
Bongartz, who said he stood firmly behind his work negotiating legislation on voluntary school district mergers this past session, told VTDigger that the mailers’ accusations were “off the wall.”
“Everybody knows it’s garbage,” said the Manchester resident. “It has actually backfired and really inspired our fundraising.”
In addition to the incumbents’ increased profile in the district compared with two years ago, both Democrats said they perceived less of a singular focus on property taxes among voters — something Bongartz said could foreshadow less electoral volatility come Nov. 3. Plunkett expressed eagerness to get back to working on his policy priorities, including education and reducing the cost of primary healthcare.
The four major party candidates will face a challenge from Progressive Rachel Shaw, who is also running for secretary of state and did not respond to requests for comment.
‘A unique set of circumstances’
In Orange County, Rep. Monique Priestley, D-Bradford, is challenging Republican Sen. John Benson, who was appointed by Scott after Larry Hart resigned the seat he had won in 2024.
“It’s certainly a unique set of circumstances,” said Dame of the contest. “Monique Priestley has been serving in the Legislature longer than John, but John is technically the incumbent.”
Priestley had been considering running for the seat for some time, she said in an interview, as Mark MacDonald neared retirement. His loss in 2024 was a “major blow,” she said, but supporters — including MacDonald himself — have since encouraged her to run.
From Priestley’s perspective, Benson’s unusual position levels the playing field somewhat, reducing the often overwhelming power of incumbency.
“It’s the first time that he’s actually running, and the first time that I’m running,” she said.
Benson, a Brookfield resident, said in a written statement that his experience in the Senate this past session will allow him to hit the ground running if reelected. The full policy results of Republican wins in 2024 have yet to be realized, he added.
“There is still much more work ahead to be done,” he said.
For Ram Hinsdale, Benson’s presence in the Senate was a result of the election and swift departure of several lawmakers, including Hart, “who did not expect to win, necessarily.”
“Orange County could just really use a boost of representation,” she said, saying the contest between the two “pretty evenly matched” candidates for the job will rely heavily on turnout. 

Members of the Addison County Sporting Group listen during an Addison County Senate candidates forum in Addison on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The hard-fought race has attracted over $74,000 in donations for Benson and $65,000 for Priestley, placing it among the most monied contests in the state this year.
While nearly all of Benson’s contributions come from inside the state, nearly 40% of Priestley’s are categorized as out-of-state. The Bradford representative, whose main policy focus is technology and internet privacy, said the difference was partly due to her national profile in those areas, as well as personal and professional networks across the country.
Priestley and Dame both said that in recent years, the district may have shifted to the right. Priestley pointed to the state’s 2022 redistricting process, which moved Thetford, a relatively blue town in central Vermont, into the Windsor Senate district.
Dame, for his part, suggested that Rural Vermont Rising, a diffuse political movement that emerged this spring from resistance to Vermont’s 2024 land use overhaul, may have a concrete electoral impact in Orange County in particular.
Benson agreed, saying he helped pass partial rollbacks of the law last session and that the rural forum has “rightly become a huge part of the conversation.”
Priestley said she has been speaking with some of the group’s most visible members for months. Though she has reservations about some aspects of the movement’s online presence, she said, she was eager to continue engaging with the group on policy issues.
As far as the group’s electoral impact, she said, “there’s more questions than answers.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Jeffries joins Hines for roundtable on community concerns in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District
text:
U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Democratic congressional candidate Christina Hines take questions from reporters following a roundtable on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)In southern Macomb County, faith leaders and local government officials sat down with former special victims prosecutor Christina Hines and U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) to share the concerns they’ve heard from their communities and offer approaches Congress could take to better serve the people.
Gathering at Love Life Family Christian Center in Eastpointe, panelists from communities and congregations throughout Michigan’s 10th Congressional District pointed to a variety of concerns ranging from education to gun violence to ensuring people of all ages have access to community resources and support.
While the district is represented by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), James’ decision to run for governor has left the seat open. Democrats have taken this as an opportunity to expand their ranks, with the goal of regaining a majority of the U.S. House of Representatives. 
Voters selected Hines to carry the torch for Democrats into November, with U.S. Army Capt. Michael Bouchard Jr., who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, representing the Republican side of the ticket. While the district was initially considered to lean Republican, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report updated its rating to “toss up” at the end of August, signaling a highly competitive congressional race in the months to come.
At the start of the roundtable, Hines noted her excitement for panelists to share the concerns of their communities with Jeffries, who arrived partway through the panel due to a flight delay, and with her so that she could take those issues to Washington.
Members of the roundtable were also asked what they would like to see Congress do better and what questions they had for Jeffries, who could potentially become Speaker of the House if Democrats regain control of the chamber in November.
Here are some of their responses.
 
Pastor Kevin Lancaster of Love Life Family Christian Center
Pastor Kevin Lancaster of Love Life Family Christian Center and Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines at a roundtable on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Opening the roundtable, Lancaster said that education was a key concern for Macomb County, particularly in Eastpointe. 
“That’s one of the biggest indicators of poverty, is a lack of education, and yet our schools in Eastpointe are crumbling,” Lancaster said, before inquiring about what solutions Democrats are proposing to help schools perform.
 
Theresa McGarity, Mount Clemens city commissioner
Mount Clemens City Commissioner Theresa McGarity speaks at a roundtable on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
McGarity, who also works for the Macomb Community Action Center, listed accessibility to public resources as among the challenges she’d observed within her city and the county, noting that programs to assist residents are increasingly moving online. 
“Everybody don’t have a computer. Everybody can’t use a smartphone. And our seniors want to remain independent. They don’t want to have to call their children when they can do things themselves,” McGarity said, adding that seniors had also faced challenges with transportation to the library so they could have access to a computer to utilize those community resources.
Funding for senior services was also important, McGarity said, pointing to the need for one-on-one assistance to help them access programs that can assist with home weatherization, housing rehabilitation, utilities and food.
 
Jocelyn Howard, executive director of Citadel of Perpetual Learning
Jocelyn Howard, executive director of Citadel of Perpetual Learning at a roundtable with Macomb County faith leaders and officials on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Howard brought up three concerns, beginning with how artificial intelligence will impact frontline workers, noting her organization does training and development work in support of schools and the automotive industry.
She also noted the need for Congress to recapture the nation’s purse strings and asked what Democrats would do to bring resources back into communities that had been stripped away by the Trump Administration.
 
Michael Howard, Macomb County commissioner
Macomb County Commissioner Michael Howard discusses community concerns during a roundtable on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
While discussing top-of-mind concerns heading into the midterm elections, Howard called out the need for resources in Black communities.
“I don’t know why it’s become fearful to say we need resources in Black communities,” Howard said. “I mean, we say it, but the folks that represent us are scared to talk about bringing resources to Black communities when we know that when the tide and the water rises in Black communities, all ships rise. When we do well, everyone in this nation does well.”
Putting it plainly, Howard said this means money to invest in communities, specifically noting the need for more resources for schools.
Howard also called out tariffs as a threat to the auto industry, while noting his own personal concerns in addressing gun violence. 
“We’re seeing kids in our community getting a hold of unsecure firearms, which is a problem that we have to address,” Howard said. “There needs to be some better laws around that, and especially to protect domestic violence victims as well.”
He also noted that being present in the community is vital for a representative. 
“I don’t know if you’ve talked to my congressmember, but I’ve seen him four times maybe, and since he’s ever been elected or running for office,” Howard told Jeffries. “And if we ever needed anything, we had to reach out to Senator Peters, who is more present in my community than my own congressmember, and the whole point of Congress was to be our voice and our representative.”
There is an increasing disconnect between what happens in D.C. and what happens on the ground in communities, Howard said, noting that when residents at the local level try to elevate their issues and concerns, it feels like they fall on deaf ears.
 
Spencer Calhoun, Mount Clemens city commissioner
Spencer Calhoun, Mount Clemens city commissioner, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Calhoun told Hines that affordability was a major concern, with rising gas, grocery and utility costs placing an increased strain on the community. 
That strain has been made worse by policies at the federal level, Calhoun said, stating that the current Republican-led administration has delivered tax cuts for wealthy individuals and corporations at the expense of working-class folks.
Healthcare was also among Calhoun’s concerns, as he pointed to Medicaid changes requiring states to redetermine recipients’ eligibility every six months rather than once a year.
“You have to learn to get really good at doing paperwork, otherwise, you’re gonna lose your healthcare,” Calhoun said. “People who are eligible for their benefits are not going to receive them just because they won’t be able to keep up.”
In offering feedback for Congress, Calhoun called for leaders to make space to listen to residents, and to turn those concerns into action.
He also closed out the roundtable by asking Jeffries how the panelists, as community leaders, young people and Black leaders, could work with Hines to support work in Washington to hold President Donald Trump accountable and lower costs.
 
Jeffries, Hines pledge action over costs, community resources and accountability
Jeffries said affordability would be a top priority for House Democrats and pointed to several provisions within congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act the caucus would like to see reversed to help address those concerns.
“We believe we need to reverse these Medicaid cuts,” Jeffries said. “We need to reverse the largest cut to SNAP that was also part of the One Big Ugly Bill that literally is ripping food out of the mouths of hungry children and seniors and veterans. It’s a disgrace, and we’ll fight that battle right at the top of the new Congress.”
Former special victims prosecutor and Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines and U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) at a roundtable in Eastpointe on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Democrats will also fight to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired Dec. 31, 2025, Jeffries said, noting that people across the country are facing higher insurance premiums as a result.
Accountability will also be a major focus.
“If you’ve been stealing from the American people, screwing over the American people, shortchanging the American people — beginning on day one, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” Jeffries said.
Hines also encouraged those in attendance to keep in contact as she works to rally voters ahead of Election Day and beyond.
“For many of you, this is not the first time you’ve already seen me, right? But I want to keep this communication going,” Hines said, adding that many of the things discussed at the forum were also important to her family. 
“And so we are going to be fighting together, lockstep, marching together,” Hines said.

title: ‘Hollywood, VT’ project spotlights the Green Mountain State’s movie history
text:
A movie crew films Alfred Hitchcock’s comic mystery “The Trouble with Harry” in the Northeast Kingdom town of Craftsbury in the fall of 1954. Photo courtesy Paramount Pictures/Vermont Life magazine
Alia Quart Khan can pitch her “Hollywood, VT” project in 25 words: Los Angeles film publicist moves to small-town Vermont during the Covid-19 pandemic, only to strike upon, study and share the state’s movie history.
Ask the 45-year-old for more specifics — take an upcoming Brattleboro screenplay reading and screening of Alfred Hitchcock’s 1955 “The Trouble with Harry,” just one of several celluloid classics with Green Mountain roots — and she’ll elaborate with a personal tale worthy of its own script.
The daughter of a Canadian mother and Pakistani father, Khan was born and raised in Switzerland, then earned a bachelor’s degree in cultural studies and political science from McGill University in Montreal and a master’s in film and television studies from the University of Warwick in England.
Moving to Los Angeles, Khan promoted major movies including the 2011 Academy Award-winning best picture “The Artist,” took work trips to film festivals in Cannes, Toronto and Venice, and directed publicity for the nonprofit arts organization Film Independent and its Oscar-eve Spirit Awards.
Then came the 2020 pandemic. After a shelter-in-place order curbed access to California businesses and beaches, Khan’s aunt invited her to join extended family for six weeks in a different Orange County — the one 3,000 miles east in central Vermont.
“I didn’t realize how much my nervous system had internalized being in Los Angeles and a high-level industry,” Khan recalled of her arrival in Randolph, population 4,774. “It turns out that rural is really good for me.”
Six weeks have morphed into six years. Pandemic movie marathoning, in turn, has led to the Hollywood, VT project, which aims to focus attention on works filmed in or featuring the Green Mountain State.
Alia Quart Khan at the popcorn machine of Brattleboro’s Latchis Theatre. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger
Take Hitchcock’s comic mystery “The Trouble with Harry,” which brought the director and his cameras to the Northeast Kingdom town of Craftsbury in the fall of 1954.
Khan was surprised to learn the movie starred Shirley MacLaine in her screen debut, a 6-year-old Jerry Mathers before his 1957 sitcom start as the title character in “Leave It to Beaver” and John Forsythe in advance of his television roles in the 1970s series “Charlie’s Angels” and 1980s soap “Dynasty.”
Sightings of the cast and crew sparked headlines from Brattleboro to Burlington.
“Hitchcock, who said this is his first visit to Vermont, praised the beauty of our state,” the Caledonian-Record reported on Sept. 21, 1954.
The director hoped to capture the season’s flaming foliage using a new VistaVision widescreen filming process. But after a few sunny days, a series of storms forced everyone onto a makeshift sound stage inside Morrisville’s American Legion. There, the sound crew struggled to muffle rain beating atop the tin roof. By the time an 850-pound camera fell and nearly flattened Hitchcock, he decided to decamp.
“Hollywood’s experiment with making an entire motion picture in Vermont ended,” the local News & Citizen reported on Oct. 14, 1954, “as director-producer Alfred Hitchcock and his cast leave for their home studios after bucking Vermont’s unpredictable weather for more than a month.”
All retreated to the Paramount lot in Los Angeles, but not before raking up enough maple leaves to decorate the set for the remaining scenes. A year later, a crowd of nearly 1,000 people — including Hitchcock, MacLaine and the governors of all six New England states — attended the movie’s world premiere at Barre’s Paramount Theatre on Sept. 30, 1955.
“The film was very well received by Vermonters, who got to see some of their own backyard in the splendor of Technicolor,” film historian Steven DeRosa noted in his 2001 book “Writing with Hitchcock.”

Shirley MacLaine and Alfred Hitchcock attend the world premiere of “The Trouble with Harry” at Barre’s Paramount Theatre on Sept. 30, 1955. Photo courtesy Vermont State Archives

Today, Khan marvels at such memories.
“The fact that a film nerd like me didn’t know about ‘The Trouble with Harry’? I’ve discovered a lot of people haven’t heard of it. I like the idea of shining a light on a piece of history.”
Khan sought grants for a statewide series featuring many Vermont movies, only to receive polite rejections that questioned if she was attempting too much too soon. And so, starting small, she held screenings this past winter at Randolph’s century-old Playhouse Movie Theatre. Locals filled its 150 seats to see Hitchcock’s work as well as 1987’s “Baby Boom” (filmed in Manchester and the nearby town of Peru), 1988’s “Sweet Hearts Dance” (filmed in Hyde Park) and 1996’s “The Spitfire Grill” (filmed in Peacham, St. Johnsbury and Troy).
Khan has since received funding from the Vermont Community Foundation and the John M. Bissell Foundation, a nonprofit supporter of local films, for a two-part “The Trouble with Harry” program at Brattleboro’s Latchis Theatre:
—  A screenplay reading on Oct. 23 will feature Tom Bodett — a Dummerston resident who’s the voice of Motel 6’s “we’ll leave the light on for you” ads — and several staffers of Vermont Public performing the script by the late John Michael Hayes, a four-time Hitchcock collaborator and former associate professor of drama at Dartmouth College.
—  A subsequent movie screening on Nov. 8 will be capped by a conversation led by Bess O’Brien, a Northeast Kingdom filmmaker who lives 30 miles from the Craftsbury location.
Hitchcock may have fled the state early, but Khan hopes to stick around. She has founded her own cultural consulting firm, On Goldfish Pond Creative, and joined the governing boards of the Vermont Arts Council and Vermont Production Collective, a nonprofit that supports film professionals.
“This has been a wonderful opportunity to talk to other creatives, to collaborate and, given the state of the world right now, to play,” she said. “If I get asked what’s next, I’ve got plenty of ideas.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Jason White’s poll on vouchers ignores strong test results in Mississippi public schools
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
House Speaker Jason White – or at least the poll he commissioned – does not seem to be embracing what has become known as the “Mississippi miracle” that references the state’s dramatic gains on some national education tests.
While Mississippi still has numerous hills to climb in terms of improving its education system, there is no doubt the state has made impressive strides.
Republican Gov. Tate Reeves and others often tout those improvements.
The governor has gone across the country touting the state’s education gains, appearing on multiple national news shows. In January 2025, Reeves said in a statement, “This is another massively historic win for education in Mississippi. Mississippi fourth graders aren’t just one of the best in reading and math gains — they’re the best in the nation.”
Did Speaker White and his Republican-leaning Cygnal pollsters not get the memo?
White, perhaps the most forceful elected official pushing to spend public money on private schools, commissioned a recent poll that seemed to dismiss those education gains. By a slim 41.1% to 39.2% margin, with 19.6% having no response, poll participants supported some form of school choice or vouchers.
Apparently not satisfied with that narrow result, the pollster asked a follow-up question: “Supporters point to other states with existing school choice programs, where student test scores have improved in both public and private schools as a result of increased options and competition. Knowing this, do you support or oppose creating a school choice program in Mississippi like the one described in the last question?”
Response to that question was 50.1% to 27.1% in favor of vouchers, with 22.8% having no opinion or not being sure.
The question might influence poll results
The question completely ignored the “Mississippi miracle” that many state education experts say is more aptly described as the “Mississippi marathon,” referring to the decades-long effort to improve the public schools.
Critics of modern polling often say the wording of the question can have a dramatic influence on the outcome of a poll.
What if the question posed by the Republican polling company for White was “in light of the fact that Mississippi has received national praise for its test score improvements that has been described by many as miraculous, should a change be made to take money away from public schools and direct it to private schools?”
What would have been the answer to that very accurate question?
Studies cite negative voucher test results
Research can be found both touting the success of vouchers in terms of student improvement and lamenting the decline in test scores in states with voucher programs. 
But multiple peer-reviewed studies indicate that vouchers harm student achievement.
Research compiled by The Parents’ Campaign, a Mississippi group that supports public education and opposes vouchers, cites multiple studies revealing numerous voucher states have struggled in recent years on test scores.
Based on the analysis of test scores in multiple states, The Parents’ Campaign concluded, “voucher students experience significant losses in achievement.”
The anti-voucher National Coalition of Public Education produced a study saying “vouchers harm student achievement as much as natural disasters.” The study cited test scores declines in multiple places with vouchers, including Louisiana, Indiana, Ohio and the District of Columbia, saying they were comparable to regressions after disasters such as Hurricane Katrina and the COVID-19 pandemic.
As stated, studies can be found arguing the opposite. An EdChoice study, for instance, argues that voucher students are much more likely to pursue a college education.
But the fact remains that Mississippi has been cited for making dramatic gains on standardized tests when compared to other states, thanks to efforts in the public schools. That is happening now, even as White tries to divert money from public to private schools.
White’s poll failed to mention that.
The question is: Was that failure intentional?

name: VTDigger
title: To tax or not to tax: Two towns consider a local option tax this November
text:
Hinesburg Town Hall seen in November 2021. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Stowe’s highway foreman was driving this summer when he came upon an unpleasant sight: a hole in the deck of the Weeks Hill Road bridge.
Many Vermont towns would need to wait a long time to access state funding for bridge repairs, Will Fricke, Stowe’s assistant city manager, said.
But Stowe had a revenue source tucked away.
“Because of local option taxes, we were lucky enough to, you know, have those capital reserves in order to fix that bridge ourselves,” said Fricke, who is hoping to have the bridge construction completed by Thanksgiving.
In the past 20 years, local option taxes have become increasingly popular in municipalities across Vermont. These taxes can be adopted in three different ways. Municipalities can choose to add a 1% tax on top of the 6% state sales tax, the 9% state meals and rooms tax and the 10% state alcoholic beverage tax. The meals and alcoholic beverages tax must be applied together, according to the Vermont government website.
The tax increase proposals come with no shortage of controversy.
The taxes are touted by many city officials as a way to generate revenue, stabilize property taxes and balance out tourists’ impacts on infrastructure and services. Opponents worry about the effects on local businesses and residents and wonder if the proposals will be as effective in towns with smaller tourist presences. This November, Hinesburg and Bennington will both vote on a local option tax for sales, rooms and meals and alcohol in their communities.
The price to sustain a city is only getting higher, said Joy Dubin Grossman, Hinesburg’s assistant town manager. These taxes are an “additional lever” that the town can use to fund necessary services and projects, she said, so it will have less need to increase property taxes.
In Hinesburg, the town estimates that the local option tax could generate between $275,000 and $330,000 in revenue annually. The town would use the revenue for public safety, infrastructure and decreasing reliance on property taxes.
Hinesburg’s local option tax was a topic of discussion in a recent town meeting, according to the Hinesburg Record. Aaron Miller, a meeting attendee, said in an interview that he could see the benefits. Still, he said he would like more clarification on the amount of tax revenue coming from visitors as opposed to community members.
“I mean, obviously, Hinesburg is not Stowe, and so our ability to raise that sales tax or meals and rooms in significant amounts is much lower,” Miller said.
In Bennington, the local option tax would apply to sales, meals and alcoholic beverages and rooms, according to their proposed policy. The selectboard estimates that the tax will bring in about $1.8 million in additional revenue. The proposal requires at least 50% of annual revenue to go toward stabilizing the local property tax rate, increasing to 89% in fiscal year 2027-2028.
The idea has been controversial in Bennington, according to Jonah Spivak, the town’s communications coordinator.
A preliminary poll conducted in Bennington showed support for the local option tax, Spivak said, with 40% of people indicating they would vote yes and 18% of people saying they would likely vote yes. But around 90% of the respondents were property owners in the community, which means they’d experience more direct property tax relief, he said.
“People are asking, ‘Well, what’s in it for those who are not property taxpayers?’” Spivak said. 
But Gordon Black, Manchester’s town assessor and economic development officer, has lived and worked in both Bennington and Manchester and seen the impacts of Manchester’s local option tax since its implementation.
From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, Manchester’s local option tax generated $1,737,618 for the town, according to the Manchester Journal. The town was able to decrease overall property taxes for fiscal year 2026.
Black said the tax can be especially impactful in communities with significant tourist traffic such as Manchester, but there could also be powerful impacts in Bennington due to its large department and grocery stores.
“If you go to the Walmart, or you go to any of the grocery stores or Home Depot, there are a lot of New York cars and frequently Massachusetts cars there,” Black said. “So people come from everywhere to go to those larger stores.”
Black added that the perception that renters would not benefit is largely skewed, since higher property tax rates for landlords translate into higher rents.
“They’re paying for that higher property tax, no question about it,” Black said.
In Stowe, Fricke said the local option tax has helped the town repair infrastructure. If it embarks on a large project, Fricke said Stowe can utilize that revenue instead of taxes spiking for a year.
The biggest project that Stowe has been able to accomplish is a large-scale improvement of the sidewalks on its main street, and a project that placed the street’s power lines underground.
Wilmington’s selectboard took a different approach to infrastructure repair this year, awarding $50,000 to businesses in their town center who took revenue hits this summer due to road construction, according to the Deerfield Valley News. Businesses might also need extra help in 2029, when a planned bridge replacement will close Route 9.
Stowe passed a local option sales tax in addition to its meals and rooms tax in 2023, which Fricke said is directed to the general fund to alleviate property taxes.
Montpelier has seen positive results since the implementation of a local option tax in 2025, according to Finance Director Heather Graves. In fiscal year 2027, it will be used to provide tax relief to Montpelier’s residents, she said, and it has helped the city purchase essential equipment like a new ambulance.
Miller, the Hinesburg resident who spoke at a recent meeting, said data about visitor spending versus resident spending would make this an easier decision for Hinesburg, but the absence of that information complicates things.
“I think Hinesburg will ultimately end up needing to make an imperfect decision,” Miller said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas’ candidates for governor ignore warning from botched execution
text:
A view of the death chamber from the witness room at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility shows an electric chair and gurney in 2001. (Photo by Mike Simons/Getty Images)Given how much law-and-order rhetoric has become standard GOP talking points in Arkansas, it’s surprising that the state’s most outspoken opponent of the death penalty was also its first Republican governor after Reconstruction.
One of the last acts Winthrop Rockefeller performed as Arkansas governor was his 1970 decision to commute the death sentences of 15 men awaiting execution. It was a controversial move for the Southern state but not altogether surprising. Rockefeller had talked before about his opposition to capital punishment.
“We ourselves admit to failure when the only way we can cope with the problem is taking another man’s life,” Rockefeller said in 1966.
Rockefeller’s radical act belongs to a bygone era. That much was clear after watching the debate for Arkansas governor.
A botched lethal injection in neighboring Tennessee should have prompted a serious discussion about capital punishment. 
The three candidates for Arkansas’ top office instead are embracing the death penalty, with at least one candidate proposing expanding the methods used.



Let us know what you think...


 


“I’m for the death penalty, and I’m for the firing squad, and hopefully we can get some things solved around here in Arkansas,” Libertarian candidate Colt Shelby said.
Shelby’s answer came in response to a question about Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate whose execution was halted after two failed rounds of lethal injection drugs. 
The execution, the latest in a long line of botched lethal injections around the country, has reignited the debate over the death penalty and prompted Tennessee’s governor to pause executions through the end of the year.
But the case appeared to give little pause for Shelby, Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders as they debated on Arkansas public television last week.
Sanders cited the law she signed last year allowing the use of nitrogen gas to put inmates to death, saying she’ll judge each case individually.
“I believe in justice for the victims,” Sanders said. “I think it’s one of the most difficult, challenging things that any governor can face.”
Love, who voted against the nitrogen executions bill and legislation that kept manufacturers of the state’s lethal injection drugs a secret, signaled a change of heart.
“In the past, I have actually leaned to not being for the death penalty, but as governor, I will take each case by case, and actually judge each case because I know that justice needs to be served,” he said.
The candidates’ openness for the death penalty comes as support for capital punishment has been at record lows nationally.
It occurs as President Donald Trump abandoned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter after the idea drew bipartisan backlash.
It’s also the latest chapter in Arkansas’ checkered political history surrounding the death penalty.
In 1992, then-Gov. Bill Clinton left the presidential campaign trail to return to Arkansas for the execution of Ricky Ray Rector. The move was widely viewed as an attempt to raise his national profile and prove himself as someone who was tough on crime. 
Former Gov. Asa Hutchinson’s plan to carry out eight executions over a two-week period drew widespread condemnation from human rights advocates. The executions — whittled down to four after half of them were blocked by the courts — were scheduled to take place before the state’s supply of a lethal injection drug expired.
It’s probably unrealistic to expect candidates in a state as conservative as Arkansas to abandon capital punishment. The year of Arkansas’ execution spree, the University of Arkansas’ Arkansas Poll found that nearly three-fourths of very likely voters still supported the death penalty.
But it’s not unrealistic to expect candidates to offer more details on why they think it’s an effective option, despite experts who say it’s not a deterrent, and what steps they’d take to ensure Arkansas doesn’t have botched executions similar to Tennessee’s.
At the very least, voters should hear the answer candidates would give to the question Rockefeller asked himself when he announced the commutations:
“What earthly mortal has the omnipotence to say who among us shall live and who shall die?”
