name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The crucial marijuana question not on the ballot: Why has Massachusetts failed to educate the public on the harmful effects of cannabis and monitor the impact of its growing use, especially on young people?
authors: Sushrut Jangi, Corrine Cather, Ari Cohen, A. Eden Evins, Cheryl Y.S. Foo, Jodi Gilman, Nicole Nadeau, and Toby Raybould
text:
IN LESS THAN three weeks, Massachusetts voters will face a binary choice when it comes to the sale of recreational marijuana. Question 8 on the ballot asks whether the state should repeal the previously voter-approved ballot question legalizing recreational cannabis sales, or keep in the place the law that was passed 10 years ago. 
We are not here to answer that question, which demands consideration of many factors, including the impact marijuana laws had prior to legalization and the fact that a robust economic sector has been established following approval of the 2016 ballot question. But as health care professionals, we are sounding the alarm on what we believe has been an inexcusable failure of state officials to provide the needed regulatory oversight and public health education and monitoring of the effects of growing cannabis use, especially among young people.  
Seven years into Massachusetts’ experiment with recreational cannabis commercialization has led to economic windfalls for the cannabis industry and the state government. In 2025, cannabis sales in Massachusetts reached a record $1.65 billion, with the state collecting $289 million in tax revenue.  
Our state now ranks in the top five cannabis markets in the country. There is no end in sight to the cannabis bonanza: In June, Gov. Maura  Healey signed cannabis reform legislation that doubles the amount of cannabis people can purchase per day or possess at any time, while increasing the number of dispensaries owned by any one entity and loosening restrictions on advertising and marketing of cannabis products. Other sales-boosters coming to the market include licensing for social consumption of cannabis in “weed cafes,” lounges, and yoga studios.   
As a group of Massachusetts clinicians and public health researchers, we are increasingly concerned about the impacts of widespread cannabis availability and associated health hazards. Since legalization, cannabis use in Massachusetts steadily increased from 15 percent of people using the drug pre-legalization in 2012, to nearly 43 percent in 2023.  
Nearly half of those report using cannabis to manage mental health. However, recent research suggests that people using cannabis to treat such symptoms see no improvement in pain, anxiety, or depression, with nearly 20 percent developing an addiction – called cannabis use disorder – within the first 12 weeks of use. 
Adolescents are especially at risk for the adverse mental health effects of cannabis. Among people seeking emergency psychiatric care from a Boston hospital, people testing positive for the active ingredient in cannabis – tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) – increased significantly post-legalization. The highest rate of increase was in adolescents aged 12 to 17, who also demonstrated the largest rise in cannabis-related disorder rates over any age group. Individuals with psychosis have used more cannabis since legalization and are almost twice as likely to visit the emergency room since dispensaries opened. 
Children are also being inadvertently exposed to the drug. Among children 5 and under, emergency visits for cannabis exposure rose from fewer than 11 cases in 2016 to 45 in 2020. Those 19 and under had a 67 percent increase in cannabis-exposure visits to the emergency room following retail sales, moving from 18.5 to 31 incidents per 100,000 people. 
Cannabis not only has negative effects on the brain, but has consequences throughout the body. Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, a chronic disease causing nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, has skyrocketed in Massachusetts, leading patients to seek repeated hospitalizations and intensive care. Emergency room visits for the syndrome increased by 1,350 percent post-legalization, with young males, Hispanic, and Black individuals at highest risk.  
Hospitalization costs, estimated at $20,000 per patient, more than doubled at one Boston hospital, due to patients requiring longer inpatient stays to recover. 
California, Colorado, Michigan, and other high-use markets have similarly reported troubling trends post-legalization, with national reports showing that cannabis raises the risk for heart attacks, strokes, death from heart disease, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. 
Despite such evidence that cannabis has negative health effects in Massachusetts, our state has done little to survey and confront these harmful consequences. The Cannabis Control Commission, whose mission is to safely, equitably, and effectively implement and administer the laws enabling access to cannabis in the Commonwealth, has no prominent documentation of these hazards on its website.  
No statewide surveillance mechanism exists to evaluate the chronic medical disease burden associated with cannabis use. While Massachusetts collects hundreds of millions of dollars in state tax revenue from cannabis annually, not a single tax dollar supports independent research into the health effects of cannabis on the public. 
We are not here to decry the legalization of cannabis. But as responsible members of the medical community, we are ringing alarms that the expanding commercialization of cannabis without protective regulation and robust public education and infrastructure is harming Massachusetts residents, especially children and minorities.  
Other states have taken steps to reduce these unintended consequences. Seventeen states where legal cannabis is available have passed legislation to fund cannabis research, with six of these states directly distributing funds to independent academic institutions.  
The Minnesota Department of Public Health launched a campaign to introduce conversations about cannabis risks, including impacts of the drug on memory, decision-making, and dependence. Several states apportion cannabis revenue to promote education, prevention, and early intervention.  
Comprehensive advertising restrictions in other states have reduced exposure to youth and the vulnerable, with reductions in cannabis use in these groups. 
Massachusetts has taken none of these approaches and, in some cases, moved in the opposite direction: advertising has expanded; restrictions have loosened; and cannabis use continues to soar.  
As members of the medical community, we have long considered Massachusetts to be a beacon of public health for other states to follow. But when it comes to mitigating the harmful effects of cannabis on public health, we have unfortunately fallen to the bottom of the pack. 
Sushrut Jangi is a gastroenterologist at Tufts Medical Center. Corinne Cather is chief of the Division of Public and Community Psychiatry for Mass General Brigham and is an associate professor of psychology at Harvard Medical School. Ari Cohen is the chief of pediatric emergency medicine at Mass General Hospital. A. Eden Evins is the William Cox Family Professor of Psychiatry in the field of addiction medicine at Mass General Brigham. Cheryl Y. S. Foo is an assistant professor of psychology at Harvard Medical School and a clinician-researcher at Massachusetts General Hospital’s Psychosis Clinical and Research Program. Jodi Gilman is an associate professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School. Nicole Nadeau is an assistant professor in emergency medicine and pediatrics at Harvard Medical School. Toby Raybould is the trauma prevention and outreach manager at Massachusetts General Hospital. The opinions expressed are of the authors, not of their institutions.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: No Kings volunteers bring early voting message to Hope Street Farmers Market in Providence
text:
Dave Wolczak, left, of Cranston, shows his sign to Terri Anderson, of Johnston at a No Kings community event at the Hope Street Farmers Market on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)There were no chants, no speeches and only a handful of signs at a No Kings event Saturday morning in Providence.
Instead, a few dozen volunteers fanned out across the Hope Street Farmers Market on the East Side, weaving through booths of locally grown produce and artisan baked goods with something else for sale.
They were promoting the merits of early voting, said Joe Cook, a Providence resident and organizer with Indivisible Metro RI.
“We just wanted to meet a lot of people without being super intrusive, on a day when they might have a chance to relax and talk,” Cook said.
Across Rhode Island, other civic organizations held their own outreach events, a combination of rallies outside municipal government buildings, neighborhood canvassing or attending community events like the farmers market, all focused on highlighting the value of early voting. Nationally, No Kings organizers also rebranded the protest event to emphasize voter education and increase early voting turnout in the 2026 midterm elections.
More than 15,000 Rhode Island voters have already cast ballots through early, in-person voting hours at designated polling places in each location since the 20-day early voting period began Wednesday, Oct. 14, according to the Rhode Island Department of State’s online tracker. 
The Sept. 9 state primaries saw record numbers of early voting, with more than 37,000 people voting during the 20-day early voting period that preceded the primary day itself. While a majority of voters still cast ballots on Election Day, early voting has become increasingly popular as awareness and comfort spread since these options were introduced in 2020 and enshrined in state law in 2022.
Volunteers gather Saturday morning at the farmers market on Hope Street and Blackstone Boulevard, one of 10 locations for No Kings events across the state. Indivisible Metro RI organized the event to encourage early voting ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election. (Photos by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
“In this state we’re kind of preaching to the choir here,” said Dave Walczak, of Cranston. But, he added, “If we can bring the numbers up, even get an extra 100 people to show up and vote, that’s a good goal.”
The retired signmaker came ready with a dozen extra signs for fellow volunteers to wave at the edges of the farmers market. “Timshel ‘thou mayest’ vote,” read the yellow lettering on Walczak’s own sign, a reference to John Steinbeck’s “East of Eden.”
Other messages were more to the point: “Vote early,” or “Vote for Democracy” were two popular slogans.



Quotation







In this state we’re kind of preaching to the choir here. If we can bring the numbers up, even get an extra 100 people to show up and vote, that’s a good goal.


– Dave Walczak of Cranston, an Indivisible Metro RI volunteer


Voting early can be more convenient, avoiding long lines or last-minute complications, such as delayed opening of several Providence polling places on Sept. 9  due to poll workers not showing up.
“It could be more secure if you’re concerned about bad actors showing up on the day of the vote, and the early vote turnout is also just a wonderful signal of the power of democracy,” Cook said, offering volunteers tips on how to pitch early voting to the people at the farmers market.
Yet the audience was not entirely receptive.
“I don’t vote early,” Kay Lisle replied bluntly when approached by a volunteer.
She continued, “I’m 86, I’m old, I like to do things the old-fashioned way.”
It helps that there is an Election Day polling place at Laurelmead, the independent senior living community off Blackstone Boulevard where Lisle and her companion, Debbie Mulcare, both live.
“We literally just go downstairs,” Mulcare said.
But the pair took a flyer anyway before heading across the park in search of spinach pies and shellfish.


A few feet away, Molly Mollica rocked a double stroller, a canning jar of fresh cut flowers tucked into the cupholder. Newly returned to Rhode Island after living in Boston, Mollica, who grew up in Barrington but now lives in Pawtucket, said she planned to vote early “given these guys,” referring to the 6-month-old twins nestled in the stroller.
Top-of-mind for her partner, Andrew Parent, was revitalizing Pawtucket’s local economy
“You lose Hasbro, you lose the hospital, Pawtucket needs a change,” Parent said, referring to the impending relocation of the toymaker and the 2018 closure of Memorial Hospital.
Julie Sacks, also of Pawtucket, was most focused on the city’s school committee races due to her concerns about potential book bans in public schools.
“These local races are critical,” Sacks said. “Sometimes people focus on the national races, but it starts locally.”
Sacks usually votes on Election Day, preferring to take in the fanfare and mark the occasion with dinner with her husband.
“We cry, or we laugh, depending on the results,” Sacks said.
But this time, she voted on the first day of early voting  Wednesday in preparation for her commitment as a poll worker on Nov. 3.
All No Kings events are nonpartisan.
More information on early voting hours and locations is available on the Rhode Island Department of State website.
Lee Clasper-Torch, co-founder of Indivisible Metro RI, right, distributes a flyer promoting early voting to Debbie Mulcare, left, and Kay Lisle, center, at the Hope Street Farmers Market in Providence on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s own tradition fades amid success of nonresident pheasant hunting
text:
A pheasant stands along a South Dakota fence line in 2023. (Unmodified photo courtesy of USDA-NRCS South Dakota)South Dakota has spent decades convincing out-of-staters to come here and hunt pheasants.
Tourism campaigns market pheasant hunting as a bucket-list experience, especially during the opening of the season, which is this weekend. Later this month, elected officials, business leaders and invited guests will gather for the Governor’s Pheasant Hunt, an event devoted as much to economic development as hunting.
Yet amid that success story sits an uncomfortable fact. Fewer South Dakotans are participating in it.
Last year, the state Game, Fish and Parks Department estimated that about 57,000 South Dakota residents hunted pheasants. More than 82,000 nonresidents did.
Visitors have outnumbered resident pheasant hunters since 2002, but the more revealing comparison is with South Dakota’s past.
South Dakota wildlife officials offer hunting license refunds as deer disease reports continue

In 2000, the state had about 755,000 people and nearly 80,000 resident pheasant hunters. Since then, South Dakota has gained roughly 180,000 residents — enough to create two more Rapid Cities — while losing more than 22,000 resident pheasant hunters.
In that timeframe we have gone from roughly 1 in 10 South Dakotans hunting pheasants to 1 in 16. 
Pheasant hunting has become one of South Dakota’s more successful industries. Game, Fish and Parks estimates pheasant hunters spent $304.5 million in South Dakota in 2025.
Nonresident hunters are also the financial backbone of the pheasant system, generating far more small-game license revenue and more habitat-stamp revenue than residents. 
That success helps explain why the decline in resident hunters attracts little urgency.
A South Dakotan who decides not to hunt this fall does not create an immediate budget problem. A motel room may still be rented by someone from Minnesota. The nonresident license still gets sold, and the Governor’s Hunt still showcases another successful year.
Economic developers promote South Dakota’s quality of life because people choose where to live based on more than economics. For generations, pheasant hunting was part of that sales pitch. Families hunted together. Neighbors shared permission. Young hunters learned from parents, grandparents and family friends. Opening-weekend stories were traded in cafes, grain elevators, schools and workplaces.
Nobody claimed access was unlimited or guaranteed, but the first question was often, “Where should we hunt?”
Increasingly, the question is, “What does access cost?”
Hunting leases have become more common, and commercial hunting has expanded. During the 2024-25 season, 235 private shooting preserves reported releasing more than 632,000 pheasants and a harvest of about 380,000. Nearly 94% of the harvested birds had been released.
Preserves provide jobs and give hunters another option. But a tradition once built largely on relationships is increasingly a marketplace built on transactions.
Landowners have every right to respond to those opportunities. They provide most of South Dakota’s wildlife habitat and bear many of its costs. But a resident looking for a place to hunt after work or on a Saturday afternoon faces different circumstances than a visitor arriving with a lodge reservation, guide and substantial budget.
Game, Fish and Parks has not ignored access. It maintains public hunting land and private-land access programs, and partnerships with conservation groups continue adding acreage.
Those efforts matter. But Pheasants Forever says lack of access is widely acknowledged as a primary barrier to hunter participation.
Still, the numbers do not prove lack of access is why South Dakotans stopped hunting.
Was it access, cost, time, hunting pressure, urbanization or changing interests? Did fewer families retain connections to farms and landowners? Did older hunters leave without anyone taking their place?


Let us know what you think...


 

Game, Fish and Parks can estimate how many pheasants were harvested. Tourism officials can estimate how much hunters spent. What South Dakota does not appear to have is a recent public effort to ask former resident hunters why they stopped hunting pheasants.
That distinction matters. If resident participation were rising, state leaders would likely point to it as evidence of success. Declining participation deserves the same attention.
South Dakota tracks visitor spending, habitat acres, harvest numbers and tourism growth. Its advertising campaigns and Governor’s Hunt make clear that it has a strategy for recruiting out-of-state hunters.
What is less clear is whether it has a strategy for retaining resident hunters. How many resident pheasant hunters does South Dakota hope to have 10 years from now, and what number would state leaders consider success?
South Dakota should continue welcoming nonresident hunters. But a state cannot measure the health of its hunting tradition only by counting the people who travel here.
South Dakota has become remarkably good at inviting the rest of the country to hunt pheasants.
The more important question may be why fewer South Dakotans are accepting the invitation.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Dem US Rep. Vasquez debates 2nd Congressional District GOP challenger Cunningham
text:
KRQE anchor Dean Staley moderates a debate on Oct. 16, 2026, between Republican Greg Cunningham, left, and incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), right, who are facing off to represent New Mexico's Second Congressional District. (Screenshot)The two candidates vying to represent New Mexico’s Second Congressional District participated in a lively debate Friday evening.
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), who first won election to the seat in 2022, and Republican challenger Greg Cunningham, a retired Marine and former Albuquerque Police Department detective, spent much of a Friday evening debate on KRQE criticizing each other. Vasquez often characterized Cunningham as a MAGA devotee, while Cunningham repeatedly characterized Vasquez as an ineffectual member of Congress.
That divide was on display particularly when KRQE anchor Dean Staley asked candidates questions about border policy and controversial tactics employed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents under President Donald Trump’s administration. Vasquez lamented seeing footage of “Americans getting killed at the hands of ICE,” referring to this year’s killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, while Cunningham blamed liberal policies in sanctuary cities for infringing on ICE agents’ abilities to do their jobs.
The contested race for the district, which includes much of southern New Mexico and stretches to the north to include a small portion of Albuquerque, is considered one of the most closely contested Congressional races in the nation.
Vasquez unseated his Republican predecessor, Yvette Herrell, in 2022 by less than one percentage point. Trump endorsed Cunningham’s bid to flip the district red and U.S. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson has visited New Mexico twice to stump for him.
Throughout Friday’s debate, Vasquez several times promised to fight the “disastrous economic policies of the Trump administration.” In response, Cunningham was often quick to ask what Vasquez has done in his current term to combat the president’s agenda.
“You’re our Congressman. We sent you there to solve these problems,” Cunningham said, adding that Vasquez was acting “like it’s all somebody else’s fault.”
The two candidates discussed a number of other issues, ranging from immigration and affordability to the war in Iran and artificial intelligence.
Immigration
The discussion around immigration and the Trump administration’s emphasis on ICE raids provoked the sharpest disagreement between Vasquez and Cunningham.
The two found a brief truce. When Vasquez expressed a desire to reform the path to citizenship, Cunningham said it was the “one thing that I do agree with you on.”
Beyond that, though, the two clashed as Staley asked both candidates where the nation’s immigration policies can improve and whether they agree with Trump’s decision not to apologize when ICE agents have killed American citizens.
Cunningham said that broadly, he looks at law enforcement agencies such as ICE and sees “men and women, our brothers and sisters and family members that got into law enforcement to do the right thing and are risking their lives every day.”
Vasquez pushed back, alluding not only to the killings of Good and Pretti but to recent controversial ICE arrests in New Mexico, as well.
“I see American citizens getting killed at the hands of ICE. I see our own Native American citizens with tribal IDs being detained right here in New Mexico,” Vasquez said. “The policy of this administration is cruel. It is separating families, it is orphaning children all across our country and it’s targeting people that look like me and you, Greg.”
SNAP, Medicaid cuts
New eligibility requirements for programs like Medicaid are set to take effect in 2027, and could result in some 89,000 New Mexicans losing healthcare coverage.
Vasquez said he is “fully in support” of targeting and addressing waste, fraud and abuse in programs like Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, but said the new requirements — particularly for food assistance — will unfairly punish children.
“That is nothing but cruel policy,” he said. “We have to reverse those SNAP cuts as soon as we get the House majority.” 
Cunningham said it’s disingenuous to equate the new eligibility requirements to “throwing” people off the program.
“Asking for work requirements, asking for a healthy adult that doesn’t have children to give their time in their community or to work a few hours a week, that’s not throwing them off the program,” he said. “That’s asking them to adhere to a set of standards and requirements.” 
Republican Greg Cunningham, left, and incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), right, on Oct. 16, 2026, participated in a televised debate on KRQE as the two face off to represent New Mexico’s Second Congressional District. (Screenshot)
Affordability
When asked about how they would address affordability for New Mexicans, Cunningham said that he would have advocated for cutting taxes on tips and overtime if he were in Vasquez’s position.
“One of the ways to make things more affordable is to let people have more money in their pockets,” he said.
Vasquez said, if re-elected, he would continue working to end the Iran war and to reverse federal cuts to programs like SNAP and Medicaid.
“It is an understatement that times are tough right now,” he said, adding that he believes Trump broke his campaign promises to not start new wars and to bring down the cost of everyday goods. 
Artificial intelligence, data centers
The hot-button topic of AI provided the final thin sliver of common ground the two candidates found during the course of Friday’s debate.
Both agreed the federal government needs to play a greater role in regulating the technology. 
Cunningham said that he believes New Mexicans should scrutinize how much water and energy the costly developments consume, and acknowledged a need for “federal guardrails,” but maintained that leaders in individual communities should have the final say in whether or not they’re built.
Vasquez, who has previously advocated for moratoria in New Mexico communities with pending data center proposals, said that, “We can’t spare a drop of water for billionaires who are not going to invest in our community.”
Iran war 
Throughout the night, Vasquez touted his long-standing opposition to the ongoing war in Iran and pledged to continue fighting it, if re-elected. In fact, he opposed it so frequently throughout the debate that Staley posed his question on the matter solely to Cunningham after telling Vasquez, “I think I understand your position on this.”
As a combat veteran, Cunningham said that “nobody wants this war over faster than the men and women that are serving in it.”
But when Staley pressed him on whether he supported the war, he only said that, “I support Iran not having a nuclear weapon and being a nuclear threat to its neighbors and to the rest of the world.”
Vasquez later addressed the matter in his closing remarks.
“The disastrous economic policies of the Trump administration have hurt families far too deep, and we have got to put an end to the war in Iran,” he said. “We have got to bring sanity and civility back to Congress.”

name: VTDigger
title: Coffee for the community
text:
Debbie Scherrer greets visitors to Saturday’s pop-up café on the porch of Rochester’s Kimball building. Photo by Tim Calabro/White River Valley Herald

This story by Tim Calabro was first published in the White River Valley Herald on Oct. 8, 2026.
When the Rochester Café closed early this summer, residents worried about losing more than a place to get breakfast. The café had been a gathering spot in the village center, and its closure came just before hundreds of visitors were expected for the annual Green Mountain Suzuki Institute.
So a group of residents improvised. Beginning around the Fourth of July, volunteers turned the porch of the closed café into a weekend pop-up, serving coffee and homemade baked goods. Different local organizations took turns hosting, and what began as an effort to keep some activity in the center of town evolved into a summerlong community gathering place that raised nearly $24,000 in donations for local organizations.
“The entire goal of this, it was secondary that we raised money, but the first goal was to create visibility and vitality in the town when people were driving through,” said Peggy McKinley, one of the coordinators. “We didn’t want to look like our town was closed.”
The idea emerged shortly after the Rochester Café shuttered. About 10 or 12 people gathered for a dinner that included Chris Landis, owner of the Kendall Building, which houses the café. With the Suzuki program approaching and an estimated 400 additional people expected in town for a week, the conversation turned to what the café’s absence would mean for both visitors and the village.
“We started talking like, how are we going to feed these people?” McKinley recalled. From there came the idea of serving coffee and pastries on the café porch. Landis agreed to let the volunteers use the space for the summer.
The pop-up initially operated daily during Suzuki week and then settled into a weekend schedule.
McKinley took on much of the scheduling, making sure a group was lined up to host each weekend and helping coordinate a network of volunteer bakers. 
She emphasized, however, that the project never belonged to one person or even one organization. “It was an amazing group effort,” she said. “There really wasn’t just one person kind of driving it.”
The Valley Hub, Feeding the Valley Alliance, Rochester Farmers Market, Park House, Big Town Projects, Rochester Public Library, the Rochester Stockbridge Unified District farm-to-school project, local first responders, the parent-teacher organization, White River Valley Players, the Rochester Democrats and Rebuild Rochester Foundation all hosted pop-ups over the course of the summer.
Changing organizations each weekend brought a different circle of volunteers and customers to the porch and helped expand the pool of people supplying baked goods, McKinley said.
Along the way, a core group of bakers also emerged who contributed week after week.
“We’re not talking like boxed muffins,” McKinley said. “We’re talking coffee cakes and croissants.”

Leah Hopperstad, visiting Vermont from Minnesota, fills up her coffee cup as members of Feeding the Valley hosted a pop-up café with coffee and baked goods on the porch of the shuttered Rochester Café Saturday. Photo by Tim Calabro/White River Valley Herald

Local businesses also helped get the project started. McKinley said the Singh Shop, Valley Grocer and Maple Soul, along with Rebuild Rochester, contributed money for signs and supplies.
McKinley and her husband developed a system of four storage bins filled with supplies to make it relatively easy for a different organization to take over each weekend. With Landis’ permission, the bins stayed on the porch and contained coffee cups, coffee makers, serving utensils, tablecloths and other supplies. Written instructions explained how to set everything up.
“People’s talents rose to the surface,” McKinley said. “Everybody took the role that worked for them.”
Nearly all of that work was done by volunteers. The group also found Alix Albert and hired her to set up coffee service and, at the end of a weekend, take supplies home to wash and restock them. Startup donations initially covered that expense, with proceeds from a few later pop-ups used after that money ran out.
Feeding the Valley Alliance volunteer Ann Van Dusen said the pop-ups filled some of the social role the café had previously played.
“It’s kept the food vibe here going and it’s a place where people can gather,” Van Dusen said.
In some ways, the porch developed a social character of its own.
Debby Scherrer, another Feeding the Valley volunteer, said that inside a restaurant, customers might simply wave to someone they recognize. On the porch, strangers were more likely to strike up conversations.
“There’s so much mixing that’s going on,” she said.
Visitors passing through town sometimes stopped after seeing the activity. McKinley said some stayed for half an hour to talk with residents, while locals sometimes spent two and a half hours visiting on the porch.
She jokingly came to describe it as “a happy hour” for breakfast and coffee.
There were impromptu attractions, too. A traveler from the Midwest who was camping nearby once brought out his guitar and played, and local musician Greg Ryan performed during a pop-up hosted by the White River Valley Players.
During Suzuki week, families camping near Chittenden Mountain arrived early one morning after a large storm, looking for someplace to warm up and get coffee. On another weekend, Scherrer recalled, a visitor from Idaho met local residents on the porch and ended up making plans to help them in their garden that afternoon.
People also continued arriving at the building expecting to find the Rochester Café open. Volunteers would explain what had happened and what the pop-up was about.
“Nine times out of 10, they would hang out and have coffee and danishes and enjoy the moment,” McKinley said.
The summer experiment also became a substantial fundraiser. McKinley estimated the pop-ups raised close to $24,000 overall, distributed among the participating organizations.
For Feeding the Valley alone, Van Dusen estimated the events brought in about $2,500.
But both women returned repeatedly to the gathering place the porch provided.
Organizers initially were unsure whether people would actually sit at the outdoor tables, Van Dusen said. Instead, people began making plans to meet friends there.
“It’s not like having the café open,” she said, “but it’s as close as we’re going to get” for now.
The hope now is that the temporary substitute will once again give way to a permanent café.
The Kendall Building is being marketed for sale or lease, according to property manager Dorie Davidson.
McKinley said reopening the café would be the best outcome for next summer. If that doesn’t happen, she said, the pop-up experiment could potentially return.
“I think what we’re all thinking is we hope by next summer that the café is open again,” she said.
Whatever happens with the building, McKinley said the success of the pop-ups demonstrated what residents could accomplish without a formal organization behind the effort.
“Everybody played a role,” she said. “Without people stepping up and playing those roles, it wouldn’t have happened.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Washington stopped measuring hunger. Missouri is seeing more of it.
text:
(Jon King/Michigan Advance)For more than three decades, the federal government released an annual comprehensive report on the state of hunger in America. But that ended in 2025 when the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced it would no longer produce Household Food Security reports.
While the report has disappeared, hunger clearly hasn’t. In fact, it appears to be getting dramatically worse as people lose food assistance and face mounting economic strains.
At Operation Food Search, which works with hundreds of partners to provide food and services to people in need in 24 Missouri and Illinois counties, we have seen a striking increase in the number of individuals seeking food assistance.
From the end of October to the end of June, visits to our reduced-price mobile farmers markets more than doubled over the same period the previous year – going from 7,431 visits to a whopping 18,973, a 155% increase
More recently, the number of clicks on our website’s “Find Food” page is 17% higher this summer than it was in the spring.
We believe several factors may be contributing to the increased demand for food assistance, including stagnating wages and increasing costs of food, gasoline, utilities, housing, and health care. Gas prices are up 37%, and according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, food prices have risen more than 40% over the past decade.
The federal bill H.R.1, otherwise known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, that passed in 2025 included changes to SNAP eligibility and work requirements that are projected to reduce or eliminate benefits for some recipients nationwide. In Missouri, as of September 24, over 40,000 people have lost food assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which now requires “able-bodied” participants to document at least 80 hours a month of work or training.
And the amount of difficult paperwork for SNAP enrollees is about to increase even more. In an Aug. 31 announcement, the Missouri Department of Social Services said it will begin requiring documented proof of housing costs, such as rent, utilities, childcare expenses, and bank account information as part of recertification.
A year ago, when the U.S. Department of Agriculture cancelled its annual Household Food Security Report, it said that “trends in the prevalence of food insecurity have remained virtually unchanged” and that the report had become “politicized” and was “rife with inaccuracies.”
This survey has long been used as the gold standard for researchers, policymakers, service providers, and anti-hunger organizations like Operation Food Search, to show us the greatest areas of need, guide effective solutions, and help us mobilize support.
Imagine trying to treat a serious illness without the scans and tests to tell you where in the body it is, whether the treatments are working, and what changes are needed. The prevalence of food security does, in fact, change significantly, as it did during the Great Recession in 2008 and during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. A shift in just a few percentage points can mean thousands of local households are struggling to find their next meal.
While the loss of the annual hunger report may hide data on the fallout of severe SNAP cuts and rising prices, it’s clear we have a growing hunger problem. At OFS, more people are coming to us for help, and we are working hard to purchase, transport, and distribute additional food to meet that need.
But the charitable food system was designed to supplement the safety net, not replace it. Without reliable, consistent data, it becomes harder to see where the gaps are, how large they are and whether the solutions are working. Less information does not mean less hunger.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky can cut health premiums without spending a dime
authors: Michael F. Cannon, Caleb O. Brown, Niklas Kleinworth
text:
Territorial health insurance plans are a carveout from the Affordable Care Act.
(Getty Images)Today’s health insurance affordability crisis is a rerun of the one Kentucky faced in the 1990s. The cause is the same. The path to relief is the same. And once again, Frankfort can deliver it.
 In 1994, Frankfort enacted new controls that supporters promised would make health insurance more affordable and accessible. By 1996, the number of health insurers selling directly to consumers plummeted from 40 to two. Both of the remaining carriers requested a 28 percent premium hike.
The market’s collapse prompted the legislature to reverse course in 1996 and 1998, repealing many of the harmful regulations responsible. Eventually, the market recovered.
Twenty years later, the Affordable Care Act re-imposed substantially similar regulations. The law’s supporters promised this time would be different. Instead, Kentucky families are again facing insufficient choices and premiums they cannot pay.
 The number of insurers in Kentucky’s individual market is again down to two in most counties. In five counties, there are three. In 10 counties, there is only one.
 Obamacare premiums are rising faster than Congress can subsidize them. This year brought Kentucky residents a 30 percent premium hike. Insurers are planning another 19 percent premium hike for 2027.
 Legislation proposed in the last session would have pulled Kentucky out of this nosedive and saved Kentuckians 60 percent or more on their health insurance.
In the 2026 session, Reps. Vanessa Grossl and T.J. Roberts filed House Bill 91. The measure aimed to free Kentucky consumers and small businesses to buy health plans from carriers in U.S. territories. Why territories? Because President Obama himself exempted territories from Obamacare’s most expensive and destructive regulations.
Leading up to Obamacare’s implementation, officials in American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands foresaw that the law would do to their insurance markets what it is now doing to Kentucky’s. They warned that “insurance issuers currently serving the individual and small group markets are likely to withdraw, making coverage unavailable at any price.” One territory’s individual market collapsed before the regulations even took effect. They begged Obama for relief.
Obama obliged. In 2014, he exempted territories from the regulations that are now tearing Kentucky’s market apart. That rule remains law today.
 Permitting territorial plans in the commonwealth would allow Kentucky families to enroll in quality, affordable health plans that meet their needs. Researchers consistently find that for most consumers, premiums for Obamacare-exempt health plans are 60 percent below those for the lowest-price Obamacare plans.
The policy would have even freed millions of Kentuckians to buy coverage that respects their religious beliefs. Among the regulations from which Obama exempted territories is Obamacare’s mandate to buy coverage for contraceptives.
The only thing preventing Kentucky families and small businesses from buying territorial plans is Kentucky law. The Commonwealth’s insurance code forbids health plans unless they receive regulatory approval from the commonwealth itself. That barrier is unambiguously Frankfort’s to remove.
In effect, recognizing territorial plans applies to insurers the standard that Frankfort already applies to physicians. Kentucky law recognizes physician licenses from “another state, United States territory, or Canadian province,” if those standards “are substantially equivalent” to Kentucky’s. The fact that Obama exempted territories from Obamacare makes their standards the only standards in the United States that are substantially equivalent to what Kentucky enacted after its painful experience in the 1990s.
Expanding the market to territory plans allows Kentuckians access quality, affordable, enforceable insurance protection from established carriers, with a named regulator and an enforceable contract standing behind every policy. The law would write the licensing territory’s regulations into the insurance contract, so that Kentucky courts could enforce them.
 It would also subject the insurers now operating in Kentucky’s individual market—Anthem, WellCare, and Molina—to greater competition. Aetna, Cigna, Humana, and UnitedHealthcare already do business in the territories, and have provider networks in Kentucky. 
 Legalizing territorial health plans would not take any choices away. Kynect would remain open for Kentuckians and carriers who prefer Obamacare plans. Consumers who qualify would still receive subsidies, which would still rise along with premiums. For Kentuckians struggling to afford coverage, the bill would simply add another option.
 
Frankfort does not need to wait on Congress to act. It does not need to spend a dime. It just needs to stop standing in the way of Kentuckians enjoying the same freedom to choose their coverage that citizens in U.S. territories enjoy.
This piece was also authored by Michael F. Cannon, director of health policy studies at the Cato Institute and Niklas Kleinworth, Director of the State Health Reform Initiative at the Paragon Health Institute.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Do social media bans protect teens’ mental health? Research suggests bans aren’t the answer.
text:
Countries are banning social media in hopes of helping with the youth mental health crisis. (Photo by Anna Barclay/Getty Images)The year 2026 has been an expensive one for social media platforms.
Since March, YouTube and Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, have settled or paid out in multiple lawsuits to the tune of more than US$17 billion for allegedly acting negligently, deliberately designing their platforms to hook kids and misleading the public about safety and privacy. If these suits are any indication of how states and the public are starting to view social media platforms, more may follow.
On top of these lawsuits, social media platforms are facing a loss of business as bans for minors are accelerating and spreading worldwide. Australia was one of the first with a ban on kids under 16 on social media starting in December 2025, followed soon after by the U.K. with a similar prohibition.
The current list of countries looking to ban minors from these platforms tops more than 20, from Greece to the United Arab Emirates to Canada. The proposed and enacted bans around the world vary in terms of age restriction, parental consent rules and age verification methods. Different countries are looking at restricting different platforms, but most include a mix of Snapchat, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X.
These bans aren’t necessarily for mental health reasons only — some are motivated by political concerns about foreign-owned platforms, and others aim to protect young people’s privacy. But nearly every government banning social media platforms for young people mentions their mental health as a reason.
The question is, are these bans the solution to the mental health problems young people are facing? I research digital media and marketing and measure the impact of new technologies, and I’m skeptical about whether prohibiting access to these platforms will actually improve young people’s mental health.
 
Mental health concerns
Since Jonathan Haidt’s 2024 book “The Anxious Generation” critics of social media have increasingly focused on young people’s mental health. Haidt argues that social media disrupts kids’ social and neurological development, contributing to rising anxiety and depression through sleep loss, fragmented attention, addiction, loneliness, social comparison and perfectionism.
A 2026 study found that young people between 14 and 20 are more than 100% more likely to experience mental illness than 14- to 20-year-olds 50 years ago.
Increased use of social media and screen time is compounding an already precarious time for minors. In 2021 it was estimated that 20.5% of young people experienced elevated symptoms of anxiety, and 25.2% of youth reported elevated symptoms of depression globally.
Many factors contribute to this, including better screening and awareness of kids’ mental health problems, as well as societal disruptions as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. As the world sheltered in place and moved online for work, school and social interactions, there was an increase in isolation and loneliness.
 
Not all bad
In light of these concerns, some researchers argue that bans on social media platforms are like putting an age restriction on buying alcohol or cigarettes.
But unlike these addictive and potentially harmful substances, there are benefits to social media, especially for teens who feel disconnected from their local communities and want to build relationships with others who feel similarly.
Social media platforms allow for global connectivity and community-building with like-minded groups. They also provide a place for self-expression and civic engagement.
In a Pew survey of U.S. teens, 80% said social media helps them stay connected to what’s happening in their friends’ lives
 
Show me the money
One place where the comparison with tobacco is actually quite apt is in relation to the money from lawsuit settlements.
In 1998, states settled a lawsuit against the major tobacco companies to recover smoking-related healthcare costs. Part of the settlement was allocated to programs aimed at reducing youth smoking. In 2026, total state funding for these programs amounts to just 3.4% of the $21.7 billion in revenue states will collect from tobacco settlement payments and tobacco taxes.
Similarly, some money from an August 2026 Meta settlement with a group of states for $17 billion is slated for state-based programs focusing on mental health infrastructure, school and community programs, and public health campaigns.
However, there is no oversight or direction as to how states should use the funds, nor is there a mechanism to report how that money has improved kids’ mental health care, safety and well-being.
 
Is it even possible?
Early evidence from the Australian social media ban shows that kids are finding work-arounds: Roughly 61% of kids ages 12-15 continue to access platforms using false IDs, altered appearances or virtual private networks, or VPNs, even though millions of accounts were disabled. In fact, this has become so common that U.K. lawmakers are debating restricting consumer VPN access.
Some countries, such as Australia, require the platforms themselves to develop ways of verifying a user’s age. Some minors have bypassed scans from biometric age estimation technology by using photo manipulation software, substituting celebrity photos, using clever makeup and even utilizing older friends and parents to pass the “selfie tests” on their behalf. Others simply manipulate their birth years during registration or rely on existing adult-verified accounts managed by family members.
And all of these age-verification methods, whether developed by a government or a social media platform, rely on collecting sensitive data to estimate age accurately, which creates privacy concerns.
Australia is currently seeking to raise fines on social media platforms that fail to comply with its requirements. The Australian safety commissioner, charged with enforcing the ban, issued a compliance update that showed 7 in 10 children who held accounts in restricted platforms remained on those platforms, and more than 80% of Australian teens ages 10-15 still use social media frequently.
Beyond concerns about enacting and enforcing these restrictions, some policymakers also worry that total bans could push some kids to migrate to even riskier online spaces.
 
What could work

Based on the evidence, I’m not convinced that banning social media platforms will be an effective solution to the mental health crisis among young people today.
So what could work?
Supporting young people’s mental health is a complex endeavor that will require a combination of people, organizations and resources coming together.
I believe kids’ mental health would be better served by governments enforcing safety by default standards on social media platforms rather than outright bans. This means that the highest security and privacy options are in place by default so that minors still on a platform are protected. For instance, accounts would be unsearchable by default, so users would have to intentionally make a profile change to be found by people they don’t know in real life.
Safety by default standards also place limits on the manipulation, algorithmic restraint and other addictive mechanisms that may lead to psychological harm in vulnerable populations such as young people.
Educating kids on digital literacy and online safety as well as ensuring some screen-free time are also going to help support kids’ mental health.
It’s also important for parents and other caregivers to recognize changes in behavior as a result of addiction to social platforms and screens. And when adults start seeing signs of a problem, they need clear, easy and affordable ways to connect their kids to mental health support, which is not available in most places right now.
Finally, the United Nations recommends bringing kids into the conversation about what’s best for them online. Obviously, this does not mean putting 12-year-olds in charge of regulatory agencies. But feedback from young people about what they care about, what they get out of being online and what makes it hard for them to look away from their screens could inform changes to social media platforms and education programs that could help young people engage online more safely and maintain a healthy balance.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
Ari Lightman is a professor of digital media and marketing at the Heinz College at Carnegie Mellon University. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Georgia Recorder
title: Trump urges supporters to ‘pretend’ he’s on the ballot as he campaigns with Georgia Republicans
text:
Congressman Mike Collins, who is the the GOP nominee for Georgia's U.S. Senate seat, speaks on stage with President Donald Trump at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderDALTON, Ga. – President Donald Trump returned to conservative northwest Georgia Friday, sharing a rally stage with the GOP nominee for the U.S. Senate and the Republican who hopes to serve as Georgia’s next governor – all while repeating unfounded claims that the 2020 election was rigged. 
Early voting started Monday for the Nov. 3 election. About 700,000 Georgians have already cast a ballot as of Friday.  
Congressman Mike Collins, a Jackson Republican who has been trailing Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff in the polls, was effusive in his praise of the president.
“I want to do something real quick, and that’s just to tell you personally, personally, not just from me, but from everybody in here and across the state and across this country, sir, we appreciate your leadership, your backbone, your standing up for America and putting America first,” Collins said to Trump on stage. “Sir, you are giving the next generation the opportunity to chase their version of the American dream. Thank you.”
Rick Jackson, the GOP nominee for governor, speaks alongside President Donald Trump at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive who is running for governor, was more reserved.
“I’m running to help vulnerable people, I call them the least of these,” said Jackson, who has made his rise from a difficult childhood to a successful businessman a key part of his campaign pitch. “And there’s never been a president who has done more for foster children that are abused and neglected than this man here. And on behalf of all foster children, I want to thank you, Mr. President, for caring about our vulnerable children.”
Speaking to reporters before the rally, Collins predicted the president’s visit will help motivate conservative voters.
“This state is red; we just gotta make sure people understand that it’s time to go vote,” he said. “People are just busy, they’re busy with their lives, whether it’s raising kids or working or whatever it may be, and it’s a midterm election. You don’t have that presidential election that’s on the news every night that’s sitting there blinking like a beacon to remind them.”
“That’s why things like this are so important,” he added. “That’s why President Trump, he helps boost the morale and push that momentum, because he shows up, and it’s working. It’s hard work. He doesn’t have to do this.”
President Donald Trump gestures to the crowd at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Jackson has a slight edge over Bottoms in the governor’s race, but polling shows Ossoff with a steady lead over Collins. University of Georgia political communications professor David Clementson said Collins likely has more to gain and Jackson more to lose from a photo op with the commander in chief.
“Rick Jackson doesn’t need to worry about the strong red, Trump-friendly Dalton area voting for him,” Clementson said. “He needs to be more focused on persuadable swing voters, whereas,  Mike Collins, he wants to run up the margins in Trump country and hope that turnout is depressed in less favorable parts of the state.”
Trump is set to host another Georgia rally in Macon Oct. 24 as he tries to fire up his supporters around the country at a time when Republicans are scrambling to hold onto Congress. 
“You have to pretend I’m on the ballot. OK, the story is this: We get 49% more votes when I’m on the ballot. When I’m not on the ballot – I guess it’s a compliment – but people don’t show up so much,” Trump said Friday. Former state Sen. 
Brandon Beach, who is now serving as U.S. treasurer, put it this way: “President Trump may not be on the ballot, but his policies are, and his candidates are, and if you want him to keep winning for you, you need to send him good conservative winning candidates, and that’s what we’re asking you to do.”
Trump repeated false claims about the 2020 election 
The last time Trump came to Dalton was in early 2021, the end of his first term, for what was supposed to be a rally for then-Sens. David Perdue and Kelly Loeffler in a runoff following the 2020 election that Trump lost. 
Perdue and Loeffler went on to lose the runoff to Democrats Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff. Some Georgia Republicans blamed Trump’s talk of a stolen 2020 election for lowering Republican turnout.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks with reporters after casting his ballot at the Bessie Branham Recreation Center on the first day of early voting. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Trump echoed those false claims from the rally stage, calling Ossoff an “imposter.” 
“The whole thing was crooked,” Trump said. “But Ossoff lost that election, but they gave it to him because it was a rigged election. That’s the only reason he became a senator. He needed a rigged election.” 
Six years later, multiple recounts and court cases have found no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 election, but Trump continues to claim otherwise. Earlier this year, the FBI raided Fulton County’s elections warehouse and seized hundreds of boxes of election documents, and then later assigned hundreds of analysts to investigate the records. 
The Georgia State Election Board’s executive director James Mills wrote a letter to U.S. Attorney General Blanche requesting federal “intervention.” Trump has flirted with the idea but did not bring it up during Friday’s rally.
Does Trump help or hurt Georgia Republicans? 
A Civiqs poll puts Trump at 33% approval in Georgia. The war in Iran and other issues have put the president at odds with members of his own party, Clementson said.
State Sen. Brian Strickland, who is the Republican nominee for attorney general, speaks at President Donald Trump’s rally on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“There are certain elements of the Republican base who are disappointed that he’s not coming through on his many campaign promises,” he said. “Inflation has only gotten worse. Russia-Ukraine has only gotten worse. He started a new war with Iran. Gas prices. Electric bills. He hasn’t released all the Epstein files, and so there’s some ambivalence there among his supporters.”
Pundits predict Trump could again lower excitement among moderate voters by drawing attention to the unpopular aspects of his presidency.
Georgia GOP Chairman Josh McKoon said he’s confident the Trump bump Republicans could get among low-propensity conservative voters will outweigh the risk of Democrats tying candidates to him.
“For the last decade, all the Democratic Party has done is define itself in opposition to Donald Trump,” he said. “So I don’t think there’s anything new about that today. But what’s great about him being here is it sends a powerful message to Georgians that we have a chance to win all of these elections.”
Speaking before the rally, Republican state Sen. Brian Strickland, who is a candidate for attorney general who spoke on stage before Trump, said he was not concerned about the campaign of his opponent, Democratic state Rep. Tanya Miller, seeking to attack Strickland by tying him to Trump.
State Sen. Greg Dolezal, the GOP nominee for lieutenant governor, speaks at President Donald Trump’s rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“I’m here as Brian Strickland running for attorney general, and my goal is to get in front of as many voters as I can, and I welcome the chance at any opportunity I get,” Strickland said. 
Miller’s campaign immediately fired off a press release after the rally concluded, saying Strickland “revealed himself to be a Trump-backed extremist.” 
State Sen. Greg Dolezal, who is running for lieutenant governor, and state Rep. Tim Fleming, who is running to be state’s next top election official, also had a speaking slot and received on-stage shoutouts from Trump. 
“Election integrity is not optional; it’s a daily duty we owe to every legal voter and to every patriot who came before us,” Fleming said in a speech before also blasting his opponent from the stage. 
Penny Brown Reynolds, the Democratic candidate for secretary of state, likewise used Fleming’s appearance against him. 
“My opponent has shown Georgians that his true loyalties will always rest with President Donald Trump and those who seek to undermine the integrity of Georgia’s elections,” Brown Reynolds said in a statement Friday night.
Democrats amplify calls to vote like Trump is on the ballot 
In a Friday morning press conference, Georgia Democratic Party Chair Charlie Bailey attacked Jackson and Collins ahead of their participation in the rally and sought to attach both candidates to Trump, saying that their policies have been harmful to Georgians.
“The Trump-Collins-Jackson ticket ought to take credit,” Bailey said. “They ought to take credit for what they’ve done to the people of Georgia, what they’ve done to the people of this country, and the back-breaking, cost-raising, foolish agenda that has made the American dream less attainable now in our great state than it’s been in over two decades,”
Bailey specifically attacked Collins for staffing scandals he’s faced over his campaign, saying that Georgia voters will reject him for being too “weak” to distance himself from former staffers that have been accused of antisemitism. He pointed to Collins’ staunch support for Trump and his votes to advance policies that he said are making life unaffordable for Georgians.
“There’s no reason to be confused about why his campaign is floundering in these times, and that the people of Georgia, Democrats, independents, and a lot of Republicans are rejecting it,” Bailey said.
His attack on Jackson was just as sharp, calling the Republican for governor “another creepy billionaire that has made a career off of taxpayer dollars” and that even though he entered the race as an outsider, he has been “one of the biggest Republican donors of the past two and a half decades.” 
Jackson’s Democratic opponent, Keisha Lance Bottoms, in a press conference Thursday night also criticized Jackson for his plan to join Trump Friday. She said that despite the Jackson campaign’s outsized spending, the race remains close and that she was encouraged by record-breaking early voting numbers. And she said that Trump’s visit might motivate even more people to vote early against Republican policies.
“If Rick Jackson believes that Trump is going to motivate voters in Georgia, he’s absolutely right. He’s going to motivate people to go to the polls, who are going to imagine that Donald Trump is on the ballot, and the people of Georgia are going to vote accordingly,” Bottoms said.
Georgia Recorder editor Jill Nolin contributed to this report.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump administration moves to reopen Alaska national preserves to bear baiting by sport hunters
text:
A grizzly bear walks on a hillside on July 28, 2013, in Denali National Park and Preserve. A new Trump administration rule, to go into effect in about a month, will overturn Obama and Biden administration bans on bear baiting by sport hunters in Alaska's national preserves. (Photo by Daniel A. Leifheit/National Park Service)Sport hunters will be able to bait bears in Alaska national preserves, under a final rule the Trump administration announced on Friday.
The rule, proposed in March, overturns bans by the Biden and Obama administrations of the practice within National Park Service units.
Bear baiting, which involves use of food stockpiles to attract bears that are then killed and harvested, is a controversial practice.
Trump administration plans to end ban on bear baiting in Alaska national preserves

Supporters say that it is a standard hunting method that, as regulated by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, is conducted in a controlled and careful way, affecting only a few animals. But critics say it is unethical and dangerous to wildlife and people.
In Alaska, national preserves, which are part of the National Park Service system, are open to hunting, under the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, or ANILCA. For most of the years since the passage of that 1980 law, the federal government deferred to state management of sport hunting, which includes allowances for bear baiting at times in certain areas.
The new rule’s bear-baiting allowance in national preserves applies only to sport hunting. Subsistence hunting in federal land units is managed by the federal government, and bear baiting has been allowed for subsistence hunters.
In a statement, U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said the new rule restores that deference to Alaska management and Alaska-specific conditions.
“For more than three decades, Alaska’s national parks and preserves were managed under a framework that recognized Alaska’s unique circumstances, respected the State’s role in managing fish and wildlife, protected subsistence uses and conserved these remarkable lands and resources,” Burgum said in the statement. “This final rule restores that commonsense framework and gives Alaskans a stronger voice in decisions affecting the lands, wildlife and traditions they know best, while ensuring the National Park Service continues to protect park resources for future generations.” 
Doug Vincent-Lang, commissioner of the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, said the new rule is appropriate.
“We thank the Department of Interior and the National Park Service for making these and other changes in the rule. The change represents a necessary return to the fish and wildlife management framework established by the Alaska Constitution and reaffirmed in ANILCA, which had served Alaska for three decades,” Vincent-Lang said in a statement.
But environmentalists blasted the decision.
Jim Adams, Alaska regional director for the National Parks Conservation Association called the new rule “outrageous” and “disheartening.”
“Approving inappropriate and dangerous sport hunting methods in Denali and other treasured landscapes is another huge blow to the integrity and forever nature of our national parks, which continue to be desecrated by this administration’s policies,” he said in a statement. 
“National preserve lands at Denali, Katmai, Gates of the Arctic and others are the very places where people travel from around the world, in hopes of seeing iconic bears and wolves alive in their natural habitat,” he said. “Allowing sport hunters to lure bears with greased donut bait piles to kill them on those lands is baffling and counter to the mission of the Park Service.”
Cooper Freeman, Alaska director at the Center for Biological Diversity, called the new rule “disgraceful.”
“This rule puts sport hunters’ desires over wise and sometimes urgently needed decisions to ensure the long-term health of wildlife in national parklands in Alaska. People come from all over the world to see wildlife thriving on our treasured national parklands in Alaska, and we shouldn’t allow unsporting and unscientific practices that deplete these populations,” he said in a statement.
Aside from the bear-baiting allowance, the new rule includes some other provisions.
It restores an allowance for licensed trappers working in national preserves to harvest animals with firearms. It has an allowance for permitholders to capture live raptors. It has some other provisions concerning issues like public notice and administrative changes at the Federal Subsistence Management board.
Unlike the Obama-era and Biden-era hunting rules, the new Trump administration rule makes references to subsistence. It includes a provision removing a permit requirement for subsistence users to collect animal parts. But for the most part, the new rule maintains the status quo for subsistence activities in national park units, affirming that existing federal law granting a rural priority remains in effect.
The final rule is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Monday and to go into effect 30 days after that.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Democrats rally with Georgia US senator ahead of early voting
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Annie Andrews, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and Rep. Jermaine Johnson, the nominee for governor, rally in Columbia, S.C., on Friday Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The Democrats seeking to be South Carolina’s U.S. senator and governor rallied Friday with U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia as part of a days-long push ahead of early voting in an attempt to bring a blue wave to the Palmetto State.
Taking the stage behind a sign that read “Keep the Faith!” were Annie Andrews, who’s vying to be South Carolina’s first Democrat in the U.S. Senate in over 20 years, and Rep. Jermaine Johnson, who could make history as the state’s first Black governor, as well as the first Democrat sent to the Governor’s Mansion in 28 years.
They urged voters to go vote and prove Democrats can be elected to statewide office in South Carolina.
The two are scheduled to continue their tour with Warnock on Saturday in North Charleston and Florence, while dozens of “No Kings” rallies focused on early voting are planned across the state.
“The people of South Carolina, we are ready, we are past ready for a new South Carolina,” Johnson told more than 100 people crowded into Senate’s End, an event venue about a mile from the Statehouse. “In this moment, right now, the energy is real. People are fired up. They are ready for real, tangible change because we deserve it.”

U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia rallies in Columbia, S.C., on Friday Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

It’s been 20 years since voters elected any Democrat to statewide office in South Carolina: In 2006, Jim Rex became superintendent of education by less than 1 percentage point.
While waiting for the candidates, people chanted about a possibility of a “blue wave” for Democrats in the midterms. Several election forecasters have indicated a closer-than-anticipated race between Andrews and Republican U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed following the death of her older brother, Lindsey Graham, in July.
Graham ran for the next full term with the encouragement and endorsement of President Donald Trump, and Republicans maintain that South Carolina remains “Trump country.”
Warnock, who isn’t up for re-election in the U.S. Senate until 2028, is in South Carolina as part of a pre-midterm tour through several states in the South.
His appearances in early voting presidential states — including South Carolina, which will hold Democrats’ first primary in the nation in 2028, have fueled speculation about his presidential ambitions. Earlier this week, he was in Columbia for a “faith power hour” with local pastors, where he dodged questions about his presidential ambitions.
Warnock’s January 2021 special election win flipped a seat long held by a Republican and gave Democrats control of the U.S. Senate. He won a full term in 2022 by defeating Republican Herschel Walker, Georgia’s legendary Heisman Trophy winner.
South Carolina can do it too, he said, referring to Andrews.
“Don’t sleep on the South,” Warnock said. “Look at me and remember that they shouldn’t sleep on the South. Nobody thought Georgia could do it until we got it done.”
On the stage, Andrews said South Carolinians don’t elect dynasties. Lindsey Graham held the seat for almost 24 years when he died.
“This Senate seat belongs to South Carolina. It does not belong to one family,” she said.
Other potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders in South Carolina ahead of the midterms include Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.
Trump is scheduled to rally at Clemson University with Graham on Wednesday.
Johnson’s opponent in the gubernatorial race, GOP Attorney General Alan Wilson, on Friday announced a bus tour for the two weeks leading up until Election Day. Republicans on that tour will include U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp.
Early voting in South Carolina starts Monday and ends on Oct. 31, except for Oct. 25, a Sunday.
The crowd at a “keep the faith” rally for South Carolina Democrats in Columbia on Friday Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)Senate candidate Annie Andrews rallies in Columbia on Friday Oct. 16, 2026.
