title: New Mexico fiber project to provide high-speed internet for underserved communities
text:
The New Mexico Office of Broadband Access and Expansion announced on Oct. 14, 2026, the first of 19 projects using federal grant money to increase broadband connectivity in five northern counties. (Photo courtesy of OBAE)After delays from federal officials, New Mexico’s agency to expand broadband this week announced an agreement with an internet service provider to bring high-speed fiber internet to communities in five of the state’s northern counties through a federally funded grant. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A total of 1,970 unserved locations and 1,965 underserved locations throughout Colfax, Rio Arriba, Sandoval, Santa Fe and Taos counties will receive fiber broadband access from the project, New Mexico Office of Broadband Access and Expansion said in a news release announcing the agreement with Kit Carson Electric Cooperative, which provides internet among other utilities. Homes, businesses and community institutions — such as fire departments, libraries, schools and medical centers — in the communities will receive the upgrade, OBAE added.
Funding for roughly two-thirds of the project’s $40 million price tag comes via the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment federal grant program, which was established in the Biden-era Infrastructure and Jobs Act to achieve universal high-speed internet access nationwide. Kit Carson matched the remaining costs. This project is the first of approximately 19 projects that will be funded by the program to tackle connectivity issues throughout the state, OBAE said in a statement.
OBAE Director Jeff Lopez told Source NM that “just around 74% of New Mexico had access to broadband” when the office was first established in 2021. “Now, around 91% is connected,” he continued, adding that this project is the first step to address the remaining locations without connection.
The Trump administration delayed $293 million of the program’s total funds earlier this year after the National Telecommunications and Information Administration failed to release guidelines for how to spend the cash. 
The Biden administration “had one set of goals and the current federal administration made some pretty dramatic changes that the Office of Broadband had to accommodate in order to get access to these dollars,” Lopez said. After the federal telecommunications agency released the new guidelines in June, OBAE began its bidding process for grant money.
Lopez said he aims for the project to be completed by 2030, as Kit Carson must complete a one- to three-year process of environmental reviews and permitting before construction can begin. 
One of the areas the project will help is in northern Santa Fe County, a rural area that has “been underserved with broadband and telecommunications” for a long time, District 1 Santa Fe County Commissioner Justin Greene told Source NM. He added the fiber program will finish “the last mile” to previous broadband efforts by the Obama administration. 
“The communities up there will have better broadband access for education, for telehealth, for entertainment and for working from home,” Greene added.

name: Delaware
title: State Police Investigating Shooting in Magnolia
text:
POLICE LOG – October 17, 2026
Delaware State Police are investigating a shooting that left two 19-year-old men injured Monday evening in Magnolia.
Troopers responded to the first block of Juanita Drive at approximately 9:30 p.m. on October 12 for a reported shooting.
Police said the preliminary investigation determined that unknown suspects had arranged to meet the victims to sell THC vape cartridges. During the exchange, both victims were struck by gunfire.
The two men were taken to an area hospital by private vehicle with non-life-threatening injuries.
The Delaware State Police Troop 3 Criminal Investigations Unit is continuing the investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact Detective R. Spanier at 302-698-8569 or Delaware Crime Stoppers at 1-800-847-3333.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Tindell to step down as public safety commissioner. Gov. Reeves appoints Capitol Police chief to succeed him
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Sean Tindell will step down next month after serving six years as Mississippi’s public safety commissioner and will be replaced by Capitol Police Chief Bo Luckey, Gov. Tate Reeves announced on Friday.
Tindell, a Republican, is running for attorney general, and he confirmed with Mississippi Today that he is resigning to focus on his campaign. In a statement, Tindell said he is proud of his tenure at the Department of Public Safety and praised Reeves’ appointment of Luckey.
“Chief Luckey has led Capitol Police to a level that has exceeded everyone’s expectations, and I’m confident he will continue that success as the next Commissioner of Public Safety,” Tindell said. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together and look forward to the opportunity to serve the people of Mississippi in other capacities in the future.” 
Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones, left, listens as Capitol Police Chief Bo Luckey speaks during the Capital City Revitalization Committee meeting at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson, Miss., on Wednesday, Aug. 27, 2025.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Tindell has led DPS since Reeves nominated him to the post in 2020. Tindell previously served as a judge on the Mississippi Court of Appeals for three years and represented the Gulfport area in the state Senate for five years.
Luckey has served as chief of Capitol Police, a state-run unit that patrols parts of Jackson, since Reeves appointed him in May 2022. During that time, the Republican-controlled Legislature expanded the department’s jurisdiction, giving it more terrain to patrol in Jackson amid concerns over crime.
Capitol Police is a division of the Department of Public Safety.
Before his time as Capitol Police chief, Luckey was an investigator in the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office. He has also worked for the Brandon Police Department, Rankin County Sheriff’s Department, U.S. Department of Homeland Security Investigations and the Drug Enforcement Administration.
“I am deeply honored and humbled to accept Governor Reeves’ appointment as Commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Public Safety,” Luckey said in a statement. “I am grateful for his trust and the opportunity to continue serving the people of Mississippi.”
Reeves said Luckey is ready to lead DPS.
“His work has made our capital city and state safer,” Reeves said. “He has years of law enforcement experience and is the right person to lead the Mississippi Department of Public Safety. I’d like to thank Sean for admirably serving our state and wish him well in the next chapter of his career.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Open Studios fosters cultural community in New Haven
text:
Niko Scharer paused by a rack of finished pottery, lifting a small bowl off the shelf. She took a moment to marvel at the small, crackly finish that had formed in the firing process. Around her, the studio bustled with activity. 
Nearby, potter Annie de Graff dipped a mug into a beige glaze, inspecting a thick drip that ran down one side. Susan Rogol settled into her nook, surrounded by small gem-colored bowls and vases. In the parking lot, Margaret Ulecka-Wilson had nearly finished loading pieces into a gas kiln that the group uses to fire its work outside.   
All four — and particularly Scharer — are part of an artist-led, grassroots effort behind the fourth annual Open Studios New Haven, a celebration of artists and art making that unfolds across New Haven and West Haven for the month of October. In the final two weekends of the month, artists will open the doors to their studios, galleries, art buses, music incubators and community theaters, inviting people in to see a process that is often private. 
“It feels like a party,” said Scharer, an artist at Erector Square Pottery and Ceramics who this year stepped up as a primary organizer of the event. “I love talking to people. I love showing them the process. People come into the studio, and they pick out things to talk about and look at that you would never expect. They share their own experiences working with clay. That’s what Open Studios is about. It’s about the people. ” 
For many of the artists involved, the story of Open Studios begins well before its inception in the summer of 2023. From 2005 to 2020, the now-defunct organization Artspace New Haven ran a month-long festival called City-Wide Open Studios (CWOS), which stretched from the labyrinthine, former factory complex Erector Square to the city-owned Goffe Street Armory to studios and work-live spaces in the city’s Mill River District and Westville neighborhood. 
Artist Olivia Charis, reads about at “Stop trying to fix me” by Jean Scott during the reception for Devotional Alchemy at 63 Audubon in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.  The Connecticut Group Show is part of Open Studios New Haven, a month-long event featuring two dozen locations. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
In 2021, under a new executive director at Artspace, it became the Open Source Festival, a weeks-long fête that brought in skateboarding, multi-channel film and video, and storytelling alongside a weekend at Erector Square that was part of Artspace’s long-running tradition. Then in the early months of 2023, after the departure of its executive director, Artspace closed its brick-and-mortar storefront in downtown New Haven.
Around that time, a group of artists at Erector Square began working together to reimagine the festival. They were, remembered artist Martha Lewis, a rag-tag and dedicated band of artists and makers, who rebuilt the weekend’s infrastructure over a series of planning meetings. When Artspace had a closing sale, they bought old CWOS banners that had been in the building’s basement, and frankensteined them anew with paper guillotines and color-coded duct tape. 
In October 2023, on the centennial anniversary of the building’s founding, over 150 artists welcomed visitors to the space. Over two days, roughly 1,500 people came out, according to artist and early organizer Eric March. 
“It’s been a great bonding experience,” said Lewis, who has worked in studios at Erector Square for over a decade, and now curates a group show of Open Studios artists at New Haven’s Institute Library. “Especially at this moment in time, work that the artists of New Haven are doing as outreach. For people to see inside people’s studios … it really is a gift.”     
Through the planning meetings, she’s gotten to know artists who may share the building, but are several floors away, behind a network of locked doors and steep stairwells. In her studio, which she has named “The Elaboratory,” Lewis can spend hours immersed in a single project, like her current series “Within Worlds.” The festival gives her an opportunity to emerge from her space, and see what her colleagues are working on.   

A piece from Martha Lewis’ series “Within Worlds,” in which the artist submerges crumpled, mineral-based paper in “a complex soup of colors,” and removes the pieces when the paint dries. Lewis uses thrifted glass containers, which she inverts and turns into display cases.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

Four years in, Scharer and fellow artists have helped coordinate 65 open studios and 42 guest artists for Erector Square alone, as well as pop-up events throughout the day like origami printing, family artmaking, and a “Wellness Concert” and instrument petting zoo from the youth-powered organization Music Haven. 
Scharer said she is particularly excited about a scavenger hunt in which attendees can criss-cross Erector Square’s eight buildings, scurrying up and down stairways and filling out a “passport” of objects that they find along the way. In one studio in building six, for instance, there’s a small oil painting of a brown fox, installed to look like he’s chasing a bumblebee one canvas over.   
In total, Schaerer said, the budget hovers around $8,000, an amount that comes from artist fees (it costs artists $25 to participate, or $60 if they are guests in the space), individual donations, and small fundraising events like raffles and tag sales. That money covers paying vendors and compensating collaborators.  
She was quick to add that the work has very much been a group effort. Ioana Barac, of the Erector Square-based design firm Atelier Cue, put together a color-coded map meant to make the building seem less overwhelming. Glass artist Karen Hibbs organized a dinner for artists on Friday evening, so people have a chance to get to know each other before the event begins. Liese Klein, who runs New Haven Aikikai Aikido, put together the scavenger hunt. Maxim Schmidt, who is an artist and curator, came back onboard as the event’s volunteer coordinator. 
Building Collaborative Community 

Artist Leila Daw in her studio.  Credit: Lucy Gellman Photo / CT Mirror

Just days before the celebration formally began, several artists buzzed around their studios, moving tubes of paint and baubles of thread until the spaces were cleaner than they’d been in months. On the first floor of the complex’s building five, artist Leila Daw checked in on her rendering of the element earth, still drying after a coat of resin. 
Daw, who has been working in her Erector Square studio for two decades, said she’s always excited for open studios weekend, and grateful to the organizers who have shepherded it through nearly half a decade of transition. In 2004, she moved into her current studio from a home studio in Branford, to work on a commission from Bradley Airport that now hangs in the space’s ticket lobby. 
Her arrival coincided with the early years of Artspace’s CWOS, when curator Denise Markonish was still working with the organization (Markonish left New Haven in 2007 to work for Mass MoCA, where she was until last year). Those years were amazing, Daw remembered. But after the Covid-19 pandemic and a leadership transition at Artspace, “it was sort of a disaster,” she said. 
Then several of her artistic colleagues scooped it up and began to reimagine it. Since that time, she said, she’s met artists who have been in the building for years, but have never had the chance to wander into her studio, or welcome her into theirs. 
“We are in this big building complex and we don’t know each other,” she said. “We can’t really see each other, it’s [normally] not completely open. But Open Studios is this completely cooperative group effort.”
As she spoke, large-scale works turned the studio into a wash of blue and green, with pops of color that made their way across each canvas. Daw works in the style of Burmese shwe chi doe, or golden thread tapestry.   

Artists Laura Vasu, Mark Kidd, and Shaily Menon, who refer to themselves as Beautiful Social Art Mechanics (BSAM) Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

One building away and several flights upstairs, artists Laura Vasu, Shaily Menon and Mark Kidd stood in their shared studio, the space already pristine. The three, who work across wildly different styles, call themselves Beautiful Social Art Mechanics (BSAM), a nod to their shared time painting in a house on New Haven’s Mechanic Street. By day, all of them work in the sciences: Kidd runs a lab for Wren Laboratories in Branford, Menon is the dean of arts and sciences at the University of New Haven, and Vasu does purchasing for the biotech company Arvinas. 
Twice a week, on Tuesday nights and Saturday mornings, they leave that work at the door, and meet in the studio to keep each other accountable as artists. It’s like exercise, said Kidd: if he doesn’t do it, he knows that his art muscles will atrophy . He’s not willing to do that again, after passing up art school when he was a young adult. Tuesday, he was true to his work, standing in the center of a bright studio, ready to get to work, just after 6 p.m.
For that reason, he and the other members of BSAM are especially excited to share their first open studios weekend with other artists in the building.   
“We knew we wanted to come to Erector Square,” he said, framed by a dream-like portrait of a house on the water, the lake behind it stretching out towards the horizon line. “I hope it’s a stepping stone for us within the arts community and within ourselves.”  
“For me, it’s like coming full circle,” added Menon, who has loved artmaking since she was a girl growing up in India, but ultimately chose to pursue the sciences. In the small studio, walls hung salon-style with art, she gestured to a painting of East Rock that she’s still working on, thick green foliage surrounding a glass-like Mill River as rock formations rose on one side. 
“It’s a celebration,” she added. We’re coming at it as a year of us being together [in this space].”
Satellite Events Abound

Artist Allyse Corbin, shows off bead work on her piece “Swarm” during the reception for Devotional Alchemy at 63 Audubon in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.  The Connecticut Group Show is part of Open Studios New Haven, a month-long event featuring two dozen locations. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

As Erector Square opens its doors, several satellite locations also plan to welcome artists and art enthusiasts both this weekend and next. They include, for instance, a fall festival from cARTie, a hands-on museum bus that travels to schools around the state; a guided tour of the Anita Louise House, a budding artists’ residency program from Lotta Studio founders Luke and Mustina Hanscom; and a smaller open studios showcase at the MarlinWorks Building. 
Just over the city line in West Haven, lifelong artist Jenna González is preparing for a group show with a dozen artists. They include, for instance, sculptor Susan Clinard, cycling activist and collage artist Matthew Feiner, and guest artists including printmaker Shaunda Holloway and multi-media sculptor Linda Mickens. 
In a phone call Wednesday, González called it a natural extension of her work to bring people together through the arts, which has in recent years stretched from Torrington to West Haven and back. For years, she ran the a mano gallery in Torrington, ultimately closing it after her mom’s health prompted her to move back to West Haven and take on a full time caregiving role. 
When she arrived in West Haven four years ago, she was hungry for the same creative community she’d been able to cultivate in Torrington, and before that at the Star Pin building in Shelton, which for years doubled as a studio space for dozens of artists (the building suffered a large fire in 2020). When she arrived in West Haven, she rented a studio space at 14 Gilbert St., meeting other artists in the building. 

Visitors look at pieces during the reception for Devotional Alchemy at 63 Audubon in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.  The Connecticut Group Show is part of Open Studios New Haven, a month-long event featuring two dozen locations. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

In 2024, the arts advocacy platform ArtsWest CT named González West Haven’s artist-in-residence, giving her space to work in their basement offices on the city’s Main Street (despite the tiny space, “sculpture dried really well in there,” González said with a laugh). Through that program, González was able to spearhead the Shoreline Artist Collective (SLAC), which that fall held its first exhibition during the second annual artist-led open studios effort. 
This show seeks to build on that momentum, she said. Earlier this year, SLAC dissolved, around the same time that she formally closed down her gallery in Torrington. González, who is not one to be easily discouraged, reached out to the Hurley Group, the property management company that runs 14 Gilbert St. A representative gave her access to keys and a 1500 square foot space for half the month, and the group show was born. That weekend takes place Oct. 24 and 25.             
“The arts community has truly saved my life many times,” she said. “I always come back to it when I need it, and it’s always been there. When I come somewhere new, I seek it out, and if I can’t find it, I create it.”
She added that she sees the show, and West Haven’s formal and continued participation in Open Studios New Haven, as a way to give back to the community. As a kid, González was in and out of foster care, and faced homelessness for a period of time. It was someone who gave her access to artmaking that helped her move forward. 
Years later, after raising a family as a single mother and surviving a stroke that left her with limited mobility, it’s still what keeps her going. One day a week, she still commutes back to Torrington, to run a support group as an art therapist. 
“I think that Gilbert Street is an amazing opportunity for West Haven,” she said, crediting City Council Member Ruby Melton, long a champion of the arts, for talking with her about arts advocacy when she was struggling to find a community. “I think West Haven needs arts representation.”

Potter Annie de Graff at work at  Erector Square Pottery and Ceramics.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

Just a few miles away over the Hamden town border, artist Jacquelyn Gleisner and members of Quilt Club New Haven will present, “Quilts in the Covered Bridge,” with an installation on the bridge beside the Eli Whitney Museum & Workshop. This year, the works on display will include a project, commissioned by New Haven’s America 250 Commission, with images from city residents of the people or places that they most associate with New Haven. 
In addition to many, many images of pizza — Gleisner sounded as though she was stifling a guffaw — people submitted drawings of everything from oysters to the futuristic, chrome-colored tunnel at New Haven Union Station, which may disappear as the Connecticut Department of Transportation implements a $402 million plan to update the station. 
Earlier this year, club members scanned and then translated those drawings into vector files, which they used a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine to mill onto wooden blocks. This weekend, club members plan to ink those blocks, so that people who come by can make their own commemorative woodblock prints with them.   
“I love bringing the quilts outside because it’s more or less forcing pedestrians to engage with them,” Gleisner said in a phone call Tuesday. She added that watching open studios come back to live has been “remarkable,” and despite some growing pains, “I do feel like artists are trying to band together to make the most of it.” 

Joy Bush, of Hamden,  gets a closer look at Joseph Smolinski’s piece “Mourning Sun” made of sea coal during the reception for Devotional Alchemy at 63 Audubon in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.  The Connecticut Group Show is part of Open Studios New Haven, a month-long event featuring two dozen locations. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

This year, the festival has also welcomed  the performing arts, with a two-weekend preview of “Revolutionary Haven: Myths of America,” an original, still-evolving and site-specific work from members of A Broken Umbrella Theatre Company. Performing the work in an unused wing of Elm City Montessori School, over a dozen ensemble members plan to turn back the clock to 1776, exploring the American Revolution from multiple viewpoints. 
For director Rachel Alderman, it feels like a homecoming — both in New Haven’s Westville neighborhood, where the company is based, and to open studios. Nine years ago, the company performed “Exchange,” a new work about the history of the District Telephone Company of New Haven, at three CWOS weekends. 
In that work, which A Broken Umbrella premiered in the fall of 2017, ensemble members used a truck and trailer to create a mobile set, and toured it across three weekends of a then-vibrant CWOS festival. Then, for years, the company kept making work, and looking for ways to collaborate with other artistic organizations in the city. 
Like Gleisner, Alderman said the project has been exciting because of the partnerships it has opened up, including with young people at Elm City Montessori and artists exhibiting their work across the city. With Wábi Gallery owner Kim Weston, for instance, set designer Mistina Hanscom has designed a room dedicated to Weston’s art, which centers her experience as a Black and Indigenous artist, mother, and member of the LGBTQ+ community.
“We’ve always been very close to the artist community in Westville and elsewhere, so this show is a great chance to illustrate that,” she said. 
Open Studios New Haven takes place over the month of October, with locations across the city and into West Haven and Hamden. This weekend, Erector Square Open Studios takes place Oct. 17-18 at Erector Square, 315 Peck St. in the city’s Fair Haven neighborhood. Satellite events include open studios at the 83 Willow St. Marlinworks Building; “Quilts in the Covered Bridge” at 915 Whitney Ave. in Hamden; a museum bus festival at 650 Central Ave; and the first weekend of “Revolutionary Haven” at Elm City Montessori School at 495 Blake St. Next weekend, West Haven will open its studios at 14 Gilbert St. and Westville artists will have events throughout the neighborhood. Check out the full lineup here.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Free photo IDs available at North Dakota tribal nations ahead of election
text:
Volunteers from North Dakota Native Vote set up a booth outside the Sioux County Courthouse on Election Day, Nov. 5, 2024. (Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Department of Transportation is traveling to four tribal nations next week to provide free nondriver photo identification cards ahead of the election.
The ID cards will be issued to North Dakota residents 18 and older who do not have a driver’s license. Paperwork will be processed overnight and photo IDs will be mailed to residents within five days, the department said.
“These photo ID cards are a great option for individuals wanting to vote in the upcoming elections,” said Brad Schaffer, director of the driver’s license division for the Department of Transportation, in a statement.
The ID card events will be held at:

Standing Rock Sioux Tribe: Monday from 10 a.m.–3 p.m., at the Sioux County Courthouse, Fort Yates.
Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa: Tuesday from 10 a.m.–3 p.m., at the Sky Dancer Casino, Belcourt.
Mandan, Hidatsa, & Arikara Nation: Wednesday from 10 a.m.–3 p.m., at the North Segment Community Center, New Town.
Spirit Lake Nation: Thursday from 10 a.m.–3 p.m., at the Blue Building, Fort Totten.

Documents needed are: 

certified birth certificate, court-issued name change and, if applicable, a certified marriage certificate, divorce decree or adoption order
Social Security card
proof of North Dakota resident physical address

North Dakota requires voters to present an ID with a street address. Many tribal citizens have post office boxes as their residential address.
During a Tribal and State Relations Committee meeting last month, Secretary of State Michael Howe said tribal citizens without a physical address can work with county officials to obtain an enhanced 911 address that will tie a physical address to a phone number.
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

Howe told lawmakers he wants every qualified elector to vote in the state’s elections, and the voter ID events help accomplish that goal.
The acceptable forms of identification for voting in North Dakota are: A North Dakota driver’s license; a nondriver state-issued ID card; a tribal ID or a tribal letter, and certificate from a long-term care facility. 
During the legislative meeting, Rep. Collette Brown, D-Warwick, expressed concern to Howe about poll workers not being educated about what a tribal ID looks like. Howe said his office would raise that issue with county election officials across the state.
Daniela Aki, director of civic engagement for the Sacred Pipe Resource Center in Bismarck, said the ID roadtrip to tribal areas is important to improve relations between Native tribes and the state.
“A lot of times we are expected to come to Bismarck,” Aki said. “Kudos to them. This is really needed.”
For questions about the photo ID events, call 1-855-633-6835. For more information about North Dakota voting requirements, visit vote.ND.gov.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Closing a ‘loophole’ or ‘fearmongering’ about noncitizens voting: South Dakota’s Amendment J
text:
Voters fill out their ballots at a Sioux Falls polling place during the South Dakota primary election on June 2, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A supporter of a state constitutional amendment on South Dakota’s Nov. 3 ballot says it would close a loophole in voting eligibility, while an opponent says it engages in “fearmongering.”
The state constitution already affirms the right of U.S. citizens to vote. Amendment J, one of four questions on the ballot, asks South Dakotans to add language to the constitution specifying people who are not U.S. citizens are “disqualified from voting.”
Two years ago, state officials discovered 273 non-U.S. citizens had accidentally been registered to vote in South Dakota while their driver’s license forms were being processed. Noncitizens can obtain a driver’s license or state ID if they are lawful permanent residents or have temporary legal status. A section of the driver’s license form allows an applicant to register to vote if they’re a citizen.


South Dakota ballot questions
Visit Searchlight’s 2026 Ballot Questions page and Voter Guide to learn more about all four of South Dakota’s ballot questions in the Nov. 3 election.


One of those 273 people voted, according to the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. That was in 2016. All of the registrations were canceled after their discovery.
State Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, sponsored the legislative resolution that sent Amendment J to the ballot. She said it would close a loophole by adding a prohibition against noncitizens voting to the language affirming citizens’ right to vote.
“As long as United States citizens who meet the requirements are allowed to vote, nothing currently prohibits noncitizens also being allowed to vote,” she wrote in a pro statement.
“It’s not happening right now, but this is being proactive,” Howard said. “I hope people agree that being proactive is much better than being reactive.”
Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, opposes Amendment J. Citizenship is already required to qualify someone as a voter in South Dakota, he said.
“When proponents are bringing forward that there are loopholes or ways for folks to allow noncitizens to vote in South Dakota, frankly, the constitution doesn’t allow that,” Muckey said. “Really, this is just a matter of, for lack of a better way, fearmongering about a group of people that aren’t voting.”
In recent years, state legislators have approved other state laws that impact voting rights. A law that came into effect last year criminalizes voting for noncitizens. A new law this year requires people to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote. Legislators also passed a law this year that allows voters to challenge another voter’s citizenship. The challenge must be in the form of a signed, sworn statement and must include what state law describes as “documented evidence,” and submitted at least 90 days before an election.
A “yes” vote on Amendment J would add language to the state constitution specifying that noncitizens are disqualified from voting. A “no” vote would leave the constitution as is.
Early voting for the Nov. 3 general election is underway. The voter registration deadline is Monday.

 To learn more about Amendment J, listen to this episode of Searchlight Report, a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight.

name: Delaware
title: Successful Seniors: At 75, Michael Richards thought assisted living meant giving up. Instead, he found a new life.
text:
Image: Successful Seniors is a new series of stories about healthy, happy seniors and the options available to caregivers for their loved ones. Image created on 10/15 using AI.

After reluctantly moving to Harmony at Kent, a Navy veteran discovered that independence isn’t always about living alone. Sometimes, it’s about having the support, friendships, and encouragement to live life more fully.
Editor’s Note: Introducing “Successful Seniors”:  Delaware LIVE is launching a new series of stories designed to help caregivers and families understand the options available for their aging loved ones. Through personal stories of older Delawareans, we’ll explore how senior living communities, supportive care, and meaningful social connections can help seniors maintain independence, improve their health, and enjoy a fulfilling quality of life. Our goal is to show that growing older doesn’t have to mean giving up what makes life meaningful—sometimes, it opens the door to new opportunities.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
DOVER, Del. – When Michael Richards moved into assisted living at age 75, he wasn’t happy about it. The Navy veteran had spent his life making his own decisions, living in his own home and maintaining his independence. He wasn’t ready to give that up.
“When I first came here, I hated it, and I was mad at my stepdaughter for putting me here,” Richards recalled.
He arrived at Harmony at Kent on Veterans Day, Nov. 11, 2025, following a hospitalization and six weeks of rehabilitation.
“I didn’t think I would be ready for this kind of life till I hit 85, not 75,” he said.
But the man who reluctantly arrived in a wheelchair has discovered something unexpected. Assisted living hasn’t meant the end of his independence. In many ways, it has helped him reclaim it.
Today, Richards walks regularly, dances with his neighbors, encourages other residents and enjoys friendships that have transformed his daily life.
When living alone became a risk
Before moving to Harmony, Richards spent much of his time in a recliner watching television.
“In my house I did no exercising,” he said. “I would get up and open the back door to let the dog out — that was my exercise.”
His increasingly sedentary lifestyle contributed to mobility challenges, and several falls made living alone dangerous.
Once, after striking his head, he lost consciousness and awoke to his dog licking his face. Another time, he slid out of bed and couldn’t reach his telephone to call for help.
His stepdaughter recognized that something needed to change.
“She wanted to know that I was safe at home. I was no longer safe at home,” Richards acknowledged.
Leaving his house and giving up his car were difficult decisions. But the move ultimately provided something he had been missing: a safer environment where he could concentrate on getting stronger.
Determined to walk again
Richards arrived at Harmony using a wheelchair, but he had no intention of staying in it.
“My main goal then was to get out of the wheelchair and have somebody take it away,” he said.
He began walking daily, setting goals and pushing himself to improve.
Eventually, he graduated to a walker and then to a rollator, a wheeled walking aid.
“I called my buddy up and I said, ‘Get this wheelchair out of here.'”
Richards credits his progress to determination and the support of therapy professionals. He participates in physical therapy with Powerback three times a week and initially received occupational therapy to regain everyday skills.
Today, he independently showers, dresses and manages his personal needs.
“My stubbornness — that’s what it is,” he said. “If I set a goal, I’m going to reach that goal one way or the other.”
His next goal is to walk without the rollator.
Discovering the power of friendship
While Richards takes pride in his physical progress, he says the greatest surprise has been the friendships he’s developed.
“I’ve made a lot of friends here, a lot of friends,” he said. “I love to talk. I have no problem talking to people that I just meet about anything.”
He has become a familiar personality in the community, sometimes dancing before entering the dining room simply to make his neighbors laugh.
When live music is offered, Richards is often among the first to dance.
He especially enjoys dancing with residents who use wheelchairs, something he learned through more than 25 years of involvement with the American Legion.
When someone tells him they can’t dance because they’re in a wheelchair, he has a ready answer.
“Don’t worry about it. I know what to do.”
The experience brings joy to everyone.
“Basically, I made their day, and it made mine because they were happy and I was happy,” he said.
But friendship also means having someone nearby during difficult moments.
After a close friend at Harmony died, another resident noticed Richards’ sadness at breakfast and sat with him.
“She wanted to know what was wrong,” he recalled.
When he asked how she knew, the woman explained that she could see the pain on his face.
“Yes, they connect and they care,” Richards said.
Independence doesn’t mean doing everything alone
Another important benefit has been help managing his medications.
Richards takes 17 pills throughout the day. Before moving, he sometimes forgot doses despite using multiple pill organizers.
At Harmony, staff members manage his medication schedule, removing a responsibility that had become difficult.
He still makes decisions, sets personal goals and takes care of himself. But assistance with medications allows him to concentrate on enjoying life and improving his health.
He also encourages other residents to remain active.
Watching one neighbor progress from a wheelchair to a walker and then a rollator brought him tremendous satisfaction.
“It makes my heart feel so good to see him using that rollator,” he said.
A different picture of successful aging
For many families, the decision to move a loved one into assisted living is accompanied by uncertainty and guilt.
There is often a fear that leaving a longtime home means sacrificing independence, dignity or happiness.
Richards’ experience offers a different perspective.
At home, he was increasingly isolated, physically inactive and struggling with his health. Today, he has support when he needs it, opportunities to stay active and friendships that give meaning to his days.
Not every senior will experience the same transformation, and assisted living isn’t the right choice for everyone. But for Richards, the combination of support, encouragement and community has made a meaningful difference.
He still remembers how angry he was when he arrived.
“Now, I don’t mind being here at all,” he said.
The man who once believed assisted living was a place for people much older than himself is now dancing, making friends and encouraging others to live more actively.
For caregivers considering what comes next for someone they love, his story offers a reminder: Sometimes, the best way to preserve independence isn’t to keep everything the same. It’s to create the opportunity for a better quality of life.

Featured resident: Michael Richards, Harmony at Kent assisted living community.
For caregivers: When evaluating senior living options, consider safety, medication assistance, opportunities for physical activity, social connections and the independence residents can maintain.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC legal aid groups sue over lawmakers’ redirection of millions in funding
text:
The North Carolina General Assembly building in Raleigh. (Photo: Rachel Crumpler/NC Health News)Three North Carolina legal aid organizations are suing state legislative leaders over a budget provision that redirects millions of dollars from programs that provide low-income residents with free civil legal services to attorneys who represent people who cannot afford a lawyer in criminal cases.
“The $15 million per year that has been diverted from community legal aid is less than five one hundredths of one percent of the overall North Carolina state budget,” the Charlotte Center for Legal Advocacy wrote in a statement about the lawsuit. “But it means so much to veterans, survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, and human trafficking, disaster victims, and others who have been the recipients of civil legal services from these funds, as ordered by the NC Supreme Court.”
Charlotte Center for Legal Advocacy, Pisgah Legal Services and Legal Aid of North Carolina filed the lawsuit this past week against the state, House Speaker Destin Hall (R-Granite Falls), Senate leader Phil Berger (R-Eden) and others. They contend that the General Assembly overstepped its constitutional authority in redirecting the funds with its budget provision that changed how money that’s generated through the state’s Interest on Lawyers’ Trust Accounts program, known as IOLTA, can be used.
The lawsuit also challenged restrictions that could prevent legal aid organizations from receiving remaining IOLTA funding based on advocacy or other work they perform or have performed in the past — even when they have used money from other sources. The organizations argue those provisions violate free speech protections under the U.S. and North Carolina constitutions.
After NC lawmakers pull plug on civil legal aid, nonprofits are left searching for solutions

The case is the latest development in a fight over a funding source that has supported underserved people’s ability to defend themselves in civil court in North Carolina for decades — and one that legal aid providers say has become particularly important in western North Carolina as residents recover two years after Hurricane Helene.
From civil legal aid to criminal defense
IOLTA doesn’t rely on state tax dollars. The program collects interest generated by certain client funds that attorneys are required to temporarily hold in trust accounts. For example, it includes interest accrued on the money held in escrow for clients while loans and liens are paid off, or during real estate transactions. The North Carolina Supreme Court first established the program on a voluntary basis in 1983 and made participation mandatory in 2007.
Under the program, the money has been distributed by the North Carolina State Bar’s IOLTA program to organizations that provide civil legal assistance and to other programs that support the administration of justice.
Lawmakers froze IOLTA grantmaking for the 2025-26 fiscal year amid concerns from Republican legislators about oversight of the program and the perceived political advocacy of some organizations receiving grants. The organizations and use of funds were the center of an investigative hearing held by the House Select Committee and Oversight and Reform in October 2025.
The budget passed this summer went further. In it, lawmakers redirected IOLTA revenue received beginning July 1, 2025, to the state’s Private Assigned Counsel Fund, which pays for private attorneys appointed to represent people who cannot afford attorneys in criminal cases.
Money IOLTA received before July 1, 2025, remains available for grants for programs designed to improve the administration of justice, subject to the legislature’s new eligibility restrictions. The program can distribute up to $2.5 million from that remaining pool each fiscal year until it is depleted. (The complaint outlines $2 million but a technical correction to the budget has updated the number to $2.5 million.)
The three organizations are among six that have received more than a million dollars in the past 10 years, according to a report given by Rep. Harry Warren to the House Select Committee on Oversight and Reform. With Legal Aid of North Carolina receiving $22,066,243, Pisgah Legal Services receiving $4,517,810 and Charlotte Center for Legal Advocacy at $3,182,310 in that same time frame.
The lawsuit argues the General Assembly lacked the authority to make that change. The legal aid organizations contend that the regulation of attorneys falls within the judicial branch’s constitutional authority and that lawmakers effectively overrode the state Supreme Court’s 2007 order establishing the mandatory IOLTA program. They are asking the court to declare the budget provision unconstitutional and block its enforcement.
The lawsuit’s second claim challenges the restrictions placed on organizations seeking money from the remaining IOLTA pool. Those restrictions can make an organization ineligible based on its provision of certain immigration services, services related to gender-affirming care or forms of public advocacy. The legal aid organizations argue that the restrictions penalize them for constitutionally protected activities even when they use other money — not IOLTA funding — to perform that work.
North Carolina is the only state in the nation diverting IOLTA funds away from their intended use, according to the lawsuit.
Scrutiny before the funding shift
Lawmakers froze new grants from July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026, while the House Oversight committee examined the program. During the oversight hearing last October, Republican lawmakers questioned the IOLTA board’s grantmaking and raised concerns about organizations getting funding even as they were separately engaging in political advocacy.
Committee chair Harry Warren (R-Salisbury) characterized some recipients as groups with “leftist ideologies” and said lawmakers wanted to examine how the IOLTA board selected organizations for funding.
Rep. Grant Campbell (R-Concord) questioned whether prohibiting IOLTA dollars themselves from funding lobbying went far enough. Because money is fungible, Campbell argued, funding an organization’s legal work could free up its other resources for political advocacy.
NC House, Senate vote to freeze use of legal fund that goes to aid low-income residents

IOLTA Executive Director Mary Irvine told lawmakers that grant recipients are already prohibited from using IOLTA money for lobbying or political activity. Nevertheless, the North Carolina State Bar had considered additional restrictions on organizations engaged in grassroots lobbying, Peter Bolar, executive director of the North Carolina State Bar told lawmakers at the time.
During that hearing, lawmakers learned that IOLTA was not funded with taxpayer dollars and that the Supreme Court created the program using its authority to regulate the practice of law in North Carolina — an issue now at the center of the lawsuit’s separation of powers claim.
Some lawmakers also raised concerns about what the freeze was doing to certain legal services, such as domestic violence and human trafficking victim services. They questioned whether some money could be released for Legal Aid who provides aid in those two areas while continuing to investigate other grants.
An April 2026 audit commissioned by lawmakers, and completed by the office of Republican State Auditor Dave Boliek, found that IOLTA’s grants complied with eligibility requirements but faulted the program for inadequate oversight after the money was awarded. Auditors said IOLTA did not independently verify enough of grantees’ reported spending and outcomes to provide reasonable assurance that roughly $30.3 million was used as intended.
The State Bar noted in its response that the audit did not identify any instance of a grantee misappropriating or misusing funds. The auditor recommended stronger monitoring and independent verification of spending and outcomes.
The General Assembly seemed to ultimately choose a different course, redirecting the future IOLTA revenue entirely.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
What the funding loss means for Helene recovery
For Pisgah Legal Services, which serves 18 western North Carolina counties, the funding change comes as the region continues its recovery from Hurricane Helene two years later.
The organization got more than $1.8 million in IOLTA funding during the last full grant cycle before the freeze, according to the lawsuit. That included a $700,000 special grant for legal needs created by Helene.
Jackie Kiger, executive director of Pisgah Legal Services, said IOLTA represented roughly 10 percent to 15 percent of the organization’s budget and supported work ranging from housing and public benefits appeals, to domestic violence and disaster recovery.
“Our budget is personnel. Essentially, it is the people,” Kiger said in an interview when the budget was passed in July.
Pisgah receives hundreds of calls every week from people seeking help across its service area, Kiger said. Losing IOLTA funding ultimately means fewer attorneys and advocates available to take those cases.
“It’s less people we can serve — that’s the truth of it. We have to maintain our staff, and we need our funding in order to do that,” Kiger said.
“Nonprofits face funding challenges frequently, and certainly, these last couple of years have been the hardest. But what I emphasize for Pisgah is that we have been through the hurricane. In addition to all the other challenges that you face as a nonprofit, we have really been a resource to our community,” she continued.
The lawsuit estimates Pisgah will serve at least 3,500 fewer people each year as a result of the IOLTA changes.
Kiger, who is an attorney and social worker, said she sees that loss of legal services as a public health issue.
IOLTA funding has supported work aimed at keeping people housed, helping survivors of intimate partner violence and child abuse, securing public benefits and protecting household income — problems often described as social determinants of health.
Those needs became even more acute after Helene. Some of the first sources of funding support for Hurricane Helene recovery came from the state’s IOLTA fund to Pisgah Legal Services and to Legal Aid of North Carolina, according to Kiger.
Pisgah has helped residents with FEMA claims and appeals, housing problems, insurance disputes, scams and other legal problems created or exacerbated by the storm.
Kiger said the organization handled “hundreds and hundreds” of FEMA appeals after Helene.
“We’ve met people who have yet to receive any assistance or know where the assistance was in the last couple of months, and that to me is very compelling. There’s a lot of folks that still haven’t been reached, and we need the funding and the people to be able to reach them,” Kiger said.
The problems have continued as western North Carolina rebuilds. Pisgah has encountered renters living with mold and water damage after temporary repairs, homeowners struggling with insurance claims and older adults targeted by scammers, Kiger said.
“Long-term recovery with people who’ve lost their homes, their resources, income, or who’ve been impacted in other ways from Helene — that is also at stake,” Kiger said.
Pisgah appealed directly to legislators representing western North Carolina in July, explaining those stakes in an email sent to what she said she believed was every member of the western North Carolina delegation. The email outlined Pisgah’s work and warned about the consequences of losing IOLTA.
“The people most affected would be your constituents,” Kiger wrote.
Kiger told NC Health News she heard back from some lawmakers, but not all. She did not say which legislators responded.
During floor debate over the budget, Sen. Julie Mayfield, (D-Asheville), raised similar concerns. She pointed specifically to the roughly $2 million Pisgah stood to lose and the $700,000 that had supported Helene recovery.
“Who is going to help those people now?” Mayfield asked.
That question may now be answered by the courts.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Your Weekly Michigan Political Brief
text:
Illustration by States Newsroom 3rd Quarter Fundraising
U.S. Senate
Abdul El-Sayed more than tripled the fundraising haul of his Republican challenger, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-White Lake), for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat. Online records show El-Sayed raised $30,659,157 in the reporting period from July 16 to Sept. 30, while Rogers brought in $9,662,538. Despite that, Rogers’ campaign maintains a nearly $3 million cash on hand advantage: $6,527,471 to $3,792,203.
 
Democratic congressional challengers outraise Republican incumbents
Callie Barr, Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 1st Congressional District, outraised incumbent U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watermeet). Online records show Barr raised $725,371 in the reporting period from July 16 to Sept. 30, nearly double Bergman’s haul of $395,839. Barr’s campaign reported $768,511 cash on hand to Bergman’s $563,458.
State Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo), Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 4th Congressional District, outraised incumbent U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township). Online records show McCann raised $1,690,688 in the reporting period from July 16 to Sept. 30, while Huizenga brought in $1,273,480. However, Huizenga’s campaign still led in cash on hand over McCann: $1,856,768 to $1,320,322.
William Lawrence, Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, outraised incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). Online records show Lawrence raised $2,545,611 in the reporting period from July 16 to Sept. 30, nearly $1 million more than Barrett’s $1,584,553. However, Barrett maintains a more than $1.3 million cash on hand advantage over Lawrence: $2,362,085 to $1,033,485.
 
Endorsements
 Bend the Arc: Jewish Action, the nation’s largest domestic-focused progressive Jewish advocacy organization, announced its endorsement for Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate in Michigan. El-Sayed was also endorsed by Serious About Safety PAC.
The congressional campaign of State Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo), the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 4th Congressional District, was endorsed by the League of Conservation Voters Action Fund, the Sierra Club, and the Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition Political Action Committee.
Mental Health PAC announced its endorsement of Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, for governor.

name: Mississippi Today
title: SpaceX ‘pinky promises’ no bad impacts for Louisiana locals — then forced to backtrack
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
PECAN ISLAND, La. – At the front of a dimly lit cafeteria, half a dozen SpaceX high-level managers sat before a photo of a rocket. 
Facing them sat the residents of Pecan Island — fishers and hunters, many of whom could trace their family’s presence here back generations.
Mark Soltys, principal launch engineer, began telling the crowd about SpaceX’s advances in aerospace technology: “Only SpaceX is demonstrating reusability,” Soltys said. With Starship, he said, “you’re actually increasing the performance, but also lowering the cost to send something to space by multiple orders of magnitude — yes, sir?”
Craig Pitre, a retired welder sitting in the front row, had raised his hand with a question.
“I don’t think too many of us are worried about the flagship rocket and recoverability,” Pitre told Soltys. “What we are all [worried about] is the ecological damage.” He continued, “All this stuff goes out and it’s going to pollute the waters. I mean, is there going to be any accountability for anything? That’s mostly what we are concerned about.”
Craig Pitre, a retired welder, interrupted SpaceXreps to tell them that locals are not worried about rocket recoverability. He said, “We are worried about ecological damage.” Credit: Gus Bennett/The Lens
For the next two hours, residents peppered SpaceX representatives with questions about the incoming impacts of the company’s planned spaceport. Will they be able to stay in their homes? Will it kill off the wildlife? Will it worsen flooding and endanger their lives?
SpaceX reps repeatedly tried to reassure those present that the massive project would have no negative impact on their lives whatsoever. But they also were unable to answer many of the questions the residents posed. And in at least two instances, SpaceX reps were forced to backtrack, as locals held the promises up against the sheer, unprecedented scale of the planned rocket launches. 
SpaceX announced plans this summer to build a $100 billion spaceport here on the fragile coast of Vermilion Parish. The company is planning to ramp up to 10,000 annual launches of its superheavy Starship at the Louisiana site, or 30 launches a day. The 300 or so permanent residents of this village will be the closest locals — only about six miles from the planned launch pads. 
The company’s goal, Soltys told the room, is “to make space life normal. You can go have lunch in orbit. You can go spend a weekend on the moon.”
Soltys didn’t mention that if those ambitions don’t pan out, the company can terminate its lease and agreement at any time for just $1,000, according to a copy of the PILOT lease agreement reviewed by The Lens.
Pecan Island residents were largely unmoved by the visions of lunch in orbit. After all: They live here, now, in Vermilion Parish, on Earth.
“You just explained the thrust and power,” Pitre pressed. “Well, there are consequences behind thrust and power.”
“Lil Mark” Broussard, who manages cattle on land abutting SpaceX’s planned spaceport, leaves a meeting with SpaceX reps held at Pecan Island School.  Credit: Gus Bennett/The Lens
At 30 launches a day, ‘temporary means nothing’
It is difficult to square the scale of SpaceX’s promises with the reality of Vermilion Parish today. Along the single two-lane road to the school, stands of cattle graze in the sun, and smoke billows up from sugarcane fields.
SpaceX had been tightlipped about the meeting. Residents were only alerted with a phone call a day or two before, and the late notice meant some couldn’t attend.
About 150 people crowded into the room, representing around half the village’s permanent residents. Before The Lens arrived, at least two Louisiana residents had been asked to leave by the Vermilion Parish Sheriff’s Office as they were not local to Pecan Island.
Early in the meeting, Katy Groom, SpaceX’s director of environmental regulatory affairs, told those gathered that “the actual launch infrastructure is very small.” SpaceX will be building across about one-third of their 125,000 acres — land leased from the local development board after the state acquired it from Exxon through a lawsuit. The company’s construction will still sprawl across 40,000 acres, nearly three times the size of Manhattan Island.
Soon after, questions started to arise.
“Am I still going to be able to get down there to my property?” asked “Lil Mark” Broussard, about an hour into the meeting.
“Yeah, we’re not going to deny access to property,” a SpaceX rep replied immediately.
But they were soon forced to retract that promise.
Broussard was referring to a strip of land between the shoreline and the southern border of SpaceX’s property. He runs horses and manages cattle on the land. 
“We’re right in the middle. So am I still going to be able to go over there?” 
Soltys repeated, “We are not going to deny you access to land.”
“I’m going to hold you to that.”
The launch sites’ exact location is not yet known, but in SpaceX renderings they are in a row along the coast, the Starships towering above the land where Broussard keeps cattle. How could SpaceX guarantee unrestricted access to property so close to the proposed launchpads? For a few minutes, the meeting dissolved into worried crosstalk.
Soltys then acknowledged, “It’s likely that there is a point where access is restricted — ”
“But do you know where that point would be?” a woman called out.
“No ma’am,” said Soltys, and soon steered the conversation elsewhere: “Without SpaceX, China is very much ahead of America” in the space race, he went on.
But another resident soon asked for specifics about access: “How big is the exclusion zone when you actually fly the rocket?” the man asked. Exclusion zones temporarily prohibit people or vehicles from access during launches.
Ben Lancaster, SpaceX’s senior manager for government affairs in Texas, said the zone would extend three to five miles from the launch site. That means the exclusion zone would reach from the launch pads, to the shoreline and then beyond, into Gulf waters.
“If you’re launching that many times a day, then ‘temporary’ means nothing,” the man pointed out. “So if you have property between the Gulf and the [launch] pad — you say you’re not going to block access, but if you can exclude, and you’re launching that many times, then access essentially is blocked. Correct?”
Soltys hesitated, then conceded: “Correct,” he said.
“Okay. Question answered. Access is blocked.”
SpaceX will ‘figure out’ bird migration
Soltys’ admission suggests that the exclusion zone will extend into fishing waters, which many depend on for their livelihoods.
“Immediately off the coast here, within a quarter mile or so, is seasonally one of the best shrimping industries in the state, as well as crabs,” said a fisherman. SpaceX’s project is “going to severely affect some of the commercial fishing industry over here.”
Martin Broussard, raised on Pecan Island with his 13 siblings, pulls a crab trap out of the water. SpaceX’s exclusion zone, which temporarily prohibits people or vehicles from access during launches, would extend into fishing waters, which many residents depend on for their livelihoods. Credit: Courtesy Brooke Broussard
Vermilion Parish also sits at the base of the Mississippi River Flyway, a crucial migration route used by millions of shorebirds. After a 600-mile nonstop flight across the Gulf, this is the first land many of them see.
“What are y’all going to do about the Mississippi Flyway?” a resident asked a few minutes after Soltys’ about face on property access. “I’m not talking about planes, here, I’m talking about birds.”
“A big part of that we think is addressed through those required mitigations,” began Owen McDonough, SpaceX’s senior manager of government affairs. McDonough previously worked as an advisor for Chevron, and before that, was a director at the American Petroleum Institute.
“How you going to detour the birds?” the resident pressed.
Groom, SpaceX’s director of environmental regulatory affairs, began to explain that the buffer zone around the launch site — land that an outside biologist described as one of the best managed wetlands in Louisiana — will still be “a flourishing place for all the species.” She added, “The birds will momentarily flush, but they return.”
“How can they return in 30 [rocket] flights a day?”
Groom hesitated. “That is — that is one thing that we will have to figure out,” Groom conceded. “We don’t know what’s going to happen at 30 flights.”
Residents muttered in frustration. “BS, BS, BS,” said one man quietly.
“What happens if the birds don’t come back?” another asked.
Groom answered, “We’re going to go figure out where they are.”
A representative of SpaceX speaks to the audience in Pecan Island. Credit: Gus Bennett/The Lens
Flood protection or higher risks?
Other questions revolved around water. An employee of Pecan Island Waterworks asked whether the massive spaceport would be using the same aquifer that supplies the village.
SpaceX didn’t have a clear answer for that either.
“Right now we are obviously very much in the design phase,” said Groom, though she added that SpaceX recycles most of the water it uses. Groom did not pledge to not use the aquifer, but said, “If we are, then we will figure out how it does not impact your guys’ source.”
Talk then turned to flooding. When SpaceX replaces wetlands with launch pads, marsh will no longer be there to dissipate the dangers of storm surge.
“Are y’all having any plans to make some levee system that would protect Pecan Island people?” a man asked. Or would flood protection only surround the company’s interests — thereby worsening flooding in their homes? 
A barrier to protect SpaceX would “leave the far east and the far west exposed to the water going around what you’re building,” a woman chimed in. “So the ask would be to protect the entire island, and not just divert water into one side.”
McDonough, the senior manager of government affairs, later promised that SpaceX would not jeopardize the nearby lock system.
“No, I’m not talking about that,” a resident interrupted. “I’m talking about a hurricane coming in and going over locks. I mean, y’all are going to be protected with a 20-, 30-foot wall, but [the water] can go around, hit Rollover [Bayou] and come running down the road” to Pecan Island. 
That’s what happened in 2005’s Hurricane Rita, when 12 feet of storm surge damaged most of the community’s structures. Will SpaceX surround themselves with a levee that endangers Pecan Island?
The SpaceX rep said they would be building “to those anticipated storm conditions.”
But the resident pressed again: “Are you building it for y’all? Or are you building it for us?”
“We don’t have that complete design figured out,” said Brandon Conroy, senior environmental regulatory engineer at SpaceX.
The following day, Conroy applied for a state permit, showing SpaceX’s plans to build a wharf and access road to start construction. These first steps alone would result in the loss of almost 400 acres of marsh, according to the application, which did not yet address flood protection plans.
Explosions and debris are ‘developmental growing pains’
Many were worried about how the noise and vibration from launches will damage their homes.
SpaceX candidly told the residents, yes, you’ll hear and feel the launches.
“It’s going to be loud,” acknowledged Groom. People inside their homes will feel a rumble, but they shouldn’t worry: “If somebody slams the door, your house does move, right?” she said. “So when that rumble happens from the rocket, it usually lasts like a minute, and you will hear it. And hopefully, it’s exciting to you.”
But some had already heard otherwise. About 80 people filed a federal lawsuit in April over alleged damage to their home caused by Starship launches in Texas. Reported damage includes cracked foundations, warped floors and burst water pipes. One plaintiff told Reuters that the foundation needs $100,000 worth of repairs.
SpaceX reps dismissed those concerns out of hand.
“We’ve seen no property damage whatsoever. There’s certainly lawsuits — you know, Mr. Musk has a big target on his back,” said Lancaster, referring to company founder Elon Musk. “Lots of people like to get headlines.”
Debris from launches in Texas has also been documented in marshes and wetlands. SpaceX described debris as “developmental growing pains” and pledged to pick it up. 
Ultimately, none of the promises that SpaceX reps made in the room that afternoon were binding, as one local pointed out.
“If nothing’s going to happen to our homes, why did our governor put in place that we can’t sue SpaceX for damaging our homes?” a woman asked.
She was referring to recent legislation in Louisiana that means SpaceX cannot be held liable for “noise, sonic booms, overflight, vibration, light, heat, exhaust, smoke, odor, visual intrusion, temporary access restrictions, or any other disturbance.” SpaceX can only be held liable for injuries caused by falling debris if it “exceeds the normal risk” that goes with space flight.
Lancaster again dismissed concerns, saying that law was meant to stop “litigious trial attorneys who really want to make a buck.”
But Hollie Girouard, who lives part-time on a road between Pecan Island and the planned spaceport, soon asked again. “Why is there no protection written in for residents?” she said. “We’re going into this trusting people that we do not know, and [you’re] saying you’re going to pinky promise me.”
“What I can’t do is speak to anything on the legislation. I don’t have any control — I just can’t answer that,” said Groom. It was in fact SpaceX that pushed for the legislation as a condition of their arrival, per reporting by the Times-Picayune.
Groom told residents they could send SpaceX an email “if you feel that there is damage caused by the rockets.”
Residents leave the SpaceX meeting at Pecan Island School. Credit: Gus Bennett/The Lens
Girouard, like some others, left the meeting discouraged.
“I don’t think anyone was satisfied hearing that there would be an online complaint form instead of protections in the first place,” she told The Lens.
“I’m still in shock and I’m angry because of the way this deal was done,” said Brooke Broussard, a distant cousin of Lil Mark. She was especially frustrated by SpaceX’s insistence that the project wouldn’t harm wildlife. “They’re delusional. They know nothing about animals or nature. Or they do, and they’re just playing dumb,” she said. “It just all felt like such a farce.”
Broussard said members of her family “are in great despair.” The wetlands here are already damaged by the oil and gas industry.
“Can we learn from our mistakes, and maybe not pump concrete into that so-sensitive marsh that is absolutely teeming with life?” she said, her voice breaking. “Teeming with life.”
