name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Educational Television Commission member resigns
text:
Tijuanna Adetunji (seated a long table, fifth from the left) and other members of the Alabama Education Television Commission listen to speakers during a meeting in Montgomery, Alabama on April 21, 2026. Adetunji has resigned from the commission, leaving just one of the members who served on the body last month. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Tijuanna Adetunji has resigned from the Alabama Educational Television Commission, leaving just one of the seven commission members who served on the board last month.
Gina Maiola, communications director for Gov. Kay Ivey confirmed Adetunji’s resignation Thursday afternoon but did not provide a reason. A request for further comment was left with Maiola Thursday afternoon.
Alabama Public Television Executive Director Wayne Reid said in a statement early Thursday evening Adetunji submitted her resignation letter last Thursday without explanation.
“With Tijuanna Adetunji’s resignation, the commission has experienced a complete turnover over the past twelve months,” Reid said. I have confidence that the Governor’s replacement appointment will bring another strong representative to the commission. APT will make an announcement once the appointment has been made. I look forward to working with the new commission and building on the exciting future ahead for Alabama Public Television.”
A message seeking comment was left with Adetunji  Thursday afternoon. According to the Alabama Public Television website, Ivey has not yet made a new appointment. Reid said APT is “hoping to hear something very soon (from Ivey) on the appointment.”
Adetunji served as the AETC’s Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District representative. She ran for the Alabama House of Representatives as a Republican in 2014 and as an independent candidate in 2018. Adetunji also ran for Montgomery City Council in 2015; she was not successful in the campaigns. 
Adetunji’s decision comes after Ivey removed five members from the commission earlier this month and after nearly a year of sometimes heated arguments among commissioners about maintaining affiliation with the Public Broadcasting Service.
Last October, then-commissioners Ferris Stephens and Les Barnett brought the idea to disaffilitate from PBS prompting public backlash from donors. In November, the commission voted to maintain PBS programming. Adetunji was not present for the November vote.
In September, the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority voted to fund a survey conducted by Cygnal, a polling firm that mainly works with Republican candidates, on Alabamians attitudes towards PBS. Adetunji voted against doing the survey.
The survey’s results showed 54% of viewers support APT continuing its PBS affiliation and 62% said they wanted public officials to stay out of programming decisions.
Adetunji leaves commissioner Logan Glass as the only member of the board to not be dismissed or removed over the last month.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: When it comes to Medicaid cuts in Kentucky, it’s always Groundhog Day
text:
Hundreds of Kentuckians with disabilities and their loved ones and advocates came to Frankfort and pleaded with elected officials to find a way to protect the services they receive through Medicaid waivers. July 17, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)Over the next few years, Kentucky is facing the largest Medicaid cuts in the program’s history. Starting in January, the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act will take Medicaid coverage away from many thousands of Kentuckians. Separately, state Medicaid cuts will go into effect in July unless the 2027 General Assembly restores funding to the program. And in January 2028, the OBBBA will begin lowering Medicaid payments to providers with reductions that will deepen over the following decade.
If allowed to occur, these perilous cuts will worsen Kentuckians’ health and well-being, increase burdensome medical debt, and cost providers and jobs including by putting 35 rural hospitals at risk of closure.
The cuts are the latest in a long series of threats. Medicaid has faced danger ever since the Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded the program in 2010 and became a political punching bag. But here’s the thing: time after time, in the face of organized public opposition, decision makers have halted major Medicaid rollbacks before the pain to communities began.
That tells us a lot about what’s at stake. And it shows why Kentuckians should urge federal and state lawmakers to stop harmful cuts yet again.
The push to cut Medicaid and repeal the ACA began as soon as the law passed. Republicans were unified in their opposition and rode the Tea Party wave in the 2010 midterms catalyzed in part by opposition to so-called Obamacare. Opponents demonized the ACA and capitalized on all it didn’t do to fix an ailing American health care system, while obscuring the good it did.
However, then-Governor Steve Beshear expanded Medicaid under the ACA in 2013, citing an obscure state law and acting right after the General Assembly had adjourned for the year. By the time the legislature reconvened, thousands of people were already gaining coverage and getting healthcare. Republicans controlled the state Senate and could have picked a fight over blocking Medicaid expansion and refusing the federal funds. But knowing that would be devastating to constituents and providers, they stood aside.
Nevertheless, rhetorical opposition to Obamacare continued throughout the 2010s — with the U.S. House voting over 50 times to overturn it — until Republicans took control of the Congress and the presidency with Donald Trump’s election in 2016. But even with a unified government, their effort to repeal the ACA failed with then-dying Senator John McCain’s famous “thumbs down” vote on the floor of the Senate. Though Republican leaders expressed disappointment at the loss, some no doubt felt relieved when tens of millions of Americans did not lose their health care.
Back in Kentucky, the legislature kept Medicaid expansion even after Republicans took full control of the legislature in 2016. Then-governor Matt Bevin attempted to establish paperwork requirements like are now in law from the OBBBA but lost in court and then in his re-election bid, in part due to his unpopular positions on health care, education and public employees. 
The legislature also tried to put in place similar barriers to Medicaid enrollment through four different bills in 2019, 2020, 2022, and 2025. All of them failed to pass or were largely stripped of their harmful measures after concerted opposition campaigns led by health advocates.
But after Trump was elected a second time with Republican majorities in Congress, lawmakers passed the OBBBA and its major cuts to Medicaid in 2025. Yet fearing backlash, the law was designed so the pain didn’t go into effect immediately. It pushed the paperwork barriers until after this year’s midterm elections and set the payment cuts to start a year later and grow gradually over time.
Most recently, the Kentucky General Assembly passed a budget in April that underfunded Medicaid by hundreds of millions of dollars compared to the executive branch forecast of costs. That forced Governor Beshear to put in place Medicaid payment cuts this summer. After an outcry from constituents and providers, he reversed course and made extraordinary appropriations to Medicaid that are likely outside his legal authority. Legislators chose not to sue, standing aside yet again and averting the pain that would result. 
It’s always Groundhog Day when it comes to Medicaid. We see repeated efforts to cut the program and create barriers to care. But after patients, providers and communities organize, lawmakers pull back from the brink.
Will this time be different? If so, we’ll finally witness the harm long feared by so many.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Data center moratorium bills stack up ahead of Virginia legislative session in January
text:
A data center in Prince William County, Va., one of over 680 of the facilities that are operational or planned in the commonwealth. State lawmakers have filed a slate of bills that would temporarily pause all data center development in the state. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Come January, state lawmakers will debate a slate of bills that would halt data center development, including one by Sen. Russett Perry, D-Loudoun, which recommends a three -year moratorium on building the high-powered digital warehouses.
Perry has filed Senate Bill 843 alongside Sen. Danica Roem, D-Prince William. It would block localities, the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) and the State Corporation Commission (SCC) from approving any data center building permits statewide from July 2027 until July 2030. 
The bill would also prevent the advance of distribution lines, on-site power, or related projects that  solely serve data centers during the same timeframe. 
“The people of Virginia just continue to be saturated, and it’s not just with data centers,” Perry said Thursday. “In my district in particular, it’s these 765 kilovolt transmission lines. People forget it’s not just the data center that might move next door to you. But it’s all the other things that come out from that.”
Virginia is home to nearly 400 data centers in operation,with over 280 planned and more proposed each year, according to Pew Research Center. 
The growing industry is tied to exploding energy demand as well as rising tensions in communities across all of the state over water use, noise levels and concerns about siting and loss of character in rural areas. 
Roem is also filing a separate moratorium bill that is more closely tied to the interconnection queue – the list of large-load customers, namely data centers, that have requested power from Dominion Energy, which the utility is obligated to serve. 
Currently, Dominion has about 25,000 megawatts of power assigned to projects with an energized date, and an additional 75,000 MW will go to projects that don’t yet have power up dates. The utility says it will take about seven years for the customers in the queue to get power, a wait that starts when the facilities are added to the queue.
Roem’s bill would block new data centers from being approved statewide until that queue is energized and the necessary infrastructure is built to do so.
“Until the industry and Dominion Energy deal with the hundreds of data centers already awaiting power, they shouldn’t be siting more data centers or building more transmission lines that wouldn’t exist if not but for the data centers,” Roem said this week.
In the House, Del. Irene Shin, D-Fairfax, proposed a bill that was continued from the 2026 session that would block localities from approving zoning and permitting requests until “the fulfillment of all pending requests for interconnection to distribution service by an electric utility customer that is a data center” or July 2028, whichever comes first.
Across the aisle, Sen. Glen Sturtevant, R-Chesterfield, has been calling for a data center moratorium for months. He plans to file his own version to be debated during the session.
“I’m hearing it more and more from my constituency that they’ve checked their electric bill and their energy usage from last month versus the same month last year, and they are shocked at how much their electric bills have gone up,” Sturtevant said Thursday.
Virginia senators request special session to act on ’deeply alarming’ groundwater report

“One of the major driving factors is the proliferation of the data centers, and the costs of their power generation in transmission being subsidized by Virginia ratepayers in their electric bills,” he added.
Lawmakers that represent areas of the state east of Interstate 95 — where a recent groundwater report showed that water availability would start to decline in the near future if the state doesn’t change course — have criticized how much water data centers’ non-closed loop cooling systems use.
The evaporative cooling systems can use hundreds of millions of gallons of water annually. 
The groundwater report led to Perry and Sen. Richard Stuart, R-King George, to call on Gov. Abigail Spanberger to initiate a special session to pass policies that address the water concerns before the January regular session. 
Spanberger denied their request.
Language in the budget lawmakers adopted earlier this year also directed DEQ to conduct a study and identify groundwater scarcity areas, especially in the eastern coastal regions of the commonwealth. The report, due this month, will also detail how non-closed loop systems can be retrofitted to be more water efficient.
However, the closed-loop systems still take an initial large batch of water and use more energy  than the evaporative systems. 
The bills represent a possible shift in the legislature, which rejected most bills that would have taken major action on data centers, including a proposal by Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Newport News, to end sales and use tax exemption for the industry. 
Debates over the measure delayed the budget for months, with lawmakers opting to preserve data centers’ tax break and add a new tax for the facilities that is expected to generate $1.2 billion over the biennium.
Sturtevant signaled that he hopes to reopen the debate about the sales and use tax exemption in the coming session.
 Workers, data centers oppose moratorium bills

The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW), a prominent workers union that has staunchly advocated against legislation that would restrict data center growth, are already pushing back against the new bills.
Jobs in manufacturing, electrical and construction have expanded in Virginia due to the data center industry, they said, and protecting them should take priority over shutting down data center development .
“I don’t think a moratorium is gonna pass because you’re taking out your tax base, you’re taking out your jobs,” said Don Slaiman, director of communications for IBEW Local 26. “(Lawmakers are) so proud of being number three in the CNBC poll. That would be eviscerated.”
The Data Center Coalition, a national group focused on advocating for policies on behalf of the industry, said data centers have invested $80.56 billion in Virginia and generated$5.34 billion in state and local taxes.
“Local or state moratoriums could deprive communities of the opportunity to compete for investment and jobs, jeopardize multibillion projects that are in development, and force jurisdictions to relinquish significant long-term economic investment, high-wage jobs, and critical tax revenue to neighboring states,” said Nicole Riley with the Data Center Coalition.
Spanberger presents slate of data center regulation proposals, puts first directives in motion

The plans for these bills come weeks after Spanberger revealed her data center policy framework. 
Much of her plan focuses on transparency in the permitting process by limiting nondisclosure agreements, assigning more transmission costs onto data centers, limiting on-site gas generation and other objectives. To be enacted, most of the measures must be translated into legislation that the General Assembly will have to pass. 
“I think the vast majority of people here in Virginia want a comprehensive framework and guardrails put around data centers before we continue to just keep approving more of them,” Perry said. “We already have more data centers than anywhere else in the world. I don’t know how we can responsibly continue to just keep approving more.”
Like all legislation, lawmakers’ data center moratorium bills must win approval from both chambers and the governor to be made law.
The General Assembly’s regular session begins on Jan. 13.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Transgender care for young patients remains on hold at Virginia hospitals
text:
The Richmond Children's Hospital. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury)Children’s hospitals in Virginia have kept transgender services for patients younger than 19 on hold for more than a year following President Donald Trump’s January 2025 executive order. 
They include the Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU, Norfolk-based Children’s Hospital of the King’s Daughters and Charlottesville-based UVA Health Children’s Hospital. 
Trump’s order said that the U.S. will “not fund, sponsor, promote, assist or support” what he labeled “destructive” procedures. 
Transgender services for minors typically include counseling and mental health support, along with treatments such as puberty blockers or hormone therapy. Surgeries on minors are extremely rare and involve patients  ages 15 to 17 years, a Harvard study found. 
Trump’s administration also recently adopted a rule prohibiting young enrolled in Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program from having transgender services covered by their insurance. 
The president and his political allies have described transgender services for young people as ”mutilation” or “junk science,” while LGBTQ+ advocates have described the services as essential to transgender people’s well-being. 
“I am heartbreakingly aware of the challenges that you are now facing and will do all that I can to support you and your family as we monitor this situation and comply with applicable law,” CHKD president Amy Sampson wrote in a letter to affected patients and their families last year announcing compliance with Trump’s order. 
The order threatened to withhold federal funding from hospitals that continued to offer transgender care to young people, prompting the hospitals to pause those services. A multi-state lawsuit filed inFebruary 2025 has since been tied up in court. 
A judge temporarily ordered the administration to continue funding hospitals that offered this care to young people, but the administration has since appealed. 
With the case still active, hospitals remain in limbo over whether to resume those services. 
The case, led by the American Civil Liberties Union, includes Virginia residents Kristin Chapman and her daughter, identified in the filing as “W.G.” Chapman’s family moved to Virginia from Tennessee following that state’s 2023 ban on transgender care for minors to ensure that W.G. could continue to receive services. 
“I thought Virginia would be a safe place for me and my daughter. Instead, I am heartbroken, tired, and scared,” Chapman said in a statement. 
The lawsuit alleges that Trump’s order discriminates on the basis of sex and disability and exceeds the president’s authority.
Va. lawmakers, Spanberger grapple with loss of federal healthcare funds for trans youth 

Though the administration has appealed the previous ruling, ACLU lawyer Joshua Stryker emphasized that hospitals could continue to treat the order as ineffective in the meantime. 
“There is absolutely nothing in federal law preventing hospitals from providing this lawful care,” he said. 
The next court date is set for Dec. 11 in the U.S. Court of Appeals in the Fourth Circuit. 
Opposing transgender minors’ access to sports or healthcare has been a pillar of Republican campaigns and legislative agendas in recent years. 
The matter was n a flagship issue for Republican gubernatorial candidate Winsome Earle-Sears in 2025, when she lost to now-governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat. Spanberger has since quietly repealed a state rule from former Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration that would have limited transgender students’s participation in sports or use of certain facilities. 
Citing Trump’s election in 2024 amid anti-trans rhetoric, a recent memo from the American Principles Project shared with members of the press declares that Democrats are “out of step on transgender issues.” 
It called highlighting the parties’ differing stances a “smart strategy” in this year’s midterm elections. 
Though transgender policy debates have not figured prominently  in Virginia’s congressional races so far this year, the uncertain legal landscape continues to affect hospitals’ policies. 
ACLU of Virginia attorney Wyatt Rolla said the government should not be involved in families’ private healthcare decisions. 
“Decisions about healthcare, including for transgender youth, should be made by families and their doctors — not the government,” they said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger’s energy plan dazzles – and disappoints
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger unveils her administration's energy plan on Oct. 1, 2026 in Richmond. The plan models how the state can meet rising energy demands and achieve clean its energy goals. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s energy plan, released October 1, is a marvel of earnestness and hard work. Anyone plowing through its 180 pages of text and appendices can’t help but be impressed with the level of detail and the thoroughness of its coverage.
The Department of Energy even acquired the same modeling software used by Dominion Energy and ran its own scenarios. And unlike Dominion, the administration took the goals of the Virginia Clean Economy Act seriously.
Spanberger’s energy plan keys in on clean energy to meet growing demand and VCEA goals

It’s an impressive effort, and the result surely has to be considered the new gold standard for Virginia energy plans, which have seldom even met statutory requirements. Take a bow, Virginia Energy staff and chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond; you deserve it.
And yet. 
If the plan’s central purpose is to demonstrate that Virginia doesn’t need to tamp down the growth of data centers to preserve energy affordability for residents and achieve the decarbonization goals of the VCEA, it fails. 
The plan acknowledges that “rapid data center load growth is driving grid infrastructure constraints and higher costs.” Yet that unconstrained load growth is subjected to scrutiny only as to the accuracy of the forecasts, not to consider throttling back the growth. 
Indeed, the plan hypothesizes that data centers will spend more on power than utilities will spend on infrastructure, an assertion the governor repeated last week at the Virginia Clean Energy Summit in Richmond.
From this calculation flowed her equally questionable argument that a future with more data centers will mean lower costs – the reverse of what the plan admits is happening now. 
Providing enough clean energy cheaply to meet this load is a really hard circle to square, though the plan describes a few pathways heading in the right direction.
It identifies a lengthy list of ways to eliminate energy waste and smooth demand spikes, many of which have already been set in motion with 2026 legislation. (There is certainly room for improvement; the web site WalletHub just ranked Virginia 35th out of 48 states on energy efficiency.)
The plan also makes a strong case for energy storage and distributed generation as a way to harness private investment and make the grid more efficient, secure and resilient. 
It recognizes the huge potential for solar on public buildings, currently held hostage to the interconnection barriers Dominion Energy erected. It also calls out Dominion for the high price tag on its clean energy projects and proposes a state-led renewables marketplace to bring the power of competition to bear on purchasing. And it suggests interesting interim solutions like fuel cells that could replace dirty diesel generators at data centers.
Certainly, it could go further. The governor could, for example, throw her weight behind a stronger residential building code and creation of an independent energy utility like Vermont’s to consolidate programs and maximize energy savings for residents. 
She could also heed the calls of lawmakers and residents who want a moratorium on data center development.
The problem remains that all the efficiency, distributed generation and grid management in the world can’t get us out of the hole that data center demand is digging for us. We’re going to need a lot more generation, and if we also need it to be cheap and clean, we need a lot more utility-scale solar.
That brings me to my criticism of the energy modeling done by Virginia Energy’s staff, apart from its failure to include a scenario that limits data center growth. It imposes a cap on the amount of solar energy that the model was allowed to choose to achieve least-cost pathways for meeting demand. Without this artificial cap, it’s safe to say, the model would have selected a lot more cheap-and-easy solar paired with storage.  
Doing so would have undercut a claim we are already hearing from Republicans, that if we would just leave climate and health costs out of the equation — and ignore turbine shortages, pipeline constraints, and fuel price volatility — building more fossil gas plants would come out as the cheapest option. A picture of what solar could do if we let it would rebut that argument.
That the model instead imposed a cap reveals Spanberger’s own ambivalence about utility solar. The administration takes it as a given that the current resistance to utility solar in many rural counties will persist even in the face of the declining farm income that makes solar one of the few lifelines available to struggling landowners. The plan mentions agrivoltaics approvingly but misses its transformational potential. 
The plan could have proposed education and incentives to bring solar and agriculture together for the mutual benefit of both. Instead, it treats utility-scale solar as a regrettable necessity we should minimize. It’s an odd capitulation to solar NIMBYs from a governor who barely acknowledges the far greater public hostility to data centers. 
Limiting utility-scale solar hamstrings the modeling effort. Even the addition of a lot more offshore wind, which is assumed to happen once President Donald Trump exits the stage, leaves us short of what’s needed to meet a massive increase in data center load. 
Unwilling to check the growth of data centers, committed to defending the VCEA and wary of expanding energy imports, Spanberger isn’t left with a lot of great options. So, like so many governors before her, she puts her faith in nuclear. 
Apparently, the best thing about the new small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) under development today is that they are still a long way from commercial viability. That excuses leaders from having to immediately grapple with the realities of cost, siting, safety, security and waste. People can just imagine SMRs will be the perfect power source. 
I am reminded of friends who joke that their retirement plan is winning the lottery. Fortunately, my friends know not to bank on it.
Spanberger proposes to bank on it, and to pass the cost of the lottery tickets on to the public. The energy plan has numerous suggestions for ways Virginia can help develop nuclear energy, all to be paid for by Virginia residents. 
The worst proposal involves revising our renewable portfolio standard to make new nuclear an eligible technology. It’s yet another blow to solar, which Virginia has already made more expensive to develop in a way no other state has done (looking at you, House Bill 206).  
The plan’s enthusiasm for nuclear even extends to conventional large light-water reactors. Recall that Dominion pulled the plug on its proposal for a third, 1500-MW light-water reactor at North Anna in 2017, when the total cost to ratepayers had hit $19 billion (about $26 billion in today’s dollars). There is a reason nuclear companies want their projects subsidized, and a reason the rest of us should be wary of being the ones doing it. 
Really, when you consider it, wouldn’t it be better just to slow the growth of data centers?

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Social Security cost of living adjustments must be protected
text:
The 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment announced Wednesday is slightly lower than September's 3.7% inflation rate. Most people feel they would need a 5 to 7% increase to keep up with inflation in a  new AARP poll. (Photo illustration by iStock/Getty Images Plus)A 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) announced Wednesday is welcome news for older Americans facing higher prices for everyday essentials like groceries, utilities and health care. But new AARP polling finds most people feel they would need a 5% to 7% increase just to keep up with inflation, which hit 3.7% in September.
Powered by spikes in energy prices, inflation surges to 3.7%

Beginning in 2027, the COLA will increase Social Security payments, on average, $900 a year or $75 a month.
AARP fought for and won automatic, yearly COLAs in 1972 because Americans needed reliable protection from rising prices. Before then, increasing Social Security payments required an act of Congress. That protection remains essential for the 248,674 people receiving Social Security here in Rhode Island.
Currently, Social Security is the foundation of retirement security for 185 million workers nationally who are contributing with every paycheck. At AARP, we will never stop fighting to protect Social Security for today’s retirees, their children and grandchildren.
Older Americans across the political spectrum expect Congress to protect this vital cost of living protection. In AARP’s recent poll of competitive Congressional districts, 85% of voters over 50 said they would be more likely to vote for candidates who would protect Social Security from cuts, including reducing the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
One in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes the COLA critically important. It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, health care and other everyday expenses. Yet special interests in Washington still want to weaken or eliminate the COLA, which would amount to cutting tens of thousands of dollars for middle-class seniors. But as AARP Chief Executive Officer Myechia Minter-Jordan emphasized this week, “We will not let that happen.”
Earlier this week, AARP’s Public Policy Institute (PPI) released this new analysis showing how proposals to change the COLA to an alternate measure of inflation would significantly reduce lifetime benefits. The analysis found:

Changing the COLA calculation to what’s called a “chained CPI” would mean a reduction in benefits that would compound over time, resulting in benefits 3.7% lower at age 75 and 9.2% lower at age 95 for a beneficiary claiming Social Security at age 62.


This change would mean a loss of approximately $17,500 for the average male retired worker and $13,400 for the average female retired worker who retired in 2001.


AARP has previously fought against such a change successfully. 

Even a modest reduction today in overall Social Security benefits, the PPI reports, could have significant consequences for Americans’ financial security, health, and overall well-being. The . The AARP survey released this week found:

About one-third of adults 50-plus might use savings faster (36%) or save less (32%).


People who are highly reliant on Social Security would be more likely to cut health services (41%) or delay medical care (25%).
More than one in five people reliant on Social Security (22%) would provide less financial help to families, and nearly as many highly reliant recipients would visit family less often (19%).

Social Security is the only inflation-protected source of income for most seniors in retirement, and AARP has long fought to protect the COLA and ensure that retirees get the full value of the benefits that they’ve earned throughout their careers. 
AARP will never stop fighting to protect and strengthen the Social Security you earned, including its COLAs.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Could data center opposition boost Democrats in Indiana House races?
text:
A campaign advertisement from Democrat Tiffany Stoner attacking Republican Rep. Becky Cash over data centers. (Screenshot)Democrats are looking to ride a wave of widespread opposition to big data center projects across the state as they aim to pick up seats in the Indiana House.
Data center worries are a prominent part of attacks against Republicans on affordability issues in several races targeted by Democrats this fall in their bid to break the two-thirds supermajority House Republicans have held since the 2012 elections.
Mail pieces and online advertisements from Democratic candidates use similar phrases, claiming Republicans “sold us out to data centers” and “gave data centers hundreds of millions.” The Democrats say they will “end data center deals we pay for.”
Republicans argue Democrats are distorting legislative votes and that local governments have the final say over allowing data center construction.
The GOP enters this year’s elections with a 70-30 House majority. But if the data center argument resonates with voters, Democrats could pick up at least the four House seats to break the two-thirds supermajority that allows Republicans to take action without Democrats even being present.
Democrats have “same messaging in every district”
Democratic candidates are pushing the data center issue in a cluster of Republican-held districts across the northern Indianapolis suburbs — near where Meta is building a $10 billion data center campus in the LEAP District outside Lebanon.
“I am not against data centers. I am against giving them a free ride,” Democratic candidate Tiffany Stoner told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “I think this got rolling faster than probably some of the local officials really were able to even handle.”
Republican Becky Cash, left, and Democrat Tiffany Stoner are seeking the Indiana House District 25 seat. (Courtesy photos)
Stoner is in a rematch against two-term Rep. Becky Cash, R-Zionsville, of what was the tightest Indiana House race in 2024. Cash won by 64 votes out of more than 37,000 cast.
Cash counters that she voted against several of the bills criticized by Democrats as pro-data center and that she wasn’t even in the Legislature when the exemption from the state’s 7% sales tax on center equipment was enacted in 2019.
“The eighth postcard talking about this just hit the mailboxes, and every single postcard says the same thing, like, literally says the same thing,” Cash said in an interview. “The Democrats are very, very focused, and I’m learning that they have the same messaging in every district. They just slightly change the words.”
The data center issue looms as Republicans work to keep control of north suburban Indianapolis seats that have been increasingly contested over recent elections, including Rep. Danny Lopez, R-Carmel, facing Democrat Lindsay Gramlich; Rep. Hunter Smith, R-Zionsville, against Democrat Racheal Bleicher; and Rep. Chris Jeter, R-Fishers, who’s challenged by Democrat Stephanie Jo Yocum.
House utilities committee leader facing heat
Utility rate hikes and the impact of data centers is front and center in the race between 10-term Rep. Ed Soliday, R-Valparaiso, and Democrat Ryan Kominakis in northwestern Indiana.
Soliday, who is chair of the House utilities committee, was already facing heat over electric bill increases before an August storm caused tens of thousands of power outages among Northern Indiana Public Service Co. customers.
Kominakis is blunt in blaming Soliday for higher utility bills and for sponsoring the data center sales tax exemption legislation in 2019. 
“He’s the most powerful man in the state, really, as far as making laws around the utilities,” Kominakis said. “He’s quite literally authored himself, wrote every law, that is, in my opinion, screwing over regular people on the day to day.”
Republican Gov. Mike Braun has remained an advocate of data center projects even as officials in many cities and counties have imposed moratoriums on such proposals.
A Free Press Indiana poll taken this month found 69% of likely voters surveyed opposed to new data center construction, with only 18% in favor. Similar opposition is being seen across the country.
Soliday has defended the state’s data center policies, saying the Legislature has responded to concerns about their impact on electricity rates and water usage. He argues that some opponents are stoking fears for political gains.
“The state provided an opportunity for locals by being competitive with other states,” Soliday said in an interview. “It’s a local decision, but that decision should be based upon the facts, and that really boils down to two areas: Is it aesthetically acceptable to our community, and is it economically beneficial? But we are going through a hysteria right now, where at public hearings there is a lot of screaming.”
Democrat Ryan Kominakis speaks in a campaign ad attacking Republican Rep. Ed Soliday. (Screenshot)
Kominakis points to news reports of data center companies benefiting from more than $655 million in exemptions from state sales and other taxes. 
“That number is only going to grow,” he said. “Just imagine what we could do with that kind of money to help regular people.”
Soliday said a singular political focus on utility rates ignores the complexity involved in ensuring reliable electricity sources and a resilient power grid.
“They’ve got a horse and they’re going to ride it,” Soliday said. “Even though there is no (talk about) ‘What are you going to do differently, and what are the unintended consequences, and how are you going to get it done?’” 
Democrats hoping for momentum swing
Democrats have fallen short the past six election cycles in their goal of breaking the House supermajority held by Republicans.
They maintain they see greater voter enthusiasm this year for their candidates. Democrats have candidates on the ballot for 97 of the 100 Indiana House seats, which they say is the most since at least 2000.
Republicans, meanwhile, left 20 current Democratic legislators without a GOP challenger. That includes 10 districts in Indianapolis and five in Lake County.
Stoner, one of the Democratic challengers, said she feels support swinging her party’s way more than when she was campaigning in 2024.
“I do anticipate we will have some real surprises across Indiana,” Stoner said. “I think given the mood and the energy and just given where people are in comparison to two years ago, I think people feel, perhaps, duped.”



Some key Indiana House races

House District 4: Rep. Ed Soliday, R-Valparaiso, faces Democrat Ryan Kominakis, a union representative and steelworker at U.S. Steel’s Gary Works plant. Soliday has defeated active Democratic challengers before but faces criticism over electricity rate hikes as he’s the House utilities committee chair. Libertarian Travis Gearhart is also running.
House District 9: Rep. Randy Novak, D-Michigan City, faces Republican Chris Cleveland, a software engineer and entrepreneur. Novak is on the House ballot for the first time after replacing Democratic Rep. Pat Boy, who won in 2024 with 51% of the vote but later stepped down.
House District 10: Rep. Chuck Moseley, D-Portage, faces Republican Ted Uzelac, a Portage police officer. Moseley has won legislative elections since 2008 but narrowly survived with 52% of the vote two years ago.
House District 24: Rep. Hunter Smith, R-Zionsville, faces Democrat Racheal Bleicher, an executive with Junior League of Indianapolis. Smith, a former Indianapolis Colts punter, is seeking a second term. 
House District 25: Rep. Becky Cash, R-Zionsville, faces Democrat Tiffany Stoner in a rematch of the 2024 election that Cash won with 50.1% of the vote.
House District 39: Rep. Danny Lopez, R-Carmel, faces Democrat Lindsay Gramlich, CEO of Girls Inc. of Greater Indianapolis. Lopez received 54% of the vote in 2024 to win his first term.
House District 43: Rep. Tonya Pfaff, D-Terre Haute, faces Republican Amy Lore, who is a Vigo County School Board member. Pfaff first won the seat in 2018.
House District 62: Rep. Dave Hall, R-Norman, faces Democrat Amy Huffman Oliver, an attorney and Brown County School Board member. Hall is seeking a third term after winning the Bloomington-area seat in 2022 with 50.1% and in 2024 with 51%.
House District 65: Rep. Chris May, R-Bedford, faces independent Sean Steele. May is seeking a sixth term in a heavily Republican district, but has a unique challenger in Steele, a Bedford Middle School teacher and son of former GOP state Sen. Brent Steele.
House District 72: Republican Darrell Neeley, a retired Navy officer, and Democrat Michele Henry, an attorney, are running for an open seat given up by longtime GOP Rep. Ed Clere of New Albany.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: In New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, childcare policy enters affordability conversation
text:
Stefany Shaheen speaks to supporters at a primary election results watch party in Portsmouth on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin) Throughout campaigns in New Hampshire and all over the country, candidates have made affordability a key focus as the cost of living rises. In New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, both Republican nominee Anthony DiLorenzo and Democratic nominee Stefany Shaheen say rising childcare costs are impacting families.
Plans from the two candidates on how to address it in the Capitol, if elected, differ. 
The 1st Congressional District, which encompasses the eastern portion of the state, including Manchester, the Seacoast and parts of the Lakes Region, has the majority of the state’s childcare programs. Programs in the district also carry some of the highest tuition prices, and families struggle to find open slots due to high need. 
Shaheen, daughter of U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, said that on the campaign trail, families told her the biggest childcare issues they face are affordability and access. 
“The cost of housing and healthcare and childcare makes it so difficult for young families to build a life here and to make New Hampshire home,” Shaheen told the Bulletin in an interview. “We have to find ways to keep young families in New Hampshire.” 
Shaheen said she was in favor of expanding the child care tax credit for families (known as the Child and Dependent Care Credit), which allows families to receive a federal income tax return reduction for qualifying childcare expenses. She also said she supports Medicare for All as a way to reduce the burden on programs and families to pay for staff health benefits. 
“I think the greatest thing we can do to help address some of the strain on these budgets is to pass Medicare for All and eliminate the need for these programs to try to also be providing healthcare for their employees because they don’t have the numbers to make it work,” Shaheen said. “It helps, but it doesn’t solve some of the structural problems long term. I think addressing benefits like healthcare and making it more manageable for people to get the training they need without having to spend a lot of money doing it will be impactful for the field.” 
She also said she supports New Hampshire having free community college to help reduce workforce entry barriers for prospective childcare providers, who, under state law, have a mandatory minimum post-secondary education requirement. Gov. Kelly Ayotte announced this week that she is proposing to reduce community college tuition costs in her upcoming budget proposal. 
Anthony DiLorenzo speaks to supporters in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after winning the Republican nomination for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District in the Sept. 8, 2026, primary. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
DiLorenzo has been advertising himself as the candidate with the financial experience to deal with affordability concerns in Congress, drawing on his experience running multiple car dealerships on the Seacoast. 
DiLorenzo did not respond to multiple requests from the Bulletin to discuss childcare policy and whether he would push for anything if elected to Congress. However, during the Republican primary debate hosted by WMUR on Sept. 2, DiLorenzo said he “believed” in the federal child tax credit. 
“I would expand upon (the Child Tax Credit) so people are able to get good childcare so that they can go to work and support their families,” he said in response to what he would do in Congress to make childcare more affordable and accessible. 
The Child Tax Credit gives qualifying families a tax break up to $2,200 per qualifying child. An additional $1,700 break could be given to a family depending on their annual income. It is different from the Child and Dependent Care Credit. 
On the campaign trail, DiLorenzo has said little about childcare. He has criticized Shaheen for her past work experience, alleging she benefited from her mother’s political connections. Jeanne Shaheen served as governor of New Hampshire from 1997 to 2003, and took office in the U.S. Senate in 2009. 
One of Shaheen’s first jobs, she said, was co-founding and serving as executive director of Business Partners for Child Care and Early Childhood Education, now known as Early Learning New Hampshire, in 2003. The nonprofit organization aims to support early-learning programs, advocate for “effective early learning policy,” and build public-private partnerships to strengthen the field, according to its mission statement. The organization has grown to be one of the most influential childcare advocacy groups in the state since its inception. 
Shaheen said she was “incredibly proud” of her time at the organization and would bring her experience working in the field, saying there would be “no greater champion” for early childhood education if elected. 
“There’s no more important priority than ensuring that the workforce that makes it possible for people to work have what they need to be able to do their jobs,” she said. “It’s one I care deeply about, and it’s one I’m going to continue to champion.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: On the Jericho Road: ‘I was sick, and you cared for me’
text:
(Stock photo by Getty Images)In 2013, my father made a decision no one should ever have to make. He chose healthcare over his family.
My dad was born in England but had built his life in America. His daughters were here, his son-in-law, and a new granddaughter. But when his health began to deteriorate, he had to make a
heartbreaking decision.
Despite spending his life working, sometimes multiple jobs, he had never accumulated enough savings to absorb a prolonged illness. Staying meant risking financial ruin.
So he returned to Wales. Once there, a nurse visited him several days a week, at home. He had a doctor who knew him well, and when his condition worsened, he could be hospitalized for long
stretches without every decision being overshadowed by whether insurance would continue to pay.


To read more commentaries in this series, click here.


The care he received in America wasn’t poor. The system surrounding it failed him, because, as it turns out, illness doesn’t heal on an insurance timeline.
He had somewhere to go: a passport, a birth country with a different system, a family who could help him get there. He still had to choose healthcare over remaining near the people he loved,
but he did not have to choose between receiving that care and financial destitution.
Most Americans facing his exact diagnosis have no such escape. I think about that more than I would like to admit: we got six extra years with him because he had an option almost no one else in
America does.
My father’s story is deeply personal to me, but hardly unique. Most Americans have a healthcare story.
It is the mother rationing medication because her rent increased. The worker tethered to a job he hates because his family’s insurance depends on it. The roughly 200,000 medical fundraisers launched on GoFundMe in a single year by Americans forced to crowdsource the cost of illness. The families watching premiums rise faster than their paychecks. And the hundreds of thousands of families each year whose medical costs contribute to bankruptcy, a form of financial ruin nearly unheard of elsewhere in the developed world.
The financial cost is only part of the story. Americans spend nearly twice as much per person on healthcare as other wealthy countries yet live almost four years less. The gap between the richest and poorest Americans can reach 15 years.
Some of that difference begins with ordinary decisions: putting off a screening because it costs too much or waiting until an illness becomes an emergency.
In South Carolina, 403 babies died before their first birthday in 2023. Our state has one of the nation’s highest infant mortality rates, ranks eighth highest in maternal mortality, and nearly 90% of pregnancy-related deaths are considered preventable.
These are not simply healthcare statistics. They are babies who never came home and mothers who did not survive.
These facts are typically discussed separately. Maternal mortality. Infant mortality. Medical debt. Insurance premiums. Life expectancy. Bankruptcy.
We have spent decades tinkering at the edges of our healthcare system. We change eligibility requirements. Create subsidies. Adjust regulations. Add programs to fill gaps left by other programs.
Beneath every patch and program lies a more fundamental question: What should determine whether someone receives the care they need to live: their humanity or their ability to pay?
Jesus never treated healing as peripheral to his ministry. It was central to it.
One of the recurring acts in Jesus’ ministry is his willingness to interrupt whatever else he was doing to attend to someone who is sick: a blind man crying out from the roadside, a paralyzed man lowered through a torn-open roof, a woman who reaches through a crowd after bleeding for 12 years.
Again and again, Jesus stops. He never asks whether healing will be costly. He didn’t inquire about deservingness. He simply heals.
I still wonder what my dad’s final years would have been like if illness had not required him to leave the country.
Would our daughters have memories of Sunday afternoons spent watching soccer on the “telly” while grandad cooked curry on the stove? Would they laugh with abandon at his ridiculous sense of humor and his penchant for accents?
Healthcare is about more than medicine. It is depression treated before hopelessness becomes tragedy, prenatal care before a complication becomes fatal, diabetes managed before kidney failure and cancer caught before it spreads. It is whether illness separates families from the people they love.
“I was sick, and you cared for me,” Jesus said.
On the Jericho Road, the wounded man was not asked what he had earned, saved or could afford. His need was enough.
Perhaps that is where every conversation about healthcare should begin: with the conviction that a human life is worth caring for.

name: National
title: Data centers are now the largest financial bet in US history
text:
Work continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, on April 17, 2026. Today’s data center buildout has become the largest industrial boom since the railroad era of the 19th century, with $10 trillion in investment and almost twice the economic impact. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The sheer size of investment in data centers is drawing concern as it surpasses all other historical booms and crowds out other more job-creating ventures. 
Until now, no industry had driven the U.S. economy with such force since the railroad expansion of the late 1800s, when titans battled one another to lay the transcontinental tracks that would connect America from coast to coast.
Railroads in the 19th century consumed about $173 billion in today’s dollars and created more than 2% of the nation’s annual economic output (GDP) over 20 years. 
Today’s data center buildout will dwarf that amount, with $10 trillion in investment, and now have almost twice the economic impact — nearly 4% of GDP. That’s according to a report created by a Columbia Business School professor, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.
Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections

States are starting to feel left out of the windfall, many having granted tax exemptions before the boom. 
Years ago, before artificial intelligence prompted a tsunami of building, states typically welcomed data centers supporting internet traffic, offering tax abatements and other perks. Many officials now are rethinking that approach as tax revenues take a bigger hit and high energy demands take a toll on affordability. 
Nevada, for instance, trimmed tax abatements and will ask data centers to agree to foot the bill for energy and water demands, in a September executive order from Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. 
States where data center costs will be concentrated over the three years are Texas ($638 billion), Virginia ($249 billion), Ohio ($169 billion) and Georgia ($160 billion), according to projections from Industrial Info Resources, a market intelligence firm.   
Southern states dominate the landscape for the number of data centers planned, with large numbers also proposed in Arizona, California, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington state, according to a Pew Research Center report in April. 
The profitability of AI has yet to catch up with the expense of the buildout.
“It is not a pretty picture right now,” said IIR’s senior vice president of research, David Pickering. “I think it will become profitable once things settle down a bit and more legislation is put in place to regulate how we handle AI. 
“The big players will no doubt find a way to make it profitable,” he said.  
There are signs the staggering cost of data centers is crowding out other investments such as housing. 
Over the past two years new construction value for data centers has more than doubled to $85 billion annually, while all other construction value has dropped 8%, according to a Stateline analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data as of August.
As new data center value grew by $48 billion since 2024, new houses and apartments dropped by $29 billion, according to the data.
Adam Shapiro, a vice president at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, noted the change in a September social media post: “We’re seeing a pivotal shift in the US economy: investment is shifting away from residential investment and towards computers.” 
Some, like the economist Paul Krugman, see the shift as hurting employment in the long run, despite more current hiring for construction workers. 
“Because data centers employ so few workers, the vast spending on AI currently taking place will also significantly reduce the demand for labor,” Krugman wrote in an Oct. 11 analysis.
Josh Bivens, chief economist for the left-leaning Economic Policy Institute, agreed that the economy’s recent dependence on data centers and other AI spending is unhealthy, calling it “a narrow base of growth, basically one sector, and a pretty fragile one.” 
“Anything that upsets expectations about the future potential profitability of AI investments will likely lead to pretty sharp cutbacks,” Bivens said. “I’m uneasy about how durable this strength might turn out to be.” 
As for the historic nature of the buildout, Mark Higgins, author of a book on U.S. financial history, said there are parallels to the age of railroad building in the late 19th century.  
“Railroads were a huge investment,” Higgins said. “In the 1800’s most of the capital was foreign, and it would attract all this money from Europe, then everything would crash — there were several panics —and Americans would buy the distressed railroads and profit, because they knew which were the good ones.” 
More cities are pressing pause on data centers as local backlash grows

Railroad construction, which did not include trains themselves, cost $4.3 billion between 1870 and 1890, about $173 billion in today’s dollars, according to historical figures provided to Stateline by Van Nieuwerburgh and adjusted for inflation.
Other large-scale construction booms consumed only about 1% or less of annual GDP: Canals in the early 19th century, electrification in the early 20th century, highways in the mid- to late-20th century, and telecoms and fiber between 1996 and 2003.
In a report this month the International Monetary Fund warned of the risk of lower stock prices if high expectations for AI fail to materialize. 
“Although core firms in the AI ecosystem have been profitable so far … weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction,” the report warned.
The buildout will also double electricity consumption, Van Nieuwerburgh estimated, a continual thorn for data center projects that need more power to process vast data troves to power AI applications. 
An Oregon report last month, which led to a continued freeze on data center approvals in the state, said the single most frequent concern in public comments is utility affordability.
An analysis from two universities in July found that the combination of data centers and cryptocurrency mining could raise electricity bills by 8% nationally, and as much as 25% in parts of Virginia. The report came from a collaboration between Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania and North Carolina State University. 
Virginia passed an electricity consumption surcharge specifically for data centers that began in July, in a budget compromise that preserved lucrative tax breaks for the data centers. Some localities with heavy concentrations are considering pauses, and at least one city has a moratorium. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Predicting or gambling? New markets invade all areas of society
text:
The Kalshi odds as of Thursday on who will win the Indiana secretary of state’s office. (Screenshot)Prediction markets are bending the common definition of gambling — and states across the nation are pushing back.
Kalshi is the first federally regulated financial exchange in the United States dedicated to trading on the outcomes of future events. It handled billions in weekly contract volume. And it’s battling in court with 21 states.
Whether Indiana will join its name to that list could be a topic in the 2027 legislative session.
But it’s not just Kalshi. They are simply the best known. A handful of other prediction markets, such as Polymarket, are “trading” on election results, the weather, sports and even the next winner of “Dancing with the Stars.”
Here’s how it works – individuals buy “yes” or “no” contract shares on whether an event will happen. Each event has a clearly stated source on how to determine the winner. For instance, on a weather trade – yes, people trade on whether it will rain – the source might be the National Weather Service’s airport sensor in a major city.
Or, in the case of a political race, the source might be a state election division site.
Prediction markets spend millions to influence state, federal governments

For instance, on Thursday Kalshi had the Indiana secretary of state race listed in favor of Democrat Beau Bayh at 60%. Republican Max Engling is at 44%. They have swapped leads over the past months and the odds are constantly shifting as people buy contracts.
The Libertarian and Lincoln Party candidates aren’t included.
So if you buy a “yes” contract at 60 cents for Bayh and he later wins you collect $1. You can also buy “no” contracts.
I know that doesn’t equal 100%. The bigger the gap between the “yes” and “no” means the market is less confident in the price, according to several explanatory sites. In a market with lots of action, the two sides should be pretty close to 100% total.
The trades are treated like a commodity on the stock market. Warnings against insider trading are all over the sites.
One way the markets are different than straight gambling is you can sell your shares before a future event is officially decided.
For instance, if you bought for Bayh early — maybe when he was at 40 cents — you can try to sell your contracts to other users now at the higher price and pocket the small win before the election is over. But someone has to be willing to buy.
The volume of trading in the secretary of state race stood Thursday at $28,267, which is considered to be a solid market.
Another interesting Indiana-related event on Kalshi right now is where the Chicago Bears will relocate. That volume has topped $950,00.
The “odds” on Thursday were 57% in favor of a new location in Illinois with Indiana at 42%. Another 3% is on no relocation. The Illinois line has been winning most of this year with small spikes for Indiana.
The federal government contends it has sole authority to regulate these markets and that is handled through the Commodities Futures Trading Commission. But many states want to have their own say on the issue, including consumer protections.
The Kalshi odds on where the Chicago Bears will move in the future. (Screenshot)
The sports market is causing much of the concern. After all, sports gambling sites like DraftKings and others are paying state gaming taxes on the bets — something Kalshi and other prediction markets don’t have to do.
A few states have specifically banned the sports trades. At least one state, Arizona, has filed criminal charges against Kalshi.
Others are very concerned about how the issue might impact the results of an election.
Last week, 40 state attorneys general banded together to file an amicus brief urging the U.S. Supreme Court to hear New Jersey’s petition on whether federal law regulating commodity trading superseded the state’s gambling laws.
The Trump administration has sided with the prediction markets.
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita did not sign on, though. His office provided this statement on the issue:
“The issues on all sides of this situation are well-covered by the parties in this case, including some other states. We have heard little from anyone in Indiana state government advocating to us one way or the other for the issues this case presents. SCOTUS will be deciding this case soon enough, and Indiana will take action from there.”
Some people are now looking to these contract markets instead of polling to gauge the views of the electorate.
Money changing hands over the outcome of elections is corrosive to democracy and amounts to an attempt to bypass existing bans on election betting, civic organizations and some public officials say. Twenty-three states completely ban election betting, according to data from the National Conference of State Legislatures analyzed by the Pew Research Center.
I think it’s important to have some state involvement on this important issue, so I am hopeful the Supreme Court ultimately takes up the case and gives states some basic authority. From there, it would be up to state lawmakers to provide reasonable guardrails and a taxing structure.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: After the announcement, who owns the promise?
text:
In 2024, Granite Shore described plans to turn Merrimack Station into a renewable energy park. (File photo by Hadley Barndollar/New Hampshire Bulletin)Most of us know the feeling. A statement goes out from Concord or Washington, and the thing we were worried about has been saved. New Hampshire heard that news in May, when Gov. Kelly Ayotte, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced that Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest would stay open and that plans to close facilities at Bartlett Experimental Forest would be reexamined.
The relief was earned, but the harder question comes once attention moves on: Who carries the commitment now?
I ask because of where I have worked. As the Forest Service’s Federal Register notice officer, and earlier while running a geospatial system serving nearly 300,000 Homeland Security users, I learned how decisions pass between offices. One controls staff, another controls buildings, a third controls money. An outside partner may control something essential. A public commitment needs a responsible party with the authority and resources to carry it out.
The governance failure at Hubbard Brook: Why New Hampshire must demand a transition plan 

What keeping a promise requires
Hubbard Brook shows what is at stake. Scientists there have collected weekly precipitation and stream-water samples since 1963. Its physical archive holds tens of thousands of cataloged samples requiring a functioning building, environmental controls and active stewardship. A missed season cannot be collected later. Last month’s rain is gone. Keeping the research continuous requires people, money and facilities long after the announcement.
Shaheen’s May 11 release also noted that she had helped secure increased research funding and language directing the Forest Service to fill vacancies at experimental forests in the Northeast, and that she and Ayotte had requested more staffing support. That is a meaningful step. It leaves a practical question: Which vacancies were filled, and what capacity did that restore? A funding priority and an operating capability are different things.
Bartlett needs its own answer. In September, the Forest Service announced plans to close 23 research facilities, and an agency official said the work done at those stations would continue at other sites. For research tied to one forest, continuity depends on maintaining measurements at that forest. Moving staff or offices does not, by itself, establish whether that continuity survives. That assurance should be accompanied by a plain account of which Bartlett facilities remain available, who supports the research, and what the five-year research plan mentioned in May commits the agency to provide.
Development carries obligations too
The same discipline applies to the possible data center in Bow. In April, PSNH, doing business as Eversource, filed an agreement to study whether a 350-megawatt facility could connect to the grid at Granite Shore Power’s request. Reporting subsequently linked the request to a possible data center. Granite Shore owns the former Merrimack Station coal plant.
The agreement makes one responsibility explicit: Granite Shore pays for the study, with an estimated $75,000 due before work begins. It also calls for estimating the supporting infrastructure needed and the customer’s potential share of its costs. That distinction matters. Paying for an assessment does not settle the final allocation of costs for whatever is eventually built. The public should be able to follow that question into the next agreement.
Merrimack Station carries earlier public commitments, too. In 2024, Granite Shore described plans to turn the site into a renewable energy park. Residents can fairly ask how a proposed data center would relate to those plans, and which commitments are documented obligations. The answer belongs in the public record before anyone concludes that the earlier promise has been fulfilled or abandoned.
Support for a statewide moratorium crosses party lines. A pause needs an authority, a scope, a duration and a purpose. The budget proposal described by NHPR would not take effect until at least July 2027. Its eventual wording would determine what it covers. Does it pause studies, applications, approvals or construction? Those are different decisions. Calling for a moratorium leaves the work of defining and implementing it.
Who carries responsibility forward
Three questions separate a commitment from an assurance: (1) Who owns the obligation, with suitable authority and resources to meet it? (2) What evidence would show whether it is being met? (3) What survives a change in leadership, funding or ownership? If an announcement cannot answer all three, residents are holding an assurance, however sincere. Answers do not guarantee follow-through, but they make it possible to check. A forest’s staff can be reassigned. A data center can be sold. Responsibility needs to survive those changes.
A jobs forecast, a staffing request, a study agreement and a completed hire establish different things: a projection, a requested priority, an assigned obligation and a completed action. A press release records what was said on a given day. Assessing fulfillment requires evidence of what happened afterward.
Nobody can guarantee everything. A developer at the study stage cannot answer every question, and early studies have a legitimate role. But each consequential question needs an owner and an answer before the decision it affects. For a research forest, that means continuity arrangements before an irreversible reduction. For a new project, it means resolving costs and applicable impacts at the stages when the relevant commitments and approvals are made.
The people who wrote letters for Hubbard Brook, and the Bow residents who spoke at their select board meeting last month, deserve that follow-through. When the answers are public, credit the people who provided them. When they remain unclear, keep asking. Hubbard Brook’s record exists because someone showed up to collect it week after week for six decades. Public promises deserve the same sustained responsibility.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Van Orden rides with Trump in campaign for third term
text:
Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-WI) speaks to reporters on the steps of the U.S. Capitol Building. (Photo by Tierney L. Cross/Getty Images)U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden, the Republican incumbent running for reelection in Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, one of the most hotly contested House races in the country, has decided his best chance is to dance with the one who brought him — President Donald Trump. 
“Derrick, this guy he fights like hell. He’s in a little bit of a community that tends to be on slightly, a little bit more than we wanted, left, but he loves them all, and he’s very popular, and he’s going to win by a lot,” Trump said of Van Orden at a June rally in Chippewa Falls. “You’re doing well. I understand you’re really doing well. So, thank you and he’s a real fighter … we’ve been friends right from the beginning.” 
Trump’s approval ratings have hit all-time lows in Wisconsin recently, a potential problem for Van Orden, whose seat is one of the Democratic Party’s top targets for flipping this year. The two-term Republican is running for the second time against Democrat Rebecca Cooke, who two years ago lost to Van Orden by only 2.7 points, in a district where Trump beat Vice President Kamala Harris by 7.4 points. 
Between the two campaigns and outside groups, the increasingly heated race is nearing $30 million in spending on mostly negative ads. Van Orden’s ads have alliteratively accused Cooke of being “corrupt” and “communist” while calling her authenticity into question — largely over charges that she’s highlighted her work as a waitress while downplaying her previous work for Democratic political campaigns and interest groups. 
“I think the campaign has gotten intensely negative, with authenticity being a core theme,” Anthony Chergosky, a political science professor at the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse, said. “I’m seeing authenticity come up on both sides, where Congressman Van Orden and his allies are going after the persona or biography of Rebecca Cooke, particularly her waitressing, has become kind of a flashpoint in this campaign. And for Congressman Van Orden, Democrats are going after him as kind of saying that he’s part of the problem in Washington, and that’s a tried and true strategy for unseating an incumbent, to portray them as part of the problem.”
Congress, Chergosky continued, “has rock bottom approval ratings as an institution, so incumbents are often targeted due to their membership in an unpopular institution. Chergosky expects the attack ads will blanket the airwaves up to Election Day, he said. “I think that this is going to continue to be a very negative campaign.” 
Across the country, a number of vulnerable Republicans have sought to find areas to distance themselves from an unpopular president. Even in Wisconsin, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany — despite a voting record that has been in near perfect lockstep with the Trump administration — has tried to put some breathing room between himself and Trump. 
But Van Orden, a former Navy SEAL, has gone the other way, continuing to vocally support the Trump administration, the war in Iran, Trump’s tariffs, his steering of the economy and the administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown. 
In September, Van Orden was the only member of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation to speak at Trump’s midterm convention in Texas. 
Throughout the year, the 3rd CD has hosted a parade of high-profile administration officials and top-ranking Republicans. 
Van Orden has appeared in his western Wisconsin district with Trump, Vice President JD Vance, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin, Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services Administrator Mehmet Oz and House Speaker Mike Johnson. 
“We are defending, right now, the foundational truths, and I’ve got to have warriors in the room to do it,” Johnson said at a rally in Sparta earlier this month. “There is no stronger warrior than Derrick Van Orden.” 
In recent weeks, Van Orden has made online posts suggesting he would volunteer to join the firing squad in the planned execution of Nidal Hasan, the man convicted of a mass shooting at Fort Hood, accusing Cooke of supporting the “chemical and physical castration of children and men in woman’s locker rooms” and alleging that she wants to bring “Somali fraud” to Wisconsin. 
He’s also posted a number of AI-generated videos of Cooke and other Democratic Party of Wisconsin officials, a tactic that drew a cease and desist letter from the Cooke campaign. Van Orden called the letter a “publicity stunt.” 
A spokesperson for Van Orden did not respond to a request for comment, but in an interview with Channel 3000, Van Orden strongly endorsed Trump’s ongoing war in Iran and argued that the high price of gas and diesel is not only because of the war causing shocks to global oil markets but also due to Democrats “chasing the green new scam” and U.S. oil companies “profiteering.” 
“Is this politically convenient right now? Absolutely not,” Van Orden said in the interview, in which he also referenced the “radical Muslim mullahs” who led the Iranian revolution in the 1970s. “Would it be much easier for Republicans to maintain the House and the Senate if we weren’t involved in this conflict in Iran? Yes. I would be a fool not to acknowledge that. But at some point, we have to deal with this issue that’s been going on for a half a century.”
Chergosky said that Van Orden “doubling down on Trumpism” might be a valid strategy in a district that’s voted for Trump three times. 
The problem, he said, is that those Trump voters haven’t always been reliable when Trump isn’t on the ballot. 
“I think Republicans in this district are making a play to turn out the pro-Trump base, and it’s a base that has delivered for Trump three times, but with any midterm election, we’re going to see a significant drop-off in voter turnout,” Chergosky said. “So a lot of times these midterms come down to the question of, among the voters who voted in the presidential election, which of them stay home this time around? In other words, who drops out of the electorate compared to the presidential election? And so I think the concern for Republicans is that a lot of these pro-Trump, low-propensity voters are going to drop out of the electorate, and I can see them trying to avoid that certainly through Congressman Van Orden’s strategy.” 
But the 3rd CD is also a district that for decades was represented by Ron Kind, a moderate Democrat. Van Orden, with his divisive and confrontational style, has been elected twice deploying a different approach to politics; still, joining forces with some of the most controversial members of Trump’s cabinet could alienate voters. 
At an agricultural roundtable hosted by the Cooke campaign last week, voters complained about the anti-vaccine “conspiracy theories” espoused by figures such as Kennedy resulting in measles outbreaks in the area. At a town hall hosted by the Wisconsin Farmers Union in Gays Mills, attendees lamented the treatment of immigrant workers at the district’s farms and manufacturing plants. 
“Derrick Van Orden has not delivered a successful farm bill out of this Congress,” Cooke said last week. “I don’t think that he’s really done very much at all to support our family farms or people in agriculture across this district.”
In the Channel 3000 interview, Van Orden made the case that he’s been a serious legislator, listing the three committees he sits on. 
While in Congress, he voted in favor of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut billions from federal healthcare programs and has hurt the bottom line of rural hospitals in the 3rd CD. After voting for the law, Van Orden has touted his work to provide millions of dollars to rural hospitals in Wisconsin. But that funding provides only $200 million after the OBBBA cut $7 billion in federal healthcare funds meant for the state, an analysis by KFF found last year
From his position on the House Agriculture committee, Van Orden has suggested expanding the H2-A visa program to help the district’s dairy farms get more immigrant labor. But the H2-A program only applies to seasonal farm workers, not the year round workers needed on a dairy farm. Van Orden has also proposed the creation of a new system in which currently undocumented workers return to their home country and pay $2,500 to get in line and wait to be approved for a new visa. 
“They should expect me to work doggedly, like I have been doing. I’ve been an incredibly effective legislator,” he said.
