name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming wildlife managers want to nix the Roadless Rule. Hunters and anglers want to keep it.
text:
The Wyoming Game and Fish Department is among the few parties encouraging the Trump administration to fully eliminate the 2001 Roadless Rule, which safeguards roughly 3.3 million acres of backcountry in the state — valued habitat for wildlife and hunters alike. 
State wildlife officials took that position in an Oct. 6 comment letter signed by Game and Fish Deputy Director Jeff Davis. It’s a stance that’s related to a desire for more local control and dissatisfaction with a “blanket federal rule,” he told WyoFile in an emailed statement.
“Locally driven planning — focused on forest health, habitat restoration, and improving public access without increasing impacts to fish, wildlife, and natural landscapes — is best guided by the people of Wyoming,” Davis said. 
Sota the pudelpointer follows a ridge in the northern Wyoming Range, pictured here in 2023, which includes large chunks of inventoried roadless area. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Game and Fish’s comment letter asks federal officials to adequately staff the Forest Service so the federal agency can successfully administer the Roadless Rule cancellation. The memo also encourages deference to the state agency’s own expertise. 
“That expertise should shape decisions from the outset and should not be overridden by national-level direction without prior consultation and a transparent, science-based explanation,” the letter reads.
Regardless of its reasoning, Game and Fish’s position puts the agency at odds with the overwhelming majority of hunters, anglers and the general public. Overall, 99.1% of the 370,238 public comments received by the U.S. Forest Service opposed eliminating roadless areas. 
Nationally, there are 44 million acres of national forest with roadless area protections. It’s a class of land that’s often akin to backcountry, and the rule keeps it that way — future roadbuilding isn’t allowed under most circumstances. In Wyoming, there are big tracts of inventoried roadless areas in mountain ranges like the Absarokas, Tetons, Winds, Bighorns, Snowies, Laramie Mountains and the Wyoming Range. 




Some 3.3 million acres of nine national forests have been classified as roadless areas since the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. (U.S. Forest Service)
The Trump administration has argued that the Clinton-era land protections should be eliminated to remove a barrier for wildfire-risk reduction work. 
There were 95 organizations and government agencies that supported the repeal, according to an analysis from a Substack outlet, More Than Just Parks, which first pointed out Game and Fish’s support for the rescission. Industry groups — including timber and logging, mining and energy, ranching and grazing and motorized recreation — accounted for the majority of parties wanting to wipe out roadless area protections. 
The Wyoming Game and Fish Department appears to be the only state wildlife management agency that submitted a comment letter supporting eliminating roadless areas, though directors for Nevada’s Division of Forestry and Department of Wildlife submitted a joint letter also favoring repeal.  
Most state wildlife agencies simply didn’t comment. 
Many Wyoming conservation groups did. One coalition of 18 groups wrote they “stand in strong and unanimous support” for keeping roadless areas intact, and they partly posed a wildlife argument. 
“Roads fragment habitat and degrade the migration corridors that Wyoming’s big game herds depend on,” the letter from Wyoming Outdoor Council, Greater Yellowstone Coalition, Wyoming Wilderness Association and others states. “Roads fragment habitat and degrade the migration corridors that Wyoming’s big game herds depend on.” 
For those reasons, some Game and Fish retirees were miffed by their former employer’s position. Ecologist and longtime Wyoming Wildlife Magazine editor Chris Madson, who’s been an occasional critic of his former employer, said that it’s evident that roads do more harm than good for wildlife, but also hunting. 
“I’m alarmed,” Madson said. “Anybody who spends any time on the public domain knows, just by the seat of his jeans, that deer and elk move away from motorized disturbance. And the more disturbance, the farther away they move.”  
Craig Benjamin, executive director of the Wyoming Wildlife Federation, said that he has “tremendous respect” for Game and Fish, but he argued the agency missed its mark in asking to eliminate roadless areas. 
“Wyoming’s forests need active management, and our wildlife needs intact habitat,” Benjamin said in a statement. “We can do both. If there are barriers to good management, let’s identify them and fix them rather than eliminate the entire Roadless Rule. 
“In Wyoming, we fix things,” he added. “We don’t throw them away.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump administration expands vehicle access to Alaska’s Denali National Park
text:
Denali National Park visitors, ferried by shuttle bus, take in a view of Denali, North America's tallest peak, on Aug. 9, 2012. Seen in the background is the sole road that runs through the park. Denali is unusual among U.S. national parks for its strict limits on vehicle traffic. Vehicle use is restricted beyond the first 15 miles of the park's 92-mile road, and most of it is by shuttle bus. A new rule will increase the number of vehicles allowed past the road's first 15 miles. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)More buses and cars will be allowed to travel on the sole road through Denali National Park, under a rule announced Thursday by the U.S. Department of the Interior and the National Park Service.
The new rule sets a limit of 160 permitted vehicles a day for the season that runs from the week before Memorial Day to the week after Labor Day. The current limit for that period is 10,512 vehicles in total, or about 100 a day.
The rule, which was proposed in May and subject to a public comment period, complies with a July 3, 2025, executive order issued by President Donald Trump and titled “Making American Beautiful Again By Improving Our National Parks.”
It includes a directive that the Secretary of Interior “review all of the Department’s recreational access rules and take steps to rescind any that unnecessarily restrict recreation in national parks,” with a special emphasis on restrictions imposed during the Biden administration.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, in a statement, said he had done that at Denali, which is one of Alaska’s top tourist destinations.
“America’s national parks belong to the American people, and we should be looking for every responsible opportunity to make these incredible places more accessible,” Burgum said in the statement. “At Denali, we’re cutting red tape, honoring a management plan shaped by years of public input, and expanding access while protecting the extraordinary landscape that makes this park so special.” 
He noted that the new vehicle limit builds on the 2012 Denali vehicle management plan.
That plan produced the seasonal 10,512-vehicle limit, but it identified a daily cap of 160 vehicles as the maximum that could be allowed while preserving Denali’s qualities.
Denali is unusual among U.S. national parks because it has just one road running though it and strict limits on vehicle traffic. Most of the vehicle traffic is by shuttle bus. Travel is restricted beyond the road’s first 15 miles; the new rule applies to the portion of the road beyond that point.
The 161 written public comments submitted to the National Park Service by organizations and individuals showed mixed opinions about the new Trump administration rule.
Some commenters, such as the Alaska Travel Industry Association, said the change to a 160-vehicle daily limit would be positive.
“Given the statewide significance of Denali National Park in Alaska’s visitor infrastructure, ATIA appreciates the opportunity to support a policy which would thoughtfully manage and expand visitor access into the park while not compromising high quality visitor experiences,” the association said in its comment letter.
Other comments that favored the change said a daily limit is preferable to a seasonal limit.
But opponents – including the state of Alaska – said the impacts of the 160-vehicle-a-day cap had not been analyzed. Negative impacts could be myriad, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources said its comment letter, dated July 17.
“The State supports the sustainable management of park resources; however, we have concerns regarding the scientific justification for the strict 160-vehicle daily limit, its impact on Alaskan residents, statutory compliance with the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA), and potential economic stagnation resulting from rigid vehicle caps,” the DNR comment letter said. “Given these concerns, the State of Alaska opposes the proposed rule as drafted because it lacks updated scientific justification, is inconsistent with statutory access requirements under ANILCA, and risks unnecessary limitations on inholder rights, subsistence activities, and public access.”
The Denali Citizens Council, a regional wildlife and wilderness advocacy group, said the 160-vehicle daily limit mentioned in the 2012 plan was based on modeling, “not from empirical before-after evidence of wildlife population response.” 
Camp Denali, a historic wilderness lodge at the end of the park road, said lighter traffic that resulted from a five-year partial road closure has benefitted wildlife, and those benefits should be analyzed.
The 92-mile road was closed to vehicles at about its midway point in late 2021 after a landslide made it unsafe. The National Park Service has just completed construction of a new bridge allowing vehicles to avoid the continually sliding slope, and the road will reopen fully next year, officials announced last month.
Hikers rest on an outcropping on the Savage Alpine Trail in Denali National Park on July 26, 2026. The sole road through the park is seen below. Travel restrictions on the 92-mile park road begin at the 15-mile mark, at the Savage River, seen in the background. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Mississippi Today
title: Amputations, ‘extortion’ and cancer treatment delays: Lawmakers hear testimony on Mississippi prison healthcare
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
From prisoners suffering amputations due to diabetes to a mother taking desperate measures to help her incarcerated son treat his debilitating pain, Mississippi lawmakers on Thursday heard stunning testimony in a more than three-hour hearing about inadequate healthcare in state prisons. 
Lawmakers presiding over a joint meeting of the House and Senate Public Health and Corrections committees peppered the CEO of Mississippi’s prison medical contractor, Kansas-based VitalCore Health Strategies, with questions about allegations of systemic failure to stop preventable deaths and illness. Their questions stemmed from stories that have poured in from their constituents, journalists and legislative watchdog reports. 
Lawmakers also condemned the absence of the Mississippi Department of Corrections at the hearing, despite having sent the agency a letter urging its officials to attend. 
The hearing came after Mississippi Today’s Behind Bars, Beyond Care series documented potentially thousands of prisoners with untreated hepatitis C and others having trouble getting cancer screenings. The series documented numerous cases of alleged neglect, including delayed care of an inmate leading to death, a prisoner’s untreated broken arm forcing an amputation, and prison officials communicating their dismay at an inmate’s rotting leg going untreated.
Lawmakers, led by House Corrections Chairwoman Becky Currie, a Republican from Brookhaven, proposed several measures earlier this year to improve prison healthcare and create stronger safeguards against the denial of care, but most of the proposed reforms died. 
The Thursday hearing centered on some of the problems the bills sought to correct as lawmakers expect to propose more reforms for the state’s troubled and expensive prison healthcare system next year. 
Lawmakers on Thursday heard about: 
Alarming delays in cancer diagnosis and treatment 
Dr. Jacob Graham, an oncologist at South Central Regional Medical Center in Laurel, said he has been alarmed by the significant delays in diagnosis and treatment faced by his patients who are incarcerated in MDOC facilities. 
One patient he described did not receive a prostate cancer diagnosis until the disease spread to his bones and caused permanent paralysis of his lower body due to compression of the spinal cord. 
Another waited nearly a year to receive prostate cancer treatment after a blood test showed dangerously high levels of a protein measured to screen for the disease. The test in fall of 2025 showed a prostate-specific antigen of 60 — significantly higher than the normal range of zero to four — but he did not receive a biopsy until April 2026, and did not begin treatment until August. Graham said it was “miraculous” the cancer had not metastasized in spite of the significant treatment delay. 
Yet another patient with lung cancer that had spread throughout his body received treatment at the University of Mississippi Medical Center and a dire prognosis of weeks to a few months to live. But prison medical staff did not arrange for him to visit a local oncologist within a week as ordered, leaving him to languish for over a month before receiving follow-up care as his condition deteriorated. He was then hospitalized again due to complications associated with the delays in care. 
Limb amputations and trip to a Motel 6
Multiple state lawmakers relayed stories of constituents who suffered amputations due to untreated diabetes in prison. 
Limb amputations are a serious complication of diabetes, though a majority of diabetes-related amputations are preventable, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
Rep. Elliot Burch, a Republican from Lucedale, testified that he received a call a year and a half ago informing him that a constituent with serious medical concerns had been released from prison to a Motel 6 on I-55 in Jackson, even though MDOC staff previously told his family they planned to refer him to long-term care. 
Burch, initially skeptical of the story, decided to investigate himself. He traveled to the motel, and after he knocked on the man’s door, he found him with both legs amputated, unable to get out of bed himself to unlock the door. At least one of the amputations occurred while the man was in MDOC custody due to uncontrolled diabetes.
The man had been dropped off with insulin, but no blood glucose monitor. And the only food he had to eat was a bag packed with carbohydrate-rich foods, including crackers and sandwiches. The man ultimately had to seek emergency care for another issue and was discharged to long-term care from the hospital. 
Rep. Steve Lott, a Republican from Lucedale, said he received a call from a constituent set to be released from South Mississippi Correctional Institution in Leakesville with serious health issues, including diabetes. Three days after the man was paroled from prison, his leg was amputated. 
A mother takes desperate measures to help treat her son’s chronic pain
Pearly White said she almost lost her home from sending money to the prison where her son was incarcerated after he lost access to critical medication.
She went on to tell lawmakers about a scheme where fellow prisoners, under the watch of guards, coerced her to pay them an ever-increasing sum of money for illegal drugs to help her son manage pain medical officials failed to manage.    
“She’s been extorted,” Currie said. 
White’s son was an amputee when he went to prison, spending time at the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman and Marshall County Correctional Facility after multiple DUI charges. He had spinal cord damage, a condition he managed with gabapentin, a prescription nerve-pain medication. The problems began when prison officials told him they couldn’t provide him with the drug. 
He couldn’t function, she said, and desperate to manage the debilitating pain, he turned to marijuana. In a plea to help her son, White transferred money to people inside the prison through an app. She could afford the payments at first, but they eventually ratcheted up the price to over $1,000, threatening to cut off her son.
“They know what they’re doing,” White said. “They have help. The officers, they know.” 
White, a veteran who works as a surgical technician in Oxford, said she has plunged into debt trying to get her son treatment he should have received through the state’s prison medical contractor.
“I stand up on this bad back and these bad knees every day so that I can pay the bills that I acquired from the inmates, because VitalCore didn’t think it was necessary that he have gabapentin,” White said.  
White’s son was eventually released from prison and now lives with her. 
White said she reported the scheme to MDOC’s Corrections Investigation Division and the FBI. She’s received no word from either entity about whether they investigated her case or the illicit flow of money into prisons. 
VitalCore responds: ‘I think it’s time to tell our story’
After over an hour of testimony from speakers outlining a wide range of prison healthcare woes, VitalCore’s leader spoke for the first time to lawmakers. 
Beth Clay, VitalCore’s lobbyist in Mississippi, introduced her client in soaring terms.
“I’m telling you, the people I’m bringing you today have hearts of gold when it comes to medical care,” Clay said.  
Viola Riggins, the company’s founder and CEO, said she doesn’t like the limelight, but feels her company’s work has been misrepresented. 
“I think it’s time to tell our story,” she said. 
Before addressing the issues raised by those who testified, Riggins described her humble beginnings in Kansas, where she began her career working in correctional facilities when she was 19. She and Dr. Lorelei Ammons founded VitalCore in 2018, and the company developed a reputation for providing medical care to places in crisis, she said. 
Riggins then extolled her company’s management of prison healthcare, distributing a packet with statistics she said show VitalCore has made progress improving outcomes inside state prisons.    
She said she was met with a “dire” state of care in 2020 when VitalCore was awarded an emergency contract to provide medical care in Mississippi prisons after the previous company terminated its contract. VitalCore was awarded over $315 million in emergency, no-bid state contracts from 2020 to 2024. The state selected the company for a three-year contract worth over $357 million in 2024. 
She described a dearth of medical staff, patients not receiving annual physicals, HIV going untreated and six years in which patients did not receive mammograms to detect breast cancer. 
“The care was not appropriate, and it was not OK,” she said.  
She claimed that many of the current challenges facing medical care are residual effects of previous contractors’ impropriety.
For example, Riggins said, reaching contractually obligated staffing levels took time, though the company is now better meeting the requirements. And as for allegations that VitalCore has delayed payments to vendors are vestiges of past contractors’ behavior — she said the company pays bills within 90 days. 
Dispute over hepatitis C treatment
VitalCore has drawn criticism for treating only a handful of the hundreds of people in MDOC diagnosed with hepatitis C. 
Brian Collier, VitalCore’s executive operations advisor and former executive director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said the company is treating 50 patients diagnosed with hepatitis C each quarter.
At this rate, he said the company will by 2029 cure over 700 patients identified with the disease in 2024. This does not include new people who enter the facility or contract the contagious illness while incarcerated. 
Currie questioned those numbers, citing conversations she had with Corrections Commissioner Burl Cain and Dr. Raman Singh, VitalCore’s chief medical officer, where they purported many more people incarcerated in MDOC facilities had tested positive for the illness.
“When I first became chair, when Burl and I actually got along, we had many, many discussions, and he told me that over 5,000 inmates had hep C,” Currie said. “Somebody is not telling the truth.”
Hepatitis C is a blood-borne infection that can be cured in more than 95% of cases with an eight- to 12-week course of medication, though it is costly. 
State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney said treating a fixed amount of hepatitis C patients a year is “unacceptable,” noting that the standard of care is to universally screen for the highly contagious infection and treat it immediately. 
“If you don’t, with a confined population, you will have reinfection,” said Edney.
Edney said he could help the company access medication at lower cost through a federal program. Mississippi Today reported in 2025 that the Department of Health provided MDOC information about how to access the discounted prices, but the agency did not take steps to do so. 
A notable no-show
Even as they probed VitalCore’s leaders and questioned some of their assertions, lawmakers commended the company for at least showing up. 
The same could not be said for the agency that hired them: MDOC. On Monday afternoon, lawmakers learned that MDOC officials, most notably Cain, planned to skip the hearing over the problems that have unfolded on their watch. 
On Tuesday, the chairs of the Public Health and Corrections committees sent Cain a letter urging him to reconsider. But their overtures apparently fell on deaf ears, as Cain and agency leaders didn’t show up. 
MDOC did not provide lawmakers with an explanation for their absence, and the agency did not respond to a request for comment from Mississippi Today. 
“So they just didn’t want to stop to sit and talk to legislators, I guess,” said Sen. Jeremy England, a Republican from Vancleave. “It sounds like they’ll be OK with whatever we do then if they don’t care to be here to listen.”
Rep. Chris Bell, a Democrat from Jackson, said he believes the joint committee should demand Cain come before it to answer questions. 
“To hear the testimony of all the individuals that we’ve heard today and for him to have the audacity not to show, not to designate someone to come is totally disrespectful,” Bell said. “This is unacceptable.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont extols housing bill, brushes over past veto
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont praised Connecticut’s sweeping housing legislation on Thursday for empowering towns and suburbs — just over a year after he vetoed an earlier iteration of the bill that he said failed to do so.
At Connecticut’s annual housing conference, the governor referenced conversations with small-town mayors and first selectmen who were eager to build additional housing. Though he joked that Connecticut’s suburbs “can be a little grumpier” than cities when it comes to housing development, he cited efforts to convert suburban shopping centers into housing units.
Lamont vetoed the original bill last June, arguing that it did not have enough “buy-in” from towns and suburbs. He later signed a revised version of the bill into law after a special session last November.
“Some of the people that complained about the housing bill was sort of ‘Not in my backyard’ and ‘Stay away from the green grass, I want to keep it green,’” Lamont said at the conference, held at New Haven’s Omni Hotel. “Well, here in New Haven, and here in most of our towns and cities, we’re taking an old parking lot and reimagining it for housing. We’re taking an office building that’s only 30% occupied and converting offices back into housing.”

Attendees listen to a speaker during the Connecticut Housing Conference at The Omni Hotel in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The housing law requires towns to create housing growth plans, expands Connecticut’s fair rent commissions and eliminates most off-street parking requirements for small housing developments. The 107-page legislation includes many other provisions, including a ban on “hostile architecture,” or structures that make it difficult for people experiencing homelessness to lie down.
The law aims to address Connecticut’s housing shortage and affordability crises. Connecticut is one of just three states that have lost housing units per capita since 2020. A Pew Charitable Trusts report last month found that high housing costs are driving over 20% of poverty in Connecticut.
Pete Harrison, a housing advocate who moderated a conference panel about the housing bill, described the wide-ranging legislation as “a little bit of a Rube Goldberg machine.” 
“But really what it is at the core is a promise from the governor, from the legislature, from all the stakeholders in this room, and elsewhere, that we need to build more homes and more kinds of homes,” Harrison added.
The conference speakers brushed past or did not acknowledge Lamont’s veto of the original bill.
“You maybe heard there’s a little back and forth on the housing bill,” the governor quipped, right before praising small towns for “overwhelmingly” taking the lead on housing development since the legislation was signed into law.
Harrison noted at the start of his panel that the law had a “very colorful story” of getting passed, adding, “it’s neither here nor there.”
Cathryn Vaulman, the governor’s director of communications, said Lamont didn’t mention the veto explicitly in order to avoid giving a “play-by-play” of the bill’s passage. She also noted that some town mayors and first selectmen who opposed the initial housing legislation support the revised version that the governor signed into law.
Other speakers praised Lamont’s approach to housing, citing the housing law and state initiatives like the Time to Own program, which helps some first-time homebuyers cover down payments and closing costs.
“Nothing that I have said could have happened without the leadership of my boss, the vision that he had, and … the financial support,” Housing Commissioner Seila Mosquera-Bruno said.

State Housing Comissioner Seila Mosquera-Bruno speaks during the Connecticut Housing Conference at The Omni Hotel in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lamont, Mosquera-Bruno and other speakers alluded to headwinds that have made housing development more challenging, including tariffs and high interest rates. Mosquera-Bruno urged the developers in the audience to brainstorm innovative ways to reduce their construction costs.
“Every dollar that we do not justify is a person that we can’t provide housing for,” she said.
Lamont is up for reelection in November. His opponent, Republican Ryan Fazio, has identified housing affordability as a key issue and called for major changes to the housing law.
In a phone interview, Fazio said the law “undermines local control and also doesn’t improve housing affordability and availability.”
“I have not gone to a single small town or medium-sized town and heard any positive feedback about 8002,” he said, referring to the legislation. “All of this belies reality, and it’s a product of the fact that the governor wasn’t an assertive leader on this topic.”
Moments after Lamont stepped off stage, Mosquera-Bruno called him back. She told him some attendees had asked her if Connecticut would continue to invest the same resources in housing in the future. 
“Housing’s going to be our No. 1 priority,” he replied.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Advocates debate merits of repealing Washington’s new high-earner income tax
text:
Labor unions and other supporters of an income tax on millionaire earners rallied at the Washington state Capitol in Olympia in February. On this week's edition of "The Impact," representatives for and against repealing the tax made their cases. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)The fall election is a test of the new 9.9% state income tax on households that bring in more than $1 million a year. Initiative 645 aims to overturn the tax before it takes effect.
Championed by Gov. Bob Ferguson and passed by the Democratic majorities in the legislature, it’s now up to the voters to decide if the new tax will stand.
Senate Bill 6346, signed into law March 30, will apply to earnings above that threshold from 2028 forward. I-645 could overturn the tax before the first payment is due in 2029.
Supporters of the repeal effort say it’s an opportunity to prevent lawmakers from expanding the income tax to non-millionaire households in the future.
I-645 supporter Jaime Herrera Beutler, a former congresswoman, told “The Impact.”
“There’s already lawmakers calling to lower that threshold and we’ve heard crickets from legislative leaders about that,” she said.
“The reality is they put all the pieces in place to expand it to all of us and I think voters deserve the truth,” she added.
Herrera Beutler argues that the initiative is also a way to shield retirement plans for teachers, firefighters, and other state employees from being taxed in the future and notes that the bill which created the new tax also eliminated longstanding exemptions.
“It’s important that folks understand this is also a retirement tax,” said Herrera Beutler. “They removed the exemption protecting their retirement checks from being taxed by the state.”
I-645 opponent, April Sims, who leads the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, argues state worker retirement benefits are not at risk.
“This is a campaign slogan from a losing initiative and they’re trying to scare folks into giving a handful of the wealthiest people in our state a $13-billion tax break,” said Sims. “That was a technical fix, is my understanding, to bring this new millionaire’s tax in alignment with IRS regulations.”
Herrera Beutler contends many small business owners will be subject to the tax.
“This doesn’t really hit the large corporation which is, I think, where you see most of the animus. This will have a pretty big impact on small- and medium-sized businesses, which employ half of the Washington workforce,” she said.
Sims sees the new tax as a step towards a more equitable tax code for average state residents and small business owners.
“That’s why the millionaires tax includes things like the largest tax break for small businesses in our state’s history, and expansion of the working families tax credit to nearly a half a million more households, the elimination of sales tax on the things that we all buy like shampoo and toothpaste and conditioner, free lunch and breakfast for school kids,” said Sims.
The fate of the new tax may remain uncertain even if it survives the election, because a separate challenge is pending in the courts.
This story was update to correct the spelling of Jaime Herrera Beutler.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Bidding wars, $15,307 diamond ring sale lead to $57K auction success, says Nebraska treasurer
text:
A diamond ring yielded the highest bid amount in an online auction of unclaimed property organized by the Nebraska State Treasurer's Office. (Courtesy of Treasurer's Office)LINCOLN — A diamond ring that had been stashed in an abandoned safe-deposit box for more than a decade now has a new owner.
A Roger Maris baseball card was one of the auction items that created a stir. (Courtesy of Nebraska Treasurer’s Office)
It went for $15,307 — nearly twice its appraised value — in an online auction organized by the Nebraska State Treasurer’s Office, which by law takes custody of such forgotten property and tries to get it back into the hands of owners or heirs.
Items that remain unclaimed for a period of time can be auctioned, and the state treasurer held such an eBay event Oct. 6-14.
Materials contained in roughly 80 safe-deposit boxes involved in the auction resulted in gross proceeds of $57,305, the treasurer reported. That’s $20,331 above the appraised value of all items up for bid.
Reaping the highest amount was the two-carat diamond ring, which sold for $15,307 after a starting bid price of about $8,000.
A 14-karat gold mesh purse sold for $10,307.
Just a few items went without garnering a bid. Among those was a black rock, a spokesperson said.
 ‘Win, win, win’

Treasurer Joey Spellerberg told the Nebraska Examiner Thursday that he didn’t know what to expect, but considered the auction a success.
State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg. (Courtesy of Treasurer’s Office)
“It’s a win, win, win,” he said.
Abandoned merchandise now can be appreciated by new owners, he said. And sale proceeds have been recorded in the original owner’s name — to be held until that person or heirs come forward.
Money raised in the auction does not become state revenue. It can be held “in perpetuity” if a rightful owner does not surface, said Spellerberg.
Among other winners was the top bidder for a 1961 Topps No. 2 Roger Maris baseball card, which sold for $425 after 30 bids. Another bidding war erupted over a batch of Sports Illustrated Kids Cards, which reached 43 bids and sold for $355.
A group of Red Seal $2 bills sold for $479 in 38 bids.
Meanwhile, some space has been cleared from the area where the state treasurer stores abandoned safe-deposit boxes received from banking institutions.
By law, the treasurer is to conduct a sale of unclaimed property every five years. The last auction was held in 2017. Spellerberg said he is evaluating whether online auctions will be held more frequently under his watch.
“But I think these auctions could happen on a more frequent (basis) as we look to catch up and free up space for new items.”
Nine-year dry spell ends Tuesday when state treasurer resumes unclaimed property auction

 Waiting to be claimed

Notwithstanding the gap between auctions, the treasurer’s Unclaimed Property Division staff has not stopped trying to locate original owners of lost items and encouraging Nebraskans to search NebraskaLostCash.gov. According to a media release, staff members send letters to owners whose addresses are available and run statewide newspaper and radio ads.
Spellerberg applauded the work of his staff. The auction was managed by J&J Coins and Collections. Auction items were appraised by independent appraiser Tom Bassett of Lincoln.
State law puts the treasurer in charge of the unclaimed property as a consumer protection measure until rightful owners or heirs claim it. That property also includes dormant bank accounts, uncashed checks, unpaid wages and life insurance proceeds.
Since the law was implemented in the late 1960s, the state has returned about $320 million to rightful owners, Spellerberg said. “One in five Nebraskans has unclaimed property, with money waiting to be claimed in all 93 Nebraska counties.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Vance calls Michigan’s U.S. Senate race a ‘test’ of gratitude versus grievance in rally for Rogers
text:
Vice President JD Vances speaks at a rally to support Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers of White Lake ahead of the Nov. 3 general election on Thursday, Oct. 15 in Monroe, Mich. (Screenshot courtesy of C-SPAN)Shoring up support for former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake in Michigan’s high-stakes U.S. Senate race was the main mission for Vice President JD Vance as he visited a sports center in Monroe Thursday, all the while framing the race as a test for what he called “a battle between grievance and gratitude.”
Rogers is in a toss-up race against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Both candidates have been barnstorming across the state, sometimes in unlikely places. Rogers spent much of the week in Detroit seeking support from Black voters while El-Sayed, on Thursday, was making a swing through northern Michigan, including stops in Escanaba and Iron Mountain with U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York).
Like Ocasio-Cortez visiting rural Michigan for El-Sayed, Vance flying in to support Rogers was another show of significant support from both sides’ national parties. Although other candidates received shoutouts from Vance — including GOP gubernatorial nominee John James — Vance’s focus was squarely set on Rogers’ race against El-Sayed, and what it would mean for the nation if Michigan chose the progressive Democrat over Rogers.
“The far left, the radicals of the Democratic Party, they’re on the ascent,” Vance said. “These people are looking ahead to the future, and they’re plotting. ‘How do we seize complete control of one of America’s great political parties?’ And they’re testing with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed. They’re testing just how extreme, just how far can they go in a nice, common sense Midwestern state like this one. The people of Michigan. My message to you is: They’re not testing me. I don’t vote here. They’re testing you.”
Vance also accused El-Sayed of adopting what he called the grievance-based platforms of the far left, which the vice president described as designed to “fundamentally destroy America.” He also claimed that El-Sayed was “obsessed” with foreign nations and conflicts abroad, namely Israel and its ongoing war with Hamas in Gaza. El-Sayed has said that he supports the plight of the Palestinian people in the conflict and has called for a reexamination of America’s relationship with Israel in terms of military and defense funding.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You listen to the man talk, and it’s clear, Abdul doesn’t love this community, Democrat or Republican,” Vance said. “He doesn’t love the people who live here. He hates the history of the United States of America. He calls our nation irredeemably racist. He calls the United States of America genocidal, and he hates the people who built it — people like my grandfather, who was for 40 years a union welder at the Middletown Works of Armco Steel in Ohio. Abdul says that men like this, men like you, men like your father and grandfather, and your son, were bigots.”
Vance also insinuated that El-Sayed wasn’t loyal to the U.S. because he alleged that El-Sayed falsely claimed he had dual-citizenship with Egypt and the U.S. “just to sound less American.”
“My friends, ask yourself this: What is it that animates Abdul El Sayed and drives him to seek public office? It is not the well-being of his fellow Americans. It’s not the hopes or aspirations of the amazing auto workers of Detroit, or the students of Ann Arbor, or families in Flint,” Vance said. “No. What excites him is this prospect of wielding the power of a country he hates. He wants to litigate ancient grievances with your tax dollars, and he wants to use the grievances of faraway lands to punish you. Well, I say on Nov. 3, send a message to Abdul El Sayed. Punish him. Don’t send him to Washington D.C.”
Instead, Vance urged his supporters at the Monroe rally to send Rogers to the U.S. Senate.
“I don’t know why he resents the things that he does. Perhaps it’s because he sees them as too white or too proud or too American,” Vance said. “But what I do know is this: that Michigan deserves better. You deserve better than a little weasel who should shut his mouth and show a little gratitude to the country that gave him everything. You deserve a senator who is grateful to this country. You deserve a senator who spent his life serving it in uniform and out. You deserve a senator who looks at this state and sees something to protect and to build upon, not something to apologize for.”
Vance said that man was Rogers, who earlier in the speaking order thanked Vance for his support just a few weeks removed from the November general election.
Rogers also framed El-Sayed as “the most extreme, dangerous candidate to ever run for the United States Senate in the history of our country.”
“We have to stop him right here in Michigan. He is lying about his ties to the Muslim Brotherhood,” Rogers said. “The IRGC, the Iranian Republican Guard — that is the enforcement mechanism for the largest state sponsor of terrorism in the world — which he refuses to condemn, is telling Americans to vote for Democrats like El-Sayed. Think of it: the IRGC telling you to vote Democrat for guys like El-Sayed. Well, I know you won’t listen.”
Rogers, national Republicans and conservative media outlets have accused El-Sayed of either accepting money from members of the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist organization or individuals associated with the movement. Bridge Michigan reported in September that there was no evidence that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood or issued support for their movement, but Rogers, who mentioned the Muslim Brotherhood eight times in his address in Monroe, has made it a primary concern.
Democrats accuse Vance of trying to bail out Rogers, James
Prior to the Vance and Rogers rally, former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D-Lansing) state Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) and other state Democrats railed against the vice president and his boss, President Donald Trump, with Stabenow saying it was an attempt to parachute “into Michigan to try to bail out Mike Rogers and John James, two of the most loyal supporters of Trump’s failed agenda.”
“It’s crucial, really critical for everybody in Michigan, that we elect leaders that are going to fight back against the chaos and the corruption caused by Donald Trump and the Republicans,” Stabenow said.
Brinks is the running mate of Democratic Party gubernatorial nominee and current Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who faces James, a sitting congressman, and state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay), James’ running mate. James and Benson are set to square off in a second televised debate Thursday evening.
Detroit City Councilmember Denzel McCampbell, who has endorsed El-Sayed, was also on the call.
“Whether it was Mike Rogers’ support for a reckless war in Iran, chaotic tariffs, or healthcare cuts, the Rogers-Trump agenda has made life more expensive for working families in our state,” McCampbell said. “Mike Rogers represents everything wrong with Washington. He’s running to serve himself, Donald Trump, and the corporate special interests bankrolling his campaigns. Michigan deserves better — and that is why I’m proud to support Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to be our next United States Senator.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Oracle says it will cut Project Jupiter emissions after New Mexico org seeks to toss permit case
text:
Aerial photos taken on June 26, 2026, show construction progress for Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI data center project planned for southern New Mexico. (Courtesy of Alexa Reynaud, Food & Water Watch, with aerial support provided by LightHawk)With a hearing still pending for an air quality permit for the Project Jupiter data center in southern New Mexico, Oracle Corporation on Thursday announced plans to cut emissions from the data center’s proposed power source by 35%, citing feedback it’s received from NMED and the public.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under the newly announced plans, the power source’s annual greenhouse gas emissions would drop from about 8.8 million tons per year to 5.7 million, the company noted in a news release.
“NMED’s staff asked hard technical questions, and they pushed us to address the concerns raised by the public,” Mahesh Thiagarajan, executive vice president and head of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, said in a statement. “We have been fully cooperating with the agency to answer every question and provide all the information it requested. We studied the issues raised in the public record and came back with refinements that do even more to protect New Mexico’s air and climate.”
The corporation’s announcement followed a request from environmental advocates on Wednesday that the hearing officer presiding over the pending air quality permit toss the case after newly released documents raised questions about the project’s potential pollution levels.
The New Mexico Environment Department earlier this month published thousands of pages of documents as part of the administrative record in the pending air quality permit case. The application from Project Jupiter’s developers seeks permission to power the data center with a fuel cell system that would rely on a yet-to-be-built natural gas pipeline.
Source NM previously reported that the developer’s initial application showed the fuel cell system could emit as many greenhouse gases as New Mexico’s largest cities combined.
However, Project Jupiter opponent Mariel Nanasi, an attorney who leads the Santa Fe-based clean energy advocacy organization New Energy Economy, on Wednesday filed a motion asking the hearing officer presiding over the matter to toss the application based on new details found in the lengthy administrative record.
Contested New Mexico hearing officer for Project Jupiter air quality permit hearing recuses himself

Namely, emails between the New Mexico Environment Department and attorneys representing Project Jupiter’s developers show that recent modeling indicated the potential for a much higher concentration of pollutants in the proposed fuel cell system’s emissions.
In one of the emails, an NMED attorney wrote that the finding “calls into question whether the original use of assumptions is a defensible and conservative approach.”
To critics like Nanasi, that question ought to “stop this proceeding in its tracks.”
“The agency charged with determining whether this massive facility complies with New Mexico’s air-quality laws has itself questioned whether the assumptions underlying the original pollution modeling are defensible,” Nanasi said in a Wednesday statement. “The Air Quality Bureau cannot simply proceed toward a hearing as though nothing material has changed.”
Retired federal judge James Browning, the newly appointed hearing officer presiding over the air quality permit case, at a Thursday meeting said he intends to hold an Oct. 26 hearing regarding Nanasi’s motion to dismiss.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermonters relieved and conflicted after Trump backs off execution livestream
text:
An armed guard walks around the fortified Lawrence William Judicial Center as the sentencing phase for Maj. Nidal Hasan continues, Tuesday, Aug. 27, 2013, in Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 of his unarmed comrades in the deadliest attack ever on a U.S. military base. Photo by Eric Gay/AP

Nancy Welch was driving to the barn to see her horses when news of a planned livestreamed execution came over her car stereo. The barn is where she normally goes for an escape. This time, she couldn’t. 
So when President Donald Trump called off the livestream Thursday, Welch felt some relief. But that wasn’t the point. Not entirely, at least. 
“We won’t face the horror of an execution turned into a grisly public spectacle, but we should still feel revulsion that the execution by firing squad will still take place,” said Welch, who lived in Vermont for 27 years, taught at the University of Vermont and was a vocal advocate against the death penalty. Welch now lives in New Hampshire.
Trump’s reversal Thursday followed bipartisan criticism of plans to broadcast the Dec. 3 execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. 
But while the livestream proposal united some critics across political lines, capital punishment itself remains far more divisive. Some Vermonters believe the controversy has shifted attention away from the longstanding debate over whether the death penalty should be used at all. 
When Paul Dame, chair of the Vermont Republican Party, got the news, he was of two minds.
Although Dame knows many in his party support the death penalty, he said he personally cannot get behind it. Even after horrible crimes, he believes in the possibility of redemption.
“For me, ending, you know, ending a life is a really serious endeavor,” Dame said. “And it’s one I know I’m not sure we should take lightly.”
This case, however, is an “uncommon event and an uncommon crime,” Dame said, adding that it is “the closest thing we have to a real case of treason.”
“When you have a military member who has security clearance and access to a military base where military families live, and they turn on the people supporting them, it’s hard to imagine a crime worthy of greater punishment,” Dame said.
But livestreaming the spectacle felt to Dame to be a step too far, he said, particularly considering the fact that Hasan was paralyzed in the course of his capture and now uses a wheelchair.
“We don’t need to create a public spectacle out of something like that,” Dame said.
The decision could also have fed Hasan’s desired goal of martyrdom, according to Abe Bonowitz, executive director of Death Penalty Action, a national organization dedicated to ending the death penalty. To broadcast this execution would be to elevate it, which is often the goal of terrorist actions, he said.
“How many of us are going to know the names of any one of the 13 people that died or the 32 people that were injured?” Bonowitz said. “Everybody’s going to know his name.”
Bonowitz also argued that the timing of the announcement seemed politically significant.
“We are glad that the President succumbed to the pressure he received even from death penalty supporters, but let’s not lose sight of what this is really about,” Bonowitz later wrote in a text to VTDigger, adding that this case served as a distraction from the economy, the Iran war and the upcoming elections.
Lori Hibbard, the daughter of Teresca King, a Vermont woman who was abducted and killed by Donald Fell in 2000, wrote in a text to VTDigger that she wasn’t opposed to a public execution, although as a mother she would not let her kids watch it.
Still, Hibbard said she was skeptical of whether the livestream would act as a deterrent for future crimes, though she empathized with the families involved with the Fort Hood case.
“I know what it’s like to be a victim of random acts of violence,” Hibbard said. “Stays with you forever.”
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who said his goal was to show the consequences of actions like Hasan’s, originally proposed streaming the execution. Bonowitz said that decision was premature since Hasan could still file a habeas petition, or a challenge to the legality of one’s detainment.
Welch urged the country to still reckon with the ethics of a death sentence, even if it will no longer be broadcast.
“Capital punishment does not restore at all the lives that were taken by this gunman or by any gunman or murderer,” Welch said. “It instead robs us of the public reckoning with why we live in such a violent society, why we have mass shootings, and what needs to change in our society and our government.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermonters relieved and conflicted after Trump backs off execution livestream.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Central Arkansas congressional candidates debate independence from Trump, cost of living
text:
U.S. Congressional District 2 candidates Chris Jones (D) and incumbent Rep. French Hill (R) shake hands after the debate at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Democrat Chris Jones said Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill is too closely aligned with President Donald Trump as the two rivals running for a central Arkansas congressional seat that’s gaining national attention debated Thursday.
Hill argued that Congress has attempted to check Trump’s power during his two non-consecutive terms. Jones disagreed, pointing out that the six-term congressman’s voting record has almost always matched Trump’s priorities.
“That’s not holding him accountable,” Jones said. “That’s letting him have free reign for [his] reckless decisions.”


 

 
The candidates for Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District butted heads over a variety of issues, including the war in Iran, the $40 trillion national debt and the affordability of healthcare and housing.
Hill is a banker who chairs the House Financial Services Committee. Jones is a pastor and scientist whose first foray into politics was his unsuccessful 2022 bid for Arkansas governor.
The 2nd District includes all or part of eight counties, including part of Little Rock, where Jones and Hill both live.
The race has drawn endorsements and spending from both major parties. An August Talk Business & Politics poll indicated a tight race.

Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms

 

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has included the 2nd District among the GOP seats it aims to flip in November. Political forecasters Larry Sabato and the Cook Political Report have recently moved the race in Democrats’ favor, from safe to likely Republican.
Democrats still face long odds in a state where the party’s nominees haven’t been elected to statewide or federal office since 2010. Hill’s campaign has also outraised and outspent Jones, who would be Arkansas’ first Black member of Congress if he wins.
Hill has split with Trump on some issues, including opposing the president’s plan to allow more beef imports into the U.S. He mentioned Thursday that earlier this year, Trump abruptly canceled plans to sign bipartisan housing legislation that Hill championed.
“President Trump said it wasn’t a good bill, and I told President Trump no,” Hill said.
 Cost of living

Trump ultimately allowed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act to become law without his signature. The law removed some of the regulations on housing manufacturing and bank loans for homebuyers. Jones said the law had some good qualities but did not go far enough to make homeownership more affordable.
Jones has repeatedly criticized Hill’s support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, a sweeping budget bill Trump signed last year that is expected to cut Medicaid and food stamps by more than $1 trillion over the next decade.

More than 800,000 low-income or disabled Arkansans rely on Medicaid, and work requirements for able-bodied enrollees are expected to cut thousands of people from the Medicaid rolls when they go into effect Jan. 1.
Hill defended his support for the work requirements and touted the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Arkansas has received and distributed more than $200 million from this pot of money so far this year.
Low reimbursement rates force Arkansas hospitals to scale back services

The Rural Health Transformation Fund supports new healthcare initiatives but isn’t meant to alleviate the costs of hospital operations. Jones said the fund is a net loss for Arkansas hospitals, which already receive low reimbursement rates from Medicaid and from private insurers. Hospitals have cut services in response, including in Jacksonville, which no longer has an emergency room.
Jones said the costs of healthcare, groceries and gasoline have been voters’ primary concerns throughout his campaign. The cost of gasoline has risen since February, when Trump started the ongoing war in Iran.
Hill defended his support for the effort “to once and for all eliminate a nuclear weapon in Iran” in response to Jones’ criticism.
Both candidates said they oppose Trump’s plan to purchase diesel fuel from Russia. Jones said the move will keep gas prices high, and Hill said he would instead support waiving the federal diesel fuel tax.
 Access to elected officials

Jones and Hill also clashed during the debate over Hill’s availability to the public.
Hill said he visits the 2nd District weekly, responds to constituents’ letters consistently and holds town halls via phone. Jones said he’s heard a different story on the campaign trail.
“How many of you all have had an opportunity to not only say something to Mr. Hill, but to get an authentic response back?” Jones said. “I’ve talked to folks who have not. They’ve tried time and time again.”
In his closing statement, Hill said he has “a servant’s heart,” citing his past experience as Little Rock Rotary Club president.
“I ask everyone, in this semiquincentennial year of America, to reject this far-left, big-government approach, vote for common sense [and] support centrist policies like I’ve offered in my leadership in the House,” Hill said.

Norma Jean (Feltman) AllenSeptember 7, 1935 – October 5, 2026Shared by: Mortimore Funeral Home and Cremation ServicesNorma Jean Allen, 91, was called to eternal peace on October 5, 2026, while in her home as independent as ever!
Norma was born on September 7, 1935, in St. Louis, Michigan, to Clarence and Clara (Meyer) Feltman. On July 4, 1953, at seventeen, she married FD Allen. Over sixty-five years, they built a life of children and adventure, moving to Wyoming in 1981 to buy a hotel and farm. Norma continued the adventure after her husband passed away in 2018.
Norma loved her family! She found great joy in conversation, sharing stories and catching up on life events all while beating you at a game of rummy. Norma always had goodies, and if she knew what you liked, you can bet it would show up in her kitchen!
She was in the height of her glory as a grandma, great-grandma, and great-great-grandma! She was proud of her grandchildren and loved to share what they were up to. Pure happiness and contentment graced Norma’s face at every holiday and family gathering as she watched her loved ones spend time together (and enjoy her noodles).
Norma was preceded in death by her parents, siblings, and husband. She is survived by her five children, Ray (Alice), Debbie (Dennis Coleman), Wanda (Chuck Niersel), Tony (Jamie), Bill (Jan), nine grandchildren and spouses, twelve great-grandchildren, and three great-great-grandchildren.
In honor of Norma’s wishes, we will not hold a service. Instead, please enjoy a treat and cherish your loved ones as a way to offer respect and condolences.








Waltrina Watson AscheMay 3, 1941 – September 19, 2026Cheyenne, Wyoming.Shared by: Schrader, Aragon & Jacoby Funeral HomeWaltrina “Trina” Watson Halamka Asche completed her earthly journey on September 19, 2026. She was born on May 3, 1941, in El Paso, Texas, to John R. Watson and Julia A. (“Judy”) Pritchett Watson. She passed away in Cheyenne, Wyoming, at the Davis Hospice Center.
Trina was the oldest of three girls and was preceded in death by her parents, an infant brother John R. Watson III, and her youngest sister Barbara Links. She is survived by her children Franklyn Elliot Halamka (Lisa) and Triana Ann Halamka Burrill (Dave), four grandchildren, seven great-grandchildren, her sister Nana Wilson (John), five nieces and nephews, and countless others who loved her and called her “Grandma Trina.”
Waltrina always considered herself a Texan and cherished the rich heritage of her ancestry. Both her parents’ families settled in Texas prior to the Civil War. In later years, she took special joy in discovering more about her family’s history.
Trina graduated from Grossmont High School in El Cajon, California. She began nursing school and worked for a time as a “candy striper” and nurse’s aide at the Motion Picture Hospital. Trina married Frank Karél Halamka on December 31, 1961. This union brought forth her two children, Franklyn and Triana. Later she was married to Fred Asche from 1976 to 1982. While her children were growing up, Trina worked in various fields, finally settling into the home care industry in the Minneapolis/St Paul area. After retirement, she became a well-known Pampered Chef consultant in the Torrington, Wyoming area.
Throughout her life, one of her greatest gifts was her servant’s heart. She was always ready to help anyone in need, no matter the time or cost. Her greatest desire was to serve others and lighten their burdens.
Waltrina loved her church family and studying Scripture, participating in several Bible studies. She enjoyed sewing, doing jigsaw and crossword puzzles, visiting with friends, and most of all, keeping up with her family’s lives, no matter where they were. Listening to Southern Gospel Music was another passion; she said it reminded her of the time in her life when she came to know Jesus.
Services for Waltrina will be held at Cheyenne Evangelical Free Church, 7006 N. College Drive, Cheyenne, WY 82009 on October 21, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. A light lunch will follow.
Memorials can be made to Cheyenne Evangelical Free Church, The Gideons International, or Davis Hospice Center.








Talbert DeVaughan BowenOctober 30, 1978 – October 10, 2026Shared by: Vase Funeral HomeTalbert “Dee” DeVaughan Bowen III was born on October 30th. 1978 in Colorado Springs, Colorado. He passed away on October 10th, 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah at 47 years old. He spent the majority of his life in Wyoming, calling Green River his home.
Dee enjoyed his career working in the oilfield as a CDL driver. Cool or neat rocks often followed him home from the road to add to his collection and share with his grandkids. They would also often be found weighing down his wife’s purse.
In 2019 his “really great beard” scored him his beautiful wife. They met at Peterbilt in Rock Springs, Wyoming. Dee and Rachel were married in 2021 where he devastatingly missed his opportunity to say “Foreeeeverrrr,” at the wedding. He liked her that day.
He loved spending his time with his family, fishing, golfing with his wife, as well as riding and being free on his motorcycle. He especially enjoyed grilling, smoking, and making soups, often earning its position as a highlight of every weekend. “I cook how I like it – with love!” Dee loved his family very much and loved to express it anytime he could. You would often overhear Dee telling his grandchildren that they were ugly and to remember to use their brains. When times were tough you could find Dee at his place of peace, a river in the mountains. He always did his best thinking on the river.
Survivors include his wife, Rachel Bowen of Green River, Wyoming; father, Talbert Bowen II of Sterling, Colorado; four sons, Talbert Bowen IV companion Samantha Brough of Rock Springs, Wyoming; Christopher Bowles of Rock Springs, Wyoming; Jeffrey Bowles and wife Ashlinn of Green River, Wyoming; Kevin and Hallee Bowles of West Jordan, Utah; three daughters, Brianna Bowen of Cheyenne, Wyoming; Josephine Bowen of Cheyenne, Wyoming; Robyn Bowles and companion Hayden Larson of Rock Springs, Wyoming; two brothers, Alan Bowen and Alyssa of Lone Star, Colorado; Donnie Morgan and wife Tiffany of Casper, Wyoming; one half- sister Adra Cochran of Casper, Wyoming; ten grandchildren, Liam Bowen; Brooklyn McAllister; Harper Bowen; Daphne Williams; Brody Bowles; Brixlie Bowles; Berkley Bowles; Bristol Bowles; Skye Bowles; Rynnley Larson; several aunts, uncles, cousins, nieces and nephews.
He was preceded in death by his paternal grandfather, Talbert Bowen I; grandmother-in-law, Dorothy Wimmer “grandma Rifle”.
A celebration of life will be held at a later date. His final wish was for everyone to skip the heavy hearts and remember the good times. In lieu of tears, pour a shot of Irish Whisky to celebrate his memory.
The family respectfully requests donations be made in Dee’s memory to Support Now:  https://www.supportnow.org/the-bowen-family-7658f776-9703-4427-b433-2880939ab76c
Condolences may be left Vase Funeral Homes.










Genevieve BriandSept. 4, 1968 – Oct. 3, 2026Laramie, WyomingShared by: Haskell Funeral HomeGenevieve Briand was born in Nantes, France, and passed away suddenly but peacefully at home in Byron on October 3, 2026.
Genevieve Briand was born September 4, 1968 to Denis and Marie-Jo Briand in Nantes, France and passed away suddenly but peacefully at home in Byron on October 3, 2026. She grew up in Le Cep, France at her family’s farm and eventually made it to Ecole Superieure d’Agriculture in Angers France which is a sister school of the University of Wyoming. In 1990 she did a summer internship in Wyoming with the Ag department at the University of Wyoming. She liked it enough to return in 1992 to work on a Ph.D. in economics at the University of Wyoming. In the fall of 1995, she met her future husband Dan Bodtke and they were married May 24, 1997 in Capenter, Wyoming. After which she started her journey to become a US citizen and finish her degree.  Dan took a job in Pullman, Washington so Gen had to delay her studies. She finished her Ph.D. in Agricultural Economics at Washington State University in 2002 and became a US Citizen in April 2005. In December 2005 she welcomed her daughter Gwynff into her life. In 2015 she returned to Wyoming and settled in Byron to be closer to Dan’s parents. While she taught economics in person and online for various places including Eastern Washington, Washington State, University of Idaho, John Hopkins, Montana State and NWC, her main passion in life was family. She spent many hours doing craft projects to share memories with family members. She was vibrant and full of life and will be dearly missed.
Genevieve is survived by her father Denis Briand (France); brother Martin Briand, wife Cecilia and children (France); sister Florence Briand, partner Romuald and children (France); husband Dan Bodtke; daughter Gwynff Bodtke; parents in law Dale and Cynthia Bodtke; brother in law David Bodtke, wife Dawn and children; aunt and uncle Marie-Madeleine and Jean-Claude Choquet and children (France); and many extended family members and friends.
Viewing will be 1 to 3 PM on Sunday October 11th and 7:45 to 8:45 AM on Monday October 12th at Haskell Funeral Home in Lovell. Memorial service will be held at 9 AM on October 12th at Haskell Funeral Home in Lovell. A short graveside service will immediately follow at the Byron Cemetery. A memorial service will be held in France at a later date.








Dorthea ButlerOctober 26, 1935 – September 27, 2026Rock SpringsShared by: Vase Funeral Home
Dorothea Butler, our beloved mother, grandmother and great-grandmother of Rock Springs, Wyoming passed away September 27, 2026 in Visalia, California at age 90 after a courageous battle with cancer.
Born on October 26, 1935 in Rock Springs, Wyoming. Dorothea was the daughter of Joe and Dorothy Pivik. After graduating from Rock Springs High, she pursued a bookkeeping career at City Hall, Saint Cyril and Methodius Catholic School, and Ben’s Foodliner until retirement. She also volunteered for The American Heart Association.
In her early years, Dorothea enjoyed playing bridge with friends and camping with family. She was best known for her passions of gardening and cooking. She loved spending time outdoors taking care of her flowers and plants. When not in the yard, she was in the kitchen making dinners for family and friends. She was very proud of her grandchildren, great-grandchild and loved spending time with them. We will always remember her for her sharp wit and humor.
Dorothea is survived by three daughters Dorothy (Jerry) Smith, Mary (Kelvin) O’Malley-Holub and Kelly O’Malley; four grandchildren Jarrad Smith, Danielle (Greg) Overmohle, Anna (Mark) Brassey, Kyle Holub; one great-grandchild Elizabeth Jo Overmohle.
She was preceded in death by her parents Joe and Dorothy Pivik; sister Marilyn Scott and brother Art Pivik; stepsister Angela Rahonce; stepbrothers Joe Pivik Jr., Carl Pivik, Rudy Pivik and Edward Pivik; spouses Patrick O’Malley, Albert Nelson, Michael Butler and companion Dan Blevins.
In accordance with Dorothea’s wishes, a traditional cremation has taken place a Celebration of Life will be conducted in the spring of 2027.
Condolences may be left at Vase Funeral Homes.








Emil Dale CalvertSept 7, 1969 — Oct 6, 2026Cheyenne, WyomingShared by: Schrader, Aragon & Jacoby Funeral Home
Emil Dale “Skip” Calvert was born September 7, 1969, in Casper, Wyoming, to Floyd and Sharon K. Gums Calvert. He passed away on October 6, 2026, in Cheyenne, Wyoming. Skip left us far too soon. He gained his eternal rest with our Lord and savior Jesus Chrst.
Emil was known to some as Skip Calvert. Skip loved rodeo and rode bareback and bulls in high school.
In 1995, he moved to Cheyenne, Wyoming. He worked in heating and air conditioning in Cheyenne from 1997 to 2026. He spent more than 20 years with Climate Control.
On September 6, 1997, he married Heather Smith in Cheyenne. They had two children, Dorian K. Calvert and Matthew Allen Calvert. Heather and Skip divorced later.
He is survived by his parents, Floyd and Sharon Calvert of Casper, Wyoming; his sister, Tessa, and her husband, Eric Garnhart, of Casper; his daughter, Doriann Kay Calvert; and his son, Matthew Allen Calvert of Cheyenne, Wyoming.
He was preceded in death by an infant son, Johnathan Blaine Calvert, his grandparents; Emil and Margaret Gums, Earl and Jerrie Calvert; and one uncle, John Calvert.
As for his new granddaughter Lillian Izabella, a message from Skip’s son Matthew: “As we bring a new life into this world, she will always remember Grandpa, and he will always be a part of us and our hearts.” We will meet you in Heaven when our Lord calls us home.








Mary Lou CampbellJul 2, 1950 — Oct 5, 2026Alpine, WyomingShared by: Schwab Mortuary & CrematoryMary Lou Campbell, 76, peacefully departed this life on October 5, 2026, at her home in Alpine, Wyoming, surrounded by her loving husband and family.
Mary was born on July 2, 1950, in Jackson, Wyoming, to Phil and Pauline Baux. The third daughter of Phil and Pauline, Mary enjoyed an eventful and joyful childhood growing up in Jackson Hole. She attended Jackson Elementary School and graduated from Jackson-Wilson High School in 1968.
Shortly after graduation, Mary moved to Denver, Colorado, where she lived for a brief time. When her mother, Pauline, became ill, however, Mary returned home to Jackson to help care for her mother, father, and younger sister. It was an early example of something that would come to define Mary throughout her life: when her family needed her, she was there.
After returning to Jackson, Mary met Robert Lee Campbell, who had recently returned home after serving his country in the Vietnam War. The two fell in love and were married in 1973, beginning a marriage and partnership that would span 53 years.
Mary became a mother in 1975 with the birth of her first child. She and Robert built their life together in Jackson Hole, where their family eventually grew to include three children. Their home was one filled with love, forgiveness, laughter, and happiness, and Mary was always at its heart.
Anyone who knew Mary knew how much she loved the holidays, but Halloween and Thanksgiving held an especially dear place in her heart. She loved the colorful change of the seasons—the brilliant autumn leaves, the decorations, the gathering of family, and the feeling that came with that special time of year. An avid holiday decorator, Mary transformed her home with the seasons, creating a place where her family could gather and where memories were made year after year.
Mary also expressed her love through cooking. Over the years, she passed along cherished recipes and a love of preparing food to her children and grandchildren. Those recipes became more than instructions written on a card or remembered from time spent together in the kitchen; they became part of Mary’s legacy. Each time one of her children or grandchildren prepares one of her dishes, a little piece of Mary returns to the kitchen and to the family table.
In that way, the traditions Mary created will continue. Holidays will come, autumn leaves will change, kitchens will once again fill with familiar aromas, and her recipes will be prepared and shared by the generations who follow her. Around those tables, Mary will continue to bring her family together. Though she is no longer physically among us, in those familiar tastes, traditions, stories, and moments together, we are reunited with her in spirit.
In 1994, Mary took on another treasured role when she became a grandmother for the first time. In the years that followed, her family continued to grow with grandchildren and, eventually, great-grandchildren. Through holiday after holiday and ordinary day after ordinary day, Mary cared for her family through their successes, their celebrations, their challenges, and their sorrows. She offered the kind of love that forgave easily, welcomed people home, and remained steadfast through whatever life brought.
Mary remained the heart of her family until the very end.
She is survived by her husband of 53 years, Robert Lee Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming; her sister, Cindy (Ronnie) of Victor, Idaho; her children, Kiley (Christina) Campbell and Beau Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming; her grandchildren, Chandler (Syd) of Fort Collins, Colorado, Cassandra (Chris) of Jackson, Wyoming, Josie Campbell of Etna, Wyoming, Shaylee and Rylie Dobben of Hyrum, Utah, Ethan and Ava Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming, and Adri and Rory of North Carolina; as well as several great-grandchildren who will dearly miss her presence in their lives.
Mary was preceded in death by her parents, Phil and Pauline Baux; her sisters, Jean Davison and Carolyn Brooks; and her youngest son, Lucas Campbell of Alpine, Wyoming.
Mary’s life cannot be measured simply by the years between her birth and her passing. It can be measured in the family she nurtured, the home she created, the holidays she made magical, the people she cared for when they needed her, and the generations who will carry her memory forward.
For more than five decades, Mary and Robert built a life together. For more than half a century, she was a wife, a mother, a sister, and eventually a grandmother and great-grandmother. Through all those years and all those roles, one thing remained constant: Mary loved her family, and her family knew they were loved.
That love remains.
Graveside services for Mary Lou Campbell will be held Friday, October 9, 2026, at 1:00 p.m.








Jeffrey J. CastagnaJune 24, 1961 – Oct. 10, 2026Green River, WyomingShared by: Vase Funeral HomeJeffery James Castagna, 65, passed away peacefully at his home in Green River, Wyoming, on October 10, 2026, after a courageous walk with glioblastoma, carried out with immense strength and grace.
Born in Bemidji, Minnesota, on June 24, 1961, Jeff developed a lifelong appreciation for the outdoors, craftsmanship, and community. As an avid outdoorsman, he found true peace in nature through hunting, archery, and fishing with flies he carefully tied himself. Through his camera lens, he pursued his love of photography—documenting wildlife and landscapes, as well as capturing every highlight at his grandchildren’s sporting events. Whether out in nature enjoying God’s creation or spending time with family and close friends, Jeff was right where he wanted to be.
Jeff was also a talented carpenter and draftsman. With a keen eye for design and functionality, he took pride in crafting cherished treasures and spaces that brought utility, warmth, and a true sense of home to those around him.
Above all, Jeff was a dedicated educator. His greatest joy in life came from teaching—he derived deep fulfillment from guiding his students, helping them unlock their potential, and inspiring them to discover their own unique strengths and passions. He spent 35 years pouring into the lives of his students at Sweetwater County School District #1. He loved knowing that he was teaching them lifelong skills that they could use regardless of career choice. He stayed in touch with many of his students and took great pride when they shared the impact he had made in their lives.
Jeff possessed a deep, genuine kindness that left a lasting mark on everyone fortunate enough to know him. Embodying a true sense of “Minnesota nice”, his warmth wasn’t loud or performative. It was rooted in a quiet humility and a sincere, thoughtful consideration for others. Whether he was offering a helping hand, sharing a peaceful moment by the water, or simply listening, Jeff made people feel seen, valued, and welcome.
Jeff met the love of his life, Kelly, in 2015. Following a four-year courtship, the couple tied the knot in Tennessee in August 2019—a perfect backdrop that allowed Jeff to cross the Great Smoky Mountains off his bucket list.
He is survived by his wife Kelly Castagna; his chosen daughter, Robyn Meeks; his stepsons, Bobby Brown Jr. (Jerika) and Michael Brown (Ashley); and his cherished grandchildren, Travin, Quintin, Cazden, Raleigh, Lathan, Slayten, and Lexleigh, Sister-in-law, Barb Castagna; his niece and nephew, Laura Castagna and David Castagna; as well as his chosen family, Mark, Kristi, and Joy Hansen, who held a special place in his heart.
Jeff was preceded in death by his parents, James and Bonnie Castagna, and his brother, Steven Castagna.
In Jeff’s memory, let us carry his spirit forward by weaving his quiet kindness into our daily live by slowing down, listening deeply, and treating everyone around us with thoughtful consideration.
The family respectfully requests donations be made in Jeffrey’s memory to the Tunnel to Tower Foundation, P.O. Box 70719, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 17176, or KLOVE Radio Station, 2000 Reams Fleming Boulevard, Franklin, Tennessee 37064. 
Cremation will take place; a Private Family Remembrance will take place at a later date.
Condolences can be expressed at Vase Funeral Homes.

Ruth FalkOctober 8, 1946 – October 3, 2026Sheridan, WyomingShared by: Champion Kane Funeral HomeRuth Falk, 79, of Sheridan, Wyoming, passed away on October 3, 2026 at her home.
Born in Denver, Colorado, to Frederick and Elizabeth Falk, Ruth grew up and lived in Phoenix, Arizona, before moving to Sheridan in 2018.
Ruth worked as a nurse for more than 30 years before retiring. She was a hard worker who showed up for others. Where there was a need, she filled it.
An avid reader, Ruth also enjoyed crocheting during her night shifts at the hospital. Her family still has the blankets to prove it, lasting reminders of the time and care she put into her work.
Love was not always easy for Ruth to give or receive, but she kept trying, often expressing her care by helping others. She loved her grandchildren.
Ruth is survived by her children, Malcolm Hernandez III and Suzanne Kulvinskas, and Suzanne’s husband, Erik Kulvinskas; her grandchildren, Stasys Kulvinskas, Chrysyn Kulvinskas, Lilia Erladson, Shaheen Esmaeili, Yasmin Esmaeili; and her siblings, Mary Gawron, Helen Tyler, Thom Falk, and Margaret Gifford.
