name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi schools show progress, though higher state standards result in more C and D districts
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Half of Mississippi schools and districts are high-performing despite higher standards this year, according to state education rankings released Thursday.
The more rigorous standards underscore state leaders’ efforts to continue the gains that have rocketed Mississippi to national stardom, education leaders said at a press conference about the new grades. The scores released Thursday reflect how schools fared in the 2025-26 school year.


“I’m very proud to say this: We increased our standards, and our districts have responded,” State Superintendent Lance Evans said. “Their performance and the efforts they’ve put forth, in my opinion, have been very successful.”
Superintendent of Education Lance Evans attends a board meeting at the Mississippi Department of Education building in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, July 17, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The Mississippi Board of Education created the accountability framework to judge how well schools serve their students and communities. The system — which awards up to 1,000 points to high schools and districts and 700 points to elementary and middle schools — takes into account state test scores, graduation rates and academic growth. 
State law requires that standards increase when student proficiency rates exceed 75% or when 65% of schools or districts earn a grade of B or higher. After Mississippi met the threshold for grades in 2023, the education agency spent two years resetting the standards to be more challenging. 
The new standards raise the scores required for each letter grade and place more weight on college and career readiness, and this is the first year that doesn’t include the U.S. History assessment, which the state Board of Education voted last June to remove as graduation requirement. The state Board of Education approved the new standards in November. 


This year, 2024-25 reading scores might also be factored into accountability grades for some districts because the test was restructured. 
In the months leading up to this release, the Mississippi Department of Education has said that this year’s letter grades should not be compared to previous years’ — however, point scores are comparable, said C. Alan Burrow, associate state superintendent. 
Evans said the process is “an essential part of ensuring Mississippi students and schools continue to improve academically each year.” 
“If we’re back here at the table in two years resetting the standards again, that won’t be a bad thing,” said Paula Vanderford, chief accountability officer for the agency, while presenting the new grades at the state Board of Education meeting on Thursday.
The board set a goal in 2016 that every school and district in Mississippi is rated C or higher. This year, 121 of the state’s 138 traditional public school districts were rated a C or above, or 87.6%, and 50.7% of districts earned a B or higher.
If the agency had not reset the standards this year, Vanderford noted that 70.7% of districts would have made a B or above. 
All of the state’s public charter schools, though, were ranked C or lower.
The state’s largest school districts, such as DeSoto and Rankin County, continue to post top results. Delta schools appear to struggle in the rankings, but a closer look shows many of the region’s districts are posting improvements.
Many Jackson area and central Mississippi county school districts saw test score drops since last year. Others saw modest gains.
That wasn’t the case for the Simpson County School District. 
Simpson upped its score by 46 points since last year, improving more than any other district in central Mississippi. Mendenhall Elementary moved from a D to a C rated school. 
The district had a new superintendent this past year: Robert Sanders. He credits the improvements to dynamic building leadership and hard working students and staff. 
Simpson County School District Superintendent Robert L. Sanders talks about the district while at Mendenhall Elementary School on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Through a partnership with The Kirkland Group, a Ridgeland-based educational consulting firm, teachers had help analyzing data on student progress. As a result, teachers could focus more on instruction  and lesson planning.
“Back in the day, we had to do this work by hand,” recalled Tommy Brumfield, principal at  Mendenhall Elementary School. “So now, teachers are able to spend more time, not just analyzing data, but being able to make plans from that data and doing something with it.”
Sanders inherited a district in need of better supervision. The district’s chronic absenteeism rate ranked third highest statewide in the 2024-25 school year. In response, Sanders dispatched principals and school staff to knock on doors in the community, and better learn the root causes of absenteeism. He said he’s since seen improvement. 
Magee Middle School saw a 36% drop in its chronic absenteeism rate since last year. The school also moved 84 points on the state accountability scale.
“I’m very pleased within just one year to see a 46-point gain,” Sanders told Mississippi Today on Wednesday. “That speaks to the leadership in our schools, because that’s where it’s happening. You have to look at every child, and you have to make sure when they’re not performing where they need to be, find out why and do the things that will empower your needle to move the right way.”
And though districts closer to the Gulf Coast again dominated the list, some show slight declines.


Long Beach School District has seen the biggest drop among Gulf Coast districts in its state accountability score the past five years, though it’s held on to its A rating. Pascagoula-Gautier School District also retained its B, but the district dropped in points since last year. 
Pascagoula-Gautier’s Superintendent Caterria Payton said the state education agency’s scores and grades don’t reflect the progress happening at her district. She highlighted three schools that improved by a letter grade, and emphasized that no schools earned a D rating.
“While these improvements have not yet resulted in the districtwide gains we expect, they demonstrate that progress is possible and that our efforts must remain focused and consistent,” she said in an emailed statement.
The Mississippi Department of Education is asking for $22 million more next year from the Legislature to focus on early education programs, dyslexia and dropout prevention initiatives. 
Evans said as the state education agency prioritizes areas of improvement and raises expectations, he’s confident Mississippi districts will rise to the occasion. 
“Overall, our districts have answered the call,” he said. “I’m very pleased with the outcome.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: ADPH encourages vaccination after measles case; no new cases immediately reported
text:
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy on Jan. 26, 2015 in Mill Valley, California. Alabama public health officials said Thursday there are no new cases of measles after an Alabamian tested positive for the disease on Tuesday, and strongly encouraged vaccination. (Photo by Illustration Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Public health officials said Thursday there have been no new reported cases of measles after announcing a positive test in north Alabama earlier this week, but strongly encouraged vaccination as cases of the disease mount nationwide.
The Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) was not able to share many details of the positive test in north Alabama on Tuesday, but clarified Thursday the individual is an adult Alabamian who contracted the disease from a trip to South America. The department did not have any vaccination records for the individual.
The department said on Tuesday that the individual was out in public from Oct. 3 to 5 in the Bailey Cove area of Huntsville at a Subway and Publix.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We are conducting epidemiologic surveillance. We are continuing to inform the public. We are informing physicians, emergency rooms, urgent cares about surveillance for measles,” Dr. Karen Landers, the chief medical officer for ADPH, said at a meeting of the ADPH board Thursday. “We will know if we have any additional spread of measles when we know.”
Landers, who was filling in for State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris, said in an interview that the public is informed of a positive test “pretty immediately” after the lab report is verified.
“We verify our information, and we get our handout and our news release out immediately,” she said. “It’s our job to protect the citizens of Alabama, and secondly, we want to give people the information so that they can act accordingly for their own health and well-being.”
Symptoms of the disease can take seven to 14 days to present after infection, and can be particularly dangerous for infants and young children. Symptoms include a high fever, cough, runny nose, red, watery eyes and a rash.
According to CDC and ADPH guidance, children should get the first dose of the vaccine between 12 and 15 months, and the second dose between 4 and 6 years old before starting school. Adults should get one or two doses depending on individual risk factors, according to the department.
Landers said that people born prior to 1957 should be immune due to likely exposure to the contagious disease before the vaccine was developed in the mid-1960s, and that anyone uncertain of their vaccination status should check with their doctor.
“Be aware of this in terms of your own vaccination status, and if you are working in a high-risk situation such as a medical clinic or around patients that might be at higher risk to have severe infections,” Landers said. “I do want to remind people that this – other than persons that are severely immunocompromised – this is a very safe and effective vaccine.”
Alabamians who have received both doses of the vaccine do not need to revaccinate, Landers said. But she said additional doses are not harmful if an individual’s vaccination status is unknown.
Dr. Marquisha Jarmon, a Hoover-based pediatrician, said some of her patients’ parents do not vaccinate their children.
“Being in a pediatric practice, one of the things that I do talk to my parents about – because unfortunately, I do have patients who don’t vaccinate – I take care of other issues for them, but they have chosen not to vaccinate, or they do a delayed schedule,” she said. “One of the things I ask them not to do is that if they have signs of a rash or anything like that, not come to the clinic, and we do a lot of telemedicine for those things. Do you offer a PCR test that we can send to the patient that they can possibly do at home and send out?”
The measles test, known as a RT-PCR test, is a swab in the nose or mouth, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Landers said there is not a take-home option. She recommended Jarmon send her patients to either a private or ADPH laboratory. 
As of Friday, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed 4,080 cases reported by 47 states of the highly contagious virus. In 2025, there were 2,289 cases reported by 45 states. There are currently outbreaks in Pennsylvania, Utah, Maryland, Delaware and Wisconsin. 
One Alabamian has tested positive for the disease this year, but they were out-of-state and posed no threat of an outbreak to Alabama. There was one confirmed case of measles in Alabama in 2025: an unvaccinated child in the northern part of the state who was under five years old. The child later recovered. 
In Pennsylvania, there have been more than 1,200 cases, 225 hospitalizations and five associated deaths. There were three reported deaths in 2025 in the U.S., a 0.13% mortality rate. The CDC has confirmed two deaths so far in 2026, a 0.05% mortality rate. 
“Continue to remind people to vaccinate. This is a safe, effective vaccine. And the way we’ve gotten by in Alabama is we generally have a very high vaccination rate,” Landers said. “But as Dr. Jarmon pointed out, that’s changing.”
According to the CDC, 94.3% of Alabama kindergarteners are vaccinated against the disease for the 2025-26 school year. In the 2024-25 school year, 95.2% of kindergarteners were vaccinated. 
About 92.7% of Pennsylvania kindergarteners are vaccinated against the disease for the 2025-26 school year, according to the CDC. Herd immunity against the disease is reached at 95% vaccination.  
Landers, who was a north Alabama-based pediatrician and infectious control physician before becoming chief medical officer, said in an interview that the only way to protect against measles is to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
“It’s a generational vaccine. It’s probably been given to more people than just about any other vaccine because of the length of time, and there are not any studies that indicate that this vaccine causes side effects in people,” Landers said. “We absolutely need to inform ourselves, talk to our physicians, talk to our pharmacists, and be aware that this disease can be severe and deadly. We don’t want to see that happen in Alabama. We don’t want to see what happened in Pennsylvania happen in Alabama.”
 Weida recommended Alabamians in high-exposure professions – like healthcare providers – ensure they are vaccinated.
“If we don’t know, then they should get at least a dose. And if they’re in healthcare, they need to get two doses,” Weida said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Trump announces ‘super range’ military installment on stump for Montana GOP candidates
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Kalispell on Oct 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)KALISPELL – Crowds began lining up at Majestic Valley Arena more than seven hours before President Donald Trump touched down in the Flathead Valley on Wednesday. 
“It’s not everyday you get to see the president,” said Gayla Pettyjohn, 77, of Kalispell. “This will likely be my only chance.”
Pettyjohn said she has already voted her ballot — Republican all the way down — which is exactly how Trump told his supporters to vote on Wednesday evening. 
“Ladies and gentlemen of Montana, the golden age of America is upon us,” said Trump, who came directly from a rally he held in Arizona earlier Wednesday afternoon. “But you must get out and vote Republican if we’re going to keep it that way.”
The rally was part of a multi-state swing that has seen Trump visit reliably Republican-voting states that have federal races considered competitive this year, including Alaska, Arizona and Ohio. In Montana, the goal was to turn out Republican voters to support U.S. House candidate Aaron Flint and U.S. Senate candidate Kurt Alme. 
“Here in Montana’s first district, we’re going to defeat far-left lobbyist phony Sam Forstag, not respected at all,” Trump said. “And we’re going to elect a true American patriot, a fantastic man, a great guy, Aaron Flint, to Congress.”
During his remarks, Trump also announced that the Department of War will be establishing a new military “super range” in Montana for testing advanced weapons and technology, including autonomous weapons, space systems, electronic warfare and supersonic and hypersonic weapons. 
“Montana will continue to play a critical role in the development and testing of cutting-edge military technology,” Trump said, adding that Republican Montana Sens. Tim Sheehy and Steve Daines were behind the investment. “Steve and Tim, they were brutal. You know, I gave it just to get them to stop calling me.”
Montana’s western congressional district, a seat held by retiring Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, is the state’s most competitive federal race this cycle, with Flint, a veteran and talk radio host, facing smokejumper Sam Forstag, a Democrat. The race is rated as a toss up in the Fox News Power Rankings. 
“We’ve known this is a battleground seat since day one,” Flint told members of the media before Trump’s arrival. “Frankly, if this was easy, I’d let somebody else do it, and I would keep enjoying, you know, my role as a statewide radio talk show host.”
Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte speaks at a rally for President Donald Trump in Kalispell on Oct. 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
 Montana’s politicos show up

While the president ran a few hours behind schedule, the rally’s opening lineup of speakers included Montana’s federal delegation, Gov. Greg Gianforte, and the two hopefuls to represent Montanans in D.C.
Flint worked on Gianforte’s first campaign in 2016, and his old boss told the crowd that they were “here to get Aaron elected.” 
“(President Trump) is working hard to deliver on the promises that he made to us, the American people. But he can’t do it alone,” Gianforte said. “He needs reinforcements. He needs people like Aaron Flint, who won’t flinch at crazy far-left Democrats who attack our way of life.”
The Republicans repeatedly characterized the Democrat in the race as a member of the “crazy liberal” left, with out-of-state roots. They cited Forstag’s time lobbying at the state legislature for a firm that represented the cities of Missoula and Bozeman, and organizations such as the Montana ACLU, and his endorsements from progressive members of Congress including New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders as proof of an agenda Montanans should resist. 
Forstag has lived in Montana since 2012 when he started school at the University of Montana, where Flint also attended. Forstag held a rally in Bozeman on Wednesday evening, with another event in Lincoln County on Thursday with former Republican Gov. Marc Racicot, who has endorsed his campaign. 
Montana Rep. Troy Downing took the attacks a step further, calling Forstag a “commie” and saying “the Bolsheviks are at the door and we can’t let them in.”
“The changes these commies call for is no change at all, it’s destruction,” Downing said. “They want free groceries, free housing, free healthcare, free everything. You know we can give them all these things, but at what cost? I’ll tell you what it’ll cost. It’ll cost freedom.” 
A spokesperson for Forstag said the president’s trip to Montana shows that “Flint is scared.”
“Working people are suffering from the cruel, chaotic cuts that Aaron cheered on from his recording studio,” Forstag said through a spokesperson. “Empty words won’t fix that. We need solutions. So while Aaron bends over backwards for the party bosses who promised him a seat in Congress, I’ll be meeting with Montanans on both sides of the aisle.”
Flint and Forstag debated each other on Tuesday, and Flint repeated many of his attacks on his opponent on stage Wednesday. 
“If there was ever a race in the U.S. that’s the definition of common sense versus crazy, it’s this one,” Flint said when he took the stage, echoing national Republicans’ midterm tagline.
Montana U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke give an interview at a rally for President Donald Trump in Kalispell on Oct. 15, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
 Congressional turnover

Zinke, who is from Whitefish, told members of the press before the event that he was leaving his seat in good hands and cited one of the lessons he learned in the military: “Never leave your post unless properly relieved.”
“This is a man who will fight for us, and believe me every day I’m in Washington, D.C., I fight for us because Washington, D.C., doesn’t understand Montana,” Zinke said on stage. 
While introducing his hopeful successor, Zinke spoke about Flint’s own family history growing up on both sides of the Continental Divide, including in Whitefish. 
“I know Whitefish is the blueberry in the tomato soup, but we’ll get through that,” Zinke said. (Whitefish is represented in the Montana Legislature by both a Democratic state senator and a Democratic state representative.) 
Among jabs at his opponent, Flint also showed his alignment with the president’s values, including those of Trump’s family. 
In his recent drives across the congressional district, Flint said he’d listened to the audiobook of Eric Trump’s book; and said he saw similarities between the Trump children and his own upbringing — they were tucked into bed with the same traditional bedtime prayer: “Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep …”
“The son of hardworking single parents, being tucked away at night to the same prayer as the sons of a very successful billionaire in New York City, and what that tells you is, is that we’re Americans,” Flint said. “We still share the same hopes and the same dreams and the same prayers.”
Flint said he was running for office for his kids’ future, and for “that 105-year-old World War II veteran back there.”
“If that man can get off his feet for you, can you get off your asses and vote to save America this November?” Flint asked the crowd. 
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Kalispell on Oct 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
Neither of Montana’s current senators spoke, as they traveled with the president after attending his rally in Arizona earlier on Wednesday, but the race to replace Daines earned Trump’s first shoutout of the night when Trump said Montanans need to defeat “radical left Dumbocrat Alani Bankhead,” running for the U.S. Senate. (“Who the hell is that?”). 
Alme, who is facing the Democrat and an independent candidate in a race rated to stay in Republican hands, touted his record as a twice-nominated U.S. Attorney for Montana (“Thank you, Mr. President, for being a job reference for me three times.”) and emphasized Republicans’ control of the Senate included keeping Montana red.
As a senator, he said he would continue fighting for “common sense policies,” including reigning in government spending and confirming judicial conservatives to the U.S. Supreme Court. 
“I’m ready to step up again, make lives more affordable, make our country safer and protect the Montana way of life,” Alme said. 
Independent Senate candidate Seth Bodnar was not mentioned in any remarks at the rally. 
Earlier on Wednesday, his campaign released an open letter to the president inviting him to meet. 
 Trump stump

“Less than two years ago, our country was dead, dead, dead as a doornail. Every leader was saying it,” Trump told the Montana crowd. Now, “We’re the hottest country in the world.”
Trump’s visit came at a time when Americans — and Montanans — are deeply concerned about affordability. Flathead County has seen some of the highest increases in housing prices relative to income in the state. 
His midterm rallies are also happening as Trump has falling approval ratings nationwide, but Montana has been one of his most reliable voting bases. 
Trump won Montana’s presidential vote by margins of 21%, 16% and 20% in the last three elections. 
He said that having “record, record, record,” numbers made visiting Montana feel like coming home. 
“But I’m from 5th Avenue. It doesn’t make sense,” he said. “But actually, it makes total sense.”
Besides stumping to “get really great people in office,” Trump spent much of his hour-long speech listing  accomplishments from his two nonconsecutive terms and reasons voters should keep Republicans in office. 
He said he would, “knock this Iran thing off fast,” and that it essentially was finished as they don’t have a navy, air force or army. 
“Their leaders are gone,” he said. “I should have probably left the leaders because I don’t know who the hell we’re negotiating with.”
“One way or the other, it’s going to end very quickly, and when that happens, oil is going to come way down,” he added. 
An attendee at President Donald Trump’s rally in Kalispell on Oct. 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
Trump repeated many of his common rally refrains to great applause, including that he always draws the biggest crowds, that he won the 2020 election (there is no evidence of voter fraud in the 2020 election won by President Joe Biden), and that Democrats would take away guns and Second Amendment rights. 
“How would you like to live up here without guns?” Trump asked. “You know who would love that to happen? Some of the wild animals you have up here that like eating you.”
Trump talked about how the previous administration had led the country into the “dark ages,” and mentioned the decrease in violent crime under his administration to historic lows, according to the FBI, as well as a reduction in illegal border crossings compared to the Biden administration. 
But a few of his lines fell flat, like his remarks about Montana’s “booming” sawmills.
“American sawmills are now supplying more lumber in the United States than at any time in almost 50 years,” Trump said, adding that if he hadn’t implemented tariffs on foreign lumber, “all your sawmills all over the state and all over other states would be closed up.” 
Scattered clapping greeted these statements, as Montana has seen the closure of major mills in recent years, with only around a half dozen still operating. 
Towards the end of his speech, Trump pushed a pledge that if Republicans hold onto the House and Senate, he will give all U.S. citizens a $5,000 dividend estimated to cost more than $1.2 trillion — more than the federal government spends on the military in a year. 
“And only a Republican president can do that,” he said. “The Democrats can’t. The reason is that we’re taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs and record-setting economic success, success like we’ve never seen before.”
Tariff revenue has climbed under Trump, but in 2025 only reached $264 billion. In recent months, tariff collections have declined and even gone negative as the federal government has had to issue refunds for tariffs deemed illegal by the Supreme Court, according to the nonpartisan organization Tax Foundation.  
Trump told voters to “pretend that I’m running,” and left Kalispell around 9 p.m., exiting the stage to the “Y.M.C.A.” 
He is scheduled to be back in the White House on Thursday.

name: Delaware
title: Scouting America honors Delaware business leader as organization builds new momentum
text:
Tonight’s Citizen of the Year dinner celebrates WSFS leader Rodger Levenson while highlighting Scouting’s growing role in developing young leaders, strengthening families and serving communities across Delmarva.
 
WILMINGTON, Del. — When Delaware business and community leaders gather Thursday evening, Oct. 15, to recognize Rodger Levenson as Scouting America’s 2026 Delaware Citizen of the Year, the occasion will be about more than honoring one of the state’s prominent business executives.
It will also be an opportunity to celebrate the return of a familiar institution to a more visible role in Delaware communities.
Scouting America is experiencing renewed interest among families seeking opportunities for their children to develop leadership skills, build friendships, explore the outdoors and learn the importance of serving others.
For the Del-Mar-Va Council, the annual recognition event offers an opportunity to connect the accomplishments of today’s business and civic leaders with the development of tomorrow’s.
Levenson, chairman, president and CEO of WSFS Financial Corp., is the honoree listed for the Oct. 15 dinner on the council’s official event calendar.
The award recognizes the kind of leadership, personal responsibility and commitment to community that Scouting seeks to instill in young people.
A familiar organization finds new purpose
Scouting has been part of Delaware life for more than a century, but today’s organization looks different from the one many parents and grandparents remember.
Camping, hiking, earning merit badges and learning outdoor skills remain important. However, Scouting also introduces young people to technology, engineering, environmental conservation, career exploration and public service.
Perhaps more importantly, it gives children the opportunity to practice leadership rather than simply learn about it.
Scouts organize activities, solve problems, work in teams and take responsibility for projects. As they grow older, those responsibilities become more demanding, preparing them to make decisions, overcome setbacks and lead others.
And in an increasingly digital world, those face-to-face experiences are attracting renewed attention.
In an August interview with Delaware LIVE, Ray Teat, Scout executive for the Del-Mar-Va Council, said participation was recovering after the disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic.
“The number of scouts, scouting units and families involved with Scouting is once again growing following a challenging time for the program coming out of COVID,” Teat said. “But the number of young people, both boys and girls, is growing.”
Tim Holly, president of the council’s executive board, said parents are increasingly recognizing the value of activities that encourage children to interact, become more independent and develop confidence.
“Parents are looking for ways to reconnect their children with other kids and with their communities,” Holly said. “They want them outside, interacting face to face, learning how to work with other people and building confidence through real experiences.”



More than a comeback — a commitment to growth


The renewed interest is supported by a deliberate effort to expand Scouting’s presence throughout the Delmarva Peninsula.
The Del-Mar-Va Council launched a Campaign for Growth covering 2024 through 2026, establishing an ambitious goal of nearly doubling youth membership by the end of 2026.
The council currently reports more than 3,600 young people participating in over 200 Scouting units, supported by approximately 2,000 volunteers across 14 counties in Delaware, Maryland and Virginia. Those figures describe the scale of the program, although the council has not publicly established that its membership-doubling goal has been reached.



anization has also increased its visibility through recruitment nights, family activities and regional events.
In April, more than 1,200 people attended the Del-Mar-Va Council Jamboree at Akridge Scout Reservation near Dover. The gathering, the council’s first jamboree since 2016, brought together Scouts from Delaware and neighboring states for outdoor activities, demonstrations and an opportunity to share the Scouting experience with the public.



It was another indication that the organization is working to reconnect with families and demonstrate how its programs fit the needs of today’s young people.


Business leadership and community service
The Citizen of the Year dinner reinforces another part of Scouting’s mission: connecting individual success with responsibility to the wider community.
By recognizing leaders such as Levenson, the organization highlights the values of leadership, integrity and service that it encourages young people to develop.
Those connections are particularly relevant to Delaware’s business community.
Employers regularly emphasize the importance of communication, teamwork, problem-solving, dependability and the ability to work with people from different backgrounds.
These are skills Scouting seeks to develop through practical experiences, often long before a young person enters college or the workforce.
Whether organizing a food drive, leading a camping trip, completing an Eagle Scout service project or helping younger Scouts learn new skills, participants are expected to contribute to something larger than themselves.
The program also depends heavily on adult volunteers, local organizations, businesses and charitable supporters who provide the resources needed to make those opportunities available.
That makes the Citizen of the Year dinner more than a recognition ceremony. It is also an opportunity to strengthen the relationship between Scouting and the community leaders whose support can help the organization reach additional families.
An investment in Delaware’s future
For a new generation of Delaware families, the appeal of Scouting may be rooted in something remarkably simple: children need opportunities to experience the real world, test their abilities and discover what they can accomplish.
Those experiences can involve an outdoor adventure, a difficult team assignment, a community service project or a first opportunity to lead a group.
They can also introduce young people to careers, interests and responsibilities they might otherwise never encounter.
Scouting’s expansion to serve both boys and girls in its core programs has opened additional opportunities, while its continued emphasis on character, citizenship and personal responsibility gives the organization a consistent mission.
For Delaware’s communities, the benefits extend beyond individual participants. Scouts help maintain public spaces, support local charities, assist community organizations and contribute thousands of volunteer hours through their activities.
The result is a youth development program that seeks to strengthen both the individuals participating and the communities they serve.
Recognizing today’s leaders, preparing tomorrow’s
Tonight’s tribute to Levenson provides a timely illustration of that connection.
Honoring an accomplished Delaware business leader is one way to celebrate the importance of service and leadership. Giving more young people the opportunity to develop those qualities is the larger mission.
With growing family interest, an expanding network of programs and an ambitious membership campaign, Scouting America is working to restore and strengthen its place in Delaware’s community life.
The uniforms, campfires and merit badges may be what people recognize.
But behind those traditions is a broader purpose: helping young people become confident, capable and responsible adults who will someday lead businesses, volunteer organizations, neighborhoods and communities.
That is the larger message behind tonight’s award dinner: Scouting America is building momentum again, and Delaware’s future leaders are the reason it matters.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ramaswamy discusses death and taxes in Ohio at Columbus Metropolitan Club
text:
Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy (L) speaking with Statehouse News Bureau Chief Karen Kasler at the Columbus Metropolitan Club. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal)Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy touted his plans to cut taxes without, he says, sacrificing on schools and local services, during an appearance in Columbus on Wednesday.
He promised to respect the Second Amendment “to the fullest extent” and advance “medical freedom. Ramaswamy also said he plans to resume death penalty executions.
Ramaswamy spoke at a Columbus Metropolitan Club meeting at the National Veterans Memorial and Museum, moderated by Statehouse News Bureau Chief Karen Kasler.
Before the event, CMC CEO & President Sophia Fifner explained they’d invited both candidates to participate in CMC forums, but Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton has not agreed to one.
The Ohio Capital Journal reached out to Acton’s campaign about not accepting the invitation and requested responses to some of Ramaswamy’s comments. The campaign did not immediately respond.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Cutting taxes
Ramaswamy told attendees the root of Ohio’s property tax crisis wasn’t local levies and expanding district budgets — it was government spending in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.
“Your home is worth more on paper, but that doesn’t feel like a financial blessing. It’s a financial curse,” Ramaswamy said. “Because your Social Security payments, your pension payments, your wages have stayed flat while you owe as much as twice as much in property taxes.”
A Brookings study contends the Federal Reserve’s purchase of mortgage-backed securities played a significant role in housing inflation.
While Ramaswamy promises a rollback of property taxes in Ohio to pre-pandemic levels, the mechanism for such a reduction by state government is unclear. Property tax rates are set at the local level, and anything beyond the 10 mills (or 1%) allowed by the state constitution goes before voters for approval.
Those taxes support a wide array of local services including schools, which make up the largest share, first responders, and libraries.
Estimates suggest his rollback could cost $4 billion, but he insists vital services won’t suffer.
“I think this property tax reform that I’m planning is also going to provide an opportunity to revisit statewide funding for something that probably shouldn’t be left exclusively to local property taxes anyway,” he said.
Relying on state funding, Kasler pressed, doesn’t answer the question of where Ramaswamy is going to find $4 billion.
“We actually have the answer this year,” Ramaswamy said, referencing state lawmakers move to cut income taxes to a flat 2.75% rate.
“Ohio’s budget is running now $1.6 billion in surplus relative to prior projections,” he went on. “Why? Because we enjoyed growth as a consequence of that tax cut that resulted in expanded revenue, which then feeds a virtuous cycle.”
Ramaswamy said that budget surplus gave lawmakers the flexibility to fund a gas tax holiday through the end of the year.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Capital punishment
Following a botched execution in Tennessee — the second there this year — Ramaswamy said he remains committed to capital punishment in Ohio.
“I do intend to resume executions in Ohio in the rare cases for the most egregious of crimes,” he said.
Since Gov. Mike DeWine took office, Ohio has been operating under a de facto moratorium on capital punishment.
In June, he issued a statement explaining it is now “impossible to make the case that the death penalty is a deterrent” and so the moral justification for capital punishment “no longer exists.”
Ramaswamy called Tennessee’s failed execution “unacceptable” and said Ohio will carry out sentences in a manner that is “ethically appropriate, scientifically sound, effective, and swift.”
Ramaswamy said there were “limitations” in the way Tennessee administered its executions. In Tennessee officials follow a single drug protocol with pentobabital; Ohio’s protocol uses three drugs, but state law makes the specific drugs confidential.
In response to concerns about Ohio’s lethal injection stockpiles expiring, and with limited options to replenish them, some state lawmakers have proposed using nitrogen gas as a potential execution method. That approach effectively suffocates a person by depriving them of oxygen. Five states explicitly allow it.
In June of this year, the U.S. Supreme Court denied the state of Alabama’s request to use the method to carry out an execution of a death row inmate, which left in place a lower court’s decision ruling the method unconstitutional.
Kasler asked Ramaswamy if he was open to changing Ohio’s execution methods.
“So we’re studying this,” he said. “And it is open-mindedness to methods other than lethal injection, which have been successfully used in the past.”
Red herrings
In the meeting hall, there are large portraits of veterans hanging from the ceiling. Looking up at one of them, Ramaswamy argued that if 18-year-olds are old enough to serve they should be old enough to purchase a firearm.
“That man’s holding a gun. He might be 18 years old, and he’s serving our military, put his life on the line,” Ramaswamy said. “If that’s the case, why can’t you similarly purchase at the age of 18 in certain markets where you’re restricted from doing so before the age of 21? Doesn’t make sense.”
Later, speaking about medical freedom, Ramaswamy brought up “Right to Try” legislation.
“I believe that in certain circumstances,” he said, “patients should be able to, on a fully informed basis, in a relationship between them and their physician, have the ability to access therapies that are still investigational therapies, but nonetheless have the potential to help them, particularly if they suffer from terminal or life-threatening conditions.”
Although the minimum age to purchase a handgun in Ohio is 21, state lawmakers voted in 2008 to grant an exception to active or reserve members of the armed forces as well as those who have been honorably discharged.
Similarly, Ohio approved Right to Try legislation in 2016. That measure allows terminally ill patients to receive an “investigational drug or product,” defined in statute as a therapy which has completed phase one trials.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Jonah Bevin court case now turns to his education
text:
Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson, left, presides over a hearing in the Bevin case on Oct. 15, 2026. Jonah Bevin appeared via video call, seen at right. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd) LOUISVILLE, Ky.— Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson said she needs more information on the education that former Gov. Matt Bevin and his ex-wife, Glenna, provided for their adopted son, Jonah. 
In court Thursday morning, Johnson said: “I want proof that Jonah received an appropriate education, and we’ll go from there.” 
Lawyers for the former governor objected, which Johnson noted. 
The judge previously ordered the Bevins to disclose detailed financial information as part of a proposed settlement in their divorce case and a year-long legal battle with their son, who seeks financial support. 
“In front of me are the three binders of financial documents we produced over the last four or five months,” Jesse Mudd, one of the Bevins’ lawyers, said in court. “We didn’t see one of these at the hearing in July because that didn’t fit their agenda. This isn’t the issue. Case has been argued. Case has been submitted. It needs to be decided so the Court of Appeals can then take a look at it.”  
Johnson said she expects any decision she makes to be sent to the Court of Appeals, but she wants that decision to be based on all available information. 
Attorneys scheduled the next hearing in the case for Jan. 28, when attorneys for Jonah will present more evidence. 
“Whether he got a diploma in a crash course in a year doesn’t necessarily mean that he has the skills to be a successful adult, and that is what sufficiency of education should mean, and that would be our argument,” said Melina Hettiaratchi, one of Jonah’s attorneys, after the status hearing. 
Johnson also said Thursday she will award Jonah’s team some attorney’s fees, though she did not disclose the amount. Hettiaratchi said this money will make it easier for the team to hire an expert to evaluate Jonah’s education. 
“It would basically be just nice to recoup the costs because that would be huge,” she said. 
Neither Glenna nor Matt Bevin was present for the morning’s proceedings. Jonah was present via video call. 
This is the latest in a long court battle as Jonah seeks support from his estranged parents.  He has alleged the Bevins abandoned him at age 17 in an abusive facility in Jamaica, leaving him with no resources or education. 
His lawyers have argued Jonah is entitled to support and resources to complete his education. 
In early September Matt Bevin was arrested in Bourbon County on an outstanding warrant for contempt of court. At the time, he was on the set of a Christmas movie being filmed in Kentucky.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Election analyst: Candidate quality key to Roger Marshall’s slide, Adam Hamilton’s rise in Kansas
text:
Colleen Shogan, former archivist of the United States, draws 2026 election insights at the Dole Institute of Politics from Jacob Rubashkin, center, deputy editor of Inside Elections, and Kirk Bado, editor of The Hotline published by National Journal. (Kansas Reflector screen capture from Dole Institute video)TOPEKA — A pair of Washington political analysts traveled to the Lawrence building honoring the legacy of Republican Robert Dole — undefeated in nine consecutive campaigns for Congress — to explain the stunning reality of Kansas joining the list of states with competitive U.S. Senate races.
Jacob Rubashkin, deputy editor of Inside Elections, and Kirk Bado, editor of The Hotline published by National Journal, told a crowd Wednesday at the Dole Institute of Politics that midterm elections often hinged on status of the national economy, approval ratings of the sitting president and personal abilities of candidates nominated to run for U.S. House or U.S. Senate.
Despite President Donald Trump carrying Kansas three times since 2016 by 14-20 percentage points, Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall’s reelection campaign was transformed into a cliffhanger with emergence of Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, the founder of a Methodist megachurch.
“This is one of the ones where candidate quality matters most,” Bado said. “This is a rescue operation for Republicans on Roger Marshall, who seems to wake up and find every available rake to step on right now. Adam Hamilton had been thinking about running potentially as an independent. He’s got the profile though to make Kansas very competitive. I think this one is really going to come down to the wire and national Republicans are incredibly, incredibly concerned about it.”
Rubashkin included Kansas among nine states where Democrats had a shot at flipping a Senate seat, but he appeared less bullish on Kansas than Bado.
Marshall would have to squander the 11.4-point margin he achieved in 2020 against Democrat Barbara Bollier in the same state Trump carried in 2024 by 16.1 points against Democrat Kamala Harris.
An Oct. 9-10 poll of 1,200 likely voters by InsiderAdvantage, which doesn’t meet the New York Times criteria for select pollsters, showed Hamilton at 47.5% to Marshall’s 46.7%, which was within the 2.8% margin of error.
Rubashkin said the path to a Democratic majority in the Senate started with retention of all seats held by Democrats up for grabs in November, including Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire. Democrats would need to claim four seats from Republicans to create a 51-49 majority. A 50-50 tie would leave the GOP in charge, because Vice President JD Vance would break ties.
Both North Carolina and Maine were “low-hanging fruit” for Senate Democrats on Nov. 3, Rubashkin said.
“There’s a big gap between the next tranche of states,” he said. “We’re talking about Ohio and Alaska, which are both states Donald Trump won essentially by double digits in all three of the last presidential elections, as well as Texas and Iowa, which similarly are very Republican states at the presidential level. That’s before we even get to places like Kansas and South Carolina.”
Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932. That’s the year national unemployment hit 33%, Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal was new and Babe Ruth famously flicked his hand to telegraph a home run in the World Series.
In terms of Republicans retaining majority control of the U.S. House, Rubashkin said Democrats were “heavily favored” to retake that chamber.
“As we’ve seen the cycle play out, Democrats are starting to encroach further and further into heavily Republican territory,” Rubashkin said. “You’ve got south Texas seats that look competitive now because Hispanic voters have moved so much away from their 2024 voting margin. You have these rural districts that are being hit hard by agricultural policy — by the tariffs, by the spike in diesel prices due to the war in Iran — that are coming online for Democrats in a major way.”
Bado offered a blunt assessment of the GOP’s prospect of holding the U.S. House: “The Republican case is prayer. It’s so much more difficult to find a viable path to a majority for them.”
He said congressional redistricting championed by Trump was unlikely to deliver the number of Republican seats the tactic was designed to claim. Early in the mid-decade redistricting fight, there were predictions the GOP could gain more than a dozen House seats in 2026.
“There are very, very few slam dunks for them in redistricted races,” Bado said. “It might net them two, three, maybe four seats.”
