name: Michigan Advance
title: UAW members recall tense encounters with Mike Rogers during his time in Congress
text:
Then-House Energy and Commerce Committee member Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI) at a hearing October 30, 2013 in Washington, DC.  (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)As Mike Rogers courts Michigan voters in his bid for the open U.S. Senate seat, members of Michigan’s largest union describe a strained relationship with him when he was last in Congress.
Rogers represented the 8th Congressional District in the U.S. House from 2001 to 2015, which covered parts of Mid-Michigan. That district encompassed the General Motors Lansing Grand River Assembly plant that employed hundreds of United Auto Workers members, including during the 2008 financial crisis, a contentious time for the auto industry in which new vehicle sales fell 40% while employment dropped by 45%.
In the Senate race, the UAW and other unions including the AFL-CIO, the AFT, and Michigan Teamsters Joint Council No. 43 have endorsed Rogers’ opponent, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Rogers, meanwhile, has secured endorsements from the business community, including the Detroit Regional Chamber and Southeast Michigan Chamber of Commerce, as well as a coalition called Auto Workers for Trump.
Active and retired UAW members told Michigan Advance they recall tense meetings with Rogers’ office when they lobbied him in Congress. The UAW’s political arm, the Community Action Program, also known as CAP, convenes in Washington, D.C., every other year and members from across the country meet with legislators to advocate for the union.
GM’s Lansing Grand River Assembly Plant in Oct. 2025. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
In February 2003, Art Reyes II, a former president of UAW Local 651 in Flint, told the Advance that he led a UAW meeting with Rogers as the then-Local 651 CAP Committee chair. According to Reyes, Rogers started the meeting by saying he understood the issues the UAW was facing because his brother worked in the plant. Reyes said he responded by asking why Rogers “supported an agenda that ran counter to his brother’s interests.” 
“He did not like that and tried to reiterate a lot of the points – trickle down economics, and you know, the whole rigmarole that … as early as 2003, we had known for quite some time was a failed policy,” Reyes said.
Michigan Advance obtained a letter stored in the Michael J. Rogers Congressional Collection at Oakland University. Rogers donated the collection after he left the House. In the letter, dated June 18, 2003, addressed to then-UAW President Ron Gettelfinger, Rogers writes that some members of the union’s Michigan leadership had been “confrontational” in meetings in his Washington office, which he wrote was “highly disruptive to constructive dialogue.” Rogers then asked Gettelfinger to keep future meetings to four to six people and said he “would wholeheartedly welcome such a discussion.”
Mike Rogers claims he was an assembly line worker. The UAW said that is stretching the truth.

Alyssa Brouillet, communications director for the Rogers campaign, said in a statement to Michigan Advance when asked about the letter and UAW meetings: “The men and women actually doing the work on an auto factory floor don’t want to lose their union-negotiated healthcare to Medicare For All or risk losing jobs because of EV mandates – all of which Abdul is pushing for. What bigger siren do you need to see that Abdul’s base is crumbling?”
Reyes said that while meetings with Rogers’ office became tense, members were always respectful.
“I can say with confidence that President Gettelfinger knows full well the professionalism of the people that are sent to lobby our congresspeople,” Reyes said. “Though we may be volunteers, though we may be frontline workers and activists, we know better than to embarrass or to tarnish the name or legacy of the United Auto Workers.”
Reyes said Rogers’ “unwillingness to be questioned caused a great deal of the conflict, and the fact that we know our stuff” about his voting record and legislative issues. 
“I think that he was insulted that we dare ask him questions, that we were prepared with follow-up questions, and it was disruptive only in that the meeting did not follow the agenda that he had set in his mind,” Reyes said.
UAW members outside Mike Rogers’ Washington, D.C., office circa 2014. (Photo by Mike Huerta)
Reyes pointed to the North American Free Trade Agreement, or NAFTA, noting Flint and Lansing were cities heavily affected by the 1994 trade deal given the big manufacturing bases in both cities. El-Sayed has campaigned on Rogers’ support for NAFTA. Overall, the AFL-CIO has ranked Rogers’ House voting record at 11%, on par with the average rating for House Republicans.
Rogers also publicly opposed the September 2007 General Motors strike, a nationwide two-day walkout. The Detroit News reported that Rogers said he was “very disappointed” that the union could not reach an agreement. 
“There were numerous other options to the union that did not involve hurting the paychecks of Michigan families or letting down the future security of their members’ jobs,” Rogers said, according to The News. “As General Motors has recently taken positive steps forward, this decision is a step backward. This strike will not turn one outbound moving van around.”
By 2023, when Rogers last ran for U.S. Senate, he said he supported a UAW strike. 
His campaign has also attacked El-Sayed’s record on the auto industry, most notably using past comments in a campaign ad in which El-Sayed said “cars are the modern-day cigarette.”
UAW members recall hallway meetings
Several years into Rogers’ tenure in the House, UAW members said they often met with staffers in the hallway outside his office rather than with Rogers himself. Reyes noted some other Republicans would similarly send staffers when the UAW requested meetings.
Mike Huerta, now an international UAW staffer, said he spent more time with the trash can outside Rogers’ office than he did with the representative. 
“The arrogance to say ‘Please stop sending these workers to me. Please stop sending middle-class folks to discuss their problems,’” Huerta said. “He doesn’t want any part of that. All he wants to talk to is somebody who can feed his campaign coffers.”
United Auto Workers Local 602 President Mike Huerta rallies for U.S. House candidate and former state Sen. Curtis Hertel (D-East Lansing) in Lansing on Oct. 30, 2024. | Kyle Davidson
UAW member Julie Hartshorn, who said she didn’t see the inside of a congressional office until Elissa Slotkin was elected, also remembers standing in the hallway outside Rogers’ office.
“As a member of Congress, you should be willing to talk to people that you know you might not [agree with], but that’s an avenue of conversation,” Hartshorn said. “That’s how you still represent those people.”
Hartshorn said she has knocked on hundreds of doors for UAW-endorsed candidates and the response has been mostly positive.
Mike Green, who joined GM when he was 17 and worked there for 39 years before retiring, said UAW members would try to meet with different representatives “so our voice would be heard.” 
“We went there to meet with our representatives, and we were more received from everybody else other than him. It was like he never had time,” said Green, who was president of UAW Local 652 in Lansing.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Dean Poggiali, president of UAW Local 724 in Lansing from 1999 to 2017, recalled that, during CAP conferences, he often met with staffers in the hallway when seeking a sit-down meeting with Rogers.
“It was with staffers who really didn’t have a lot of knowledge of what some of the issues were that we were wanting to bring up at the time.”
In the current Senate race, Reyes said he sees a “clear contrast between the two candidates regarding their respect for working people.”
“We’re talking with [UAW] members, and we get some resistance from individuals who cannot see past the difference in religion. I believe that’s a bigoted opinion,” he said. 
“But the flip side of that, and it’s something that I’m seeing more of, is your non-regular voter, the low propensity voters … especially young people. They are fired up.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Office of Housing details affordable housing ‘mismatch’ along with  $97M funding request
text:
A construction worker hoses down the stucco at a newly constructed home in the Mesa Del Sol development in southeastern Albuquerque on July 13, 2026. Affordable housing developers told lawmakers they need additional tax relief and more-predictable state funding to continue to build new homes in New Mexico. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Leaders of the New Mexico Office of Housing on Wednesday released the results of a new analysis showing how the state’s existing housing supply shortchanges most low- and medium-income residents, along with a breakdown of close to $100 million in funding it plans to request next year. 
The Office of Housing has been attached administratively to the New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions, the state’s workforce development agency, since 2025. In that time, lawmakers have already provided it with more than $100 million for a variety of housing and homelessness initiatives. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During an online presentation, Department of Workforce Solutions Secretary Sarita Nair and Lisa Huval, the office’s housing initiatives manager, laid out seven policy priorities they arrived at following a series of interviews and analyses they conducted with the help of an outside consultant. 
The office’s priorities include increasing local capacity and updating local zoning codes to ensure faster housing permitting; preserving existing affordable housing units; collecting and analyzing more data; and using state subsidies to fill gaps that prevent developers from building new affordable housing.
At the moment, according to an analysis Huval provided, construction of a single apartment in a multifamily development would cost a developer in Albuquerque $348,000, a number that has steadily risen due to increased construction, regulatory and capital costs. But the only way that unit could be affordable to a tenant who makes 80% or less than the city’s median income is if it cost developers $275,000, Huval said. 
“That difference between those two numbers is really what is driving our housing shortage,” Huval said. 
Statewide, New Mexico lacks at least 50,000 units affordable to low- and moderate-income households, which refers to those who make between 30% and 150% of the area median income, officials said Wednesday. That includes two-person households statewide earning between $24,100 and $120,500. 
Roughly 60% of New Mexico households who make within that income range are “cost-burdened,” which means they spend about one-third or more of their incomes on housing. 
Overall, the analysis found that 65% of affordable housing across the state is owned by people who could afford more expensive dwellings based on their incomes.
New Mexico Legislature needs to help local governments permit more housing, report recommends

For example, 136,000 occupied housing units exist in New Mexico that are affordable to those who make 50% or less than the area median income. But 36% of those units — comprising roughly 47,000 homes — are owned by those who make more than the area median income. 
Nair said the “mismatch” pervades the statewide affordable housing market and occurs naturally. It points to a need for increased housing supply generally, but also of different types of housing across the income spectrum.
“This is not people doing bad things.This is the natural dynamic,” she said. “I myself live in a unit that’s affordable to a lower income than I make. And I own it, and I’m never moving.”
The disparity exists in the affordable rental market as well.
The Office of Housing is seeking roughly $97 million in the upcoming legislative session, most of which would go for “gap financing” for affordable housing construction. That includes $50 million for grants to developers, as well as $30 million in capital outlay. 
“Our hope is that over time less and less subsidy is needed for affordable housing for low- and moderate-income folks,” Huval said. “For now, we believe we need to continue to invest in or deploy grants that close that gap between what it takes to build housing and then what a low-moderate income household can afford to pay.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids deplores ‘for-sake-of-headlines’ ICE raids in Kansas
text:
U.S. Attorney for Kansas Ryan Kriegshauser, right, seen in this April 21, 2026, photo, says a three-day operation in southwest Kansas by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement led to 104 arrests. U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kansas, says ICE's "extreme actions" make Kansans feel less safe and puts unnecessary strain on local economies. (Photo by Grace Hills for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids said September raids in southwest Kansas by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement damaged the beef and dairy industries and demonstrated federal agents should work collaboratively with local law enforcement on immigration cases.
Trump’s immigration sweeps leave southwest Kansas communities looking for way forward

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security reported the three-day Operation Safe Community by ICE resulted in the arrest of 104 people. The office of the U.S. attorney for Kansas identified five individuals taken into custody from Sept. 22-24 had been convicted of crimes in other countries, lacked credentials to legally be in the United States and ought to be deported.
A Wichita Eagle investigation found that four of those five individuals had been deported months before the raid, and the fifth was already in federal prison at the time of the raid.
Davids, the 3rd District Democrat seeking reelection Nov. 3, said in a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that she had “grave concerns” about ICE’s work in Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal. She expressed support for enforcement of federal immigration law but argued it was unnecessary for ICE to paralyze the local agricultural economy.
“ICE’s activities led to local business closures and school absences,” Davids said. “Kansans have shared with me instances of citizens and documented persons being targeted on their way to work or going about their day, and in many cases, local law enforcement was not consulted.”
She said southwest Kansas was responsible for more than 20% of the nation’s daily cattle slaughter. ICE’s incursion into the meatpacking hub corresponded with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s reported 8.5% drop in the week-to-week slaughter of livestock.
She said the Kansas Livestock Association concluded ICE had a “chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table and keep the cattle supply chain moving.” The Kansas Dairy Association indicated ICE created uncertainty among workers, including those authorized to work in the United States.
“These extreme actions leave Kansans feeling less safe, strain local economies and disrupt national supply chains,” Davids’ letter to Mullin said. “I urge you to commit to immigration enforcement that coordinates with local law enforcement, respects legal workers and does not rely on racial profiling or significant economic disruptions for the sake of headlines or mass panic.”
Ryan Kriegshauser, the U.S. attorney for the district of Kansas, said in a statement the assertion ICE engaged in discriminatory sweeps based on skin color and race were “misguided and irresponsible.”
“Such rhetoric stokes fear and risks unnecessary harm to Kansas industries,” he said. “We encourage everyone discussing this topic, especially on social media, to pause, wait for the facts to be released and avoid amplifying sensational or unsubstantiated rumors.”
He said information about ICE arrests wasn’t always immediately disclosed to the public because of federal laws, ICE policies and other security considerations.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear issues executive order seeking to overhaul KentuckyWired board
text:
The authority overseeing the KentuckyWired broadband network has dealt with years of litigation with its private partner Accelecom. (Getty Images)FRANKFORT, Ky. — Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has issued an executive order overhauling the board overseeing the state’s broadband network KentuckyWired, throwing another wrench into a contentious lawsuit the network is entangled in.
In his Wednesday order, Beshear cited a Kentucky Supreme Court decision in June as authority to invalidate a state law passed this year by the Republican-controlled state legislature that overhauled the leadership and board for the Kentucky Communications Network Authority, or KCNA. That June decision nullified legislative attempts to shift control of the Kentucky Fair Board from the governor to the agriculture commissioner.
That state law, House Bill 314, removed the majority of Beshear appointments from the board and replaced the majority of the board with appointments made by Republican state constitutional officers. Beshear’s order would revert the board to its previous makeup before the passage of HB 314. 
Republicans argued HB 314 was needed to provide better oversight over the network that’s been entangled in a lawsuit for years with the private company Accelecom, or Open Fiber Kentucky Company LLC, which it partnered with to manage the network. The ongoing contract disputes before Franklin Circuit Court Judge Phillip Shepherd include Accelecom seeking permission to connect certain customers to the middle mile network. 
Beshear issued the executive order ahead of a Thursday morning court hearing in Shepherd’s courtroom for the lawsuit between the state and Accelecom, the last scheduled hearing before a planned trial date in November. 
KCNA is the agency administering the network of hundreds of miles of fiber optic cable built across the state to provide high-speed internet connection to every county seat. 
That network serves as a “middle mile” of internet connection, and private companies then build a “last mile” of internet connection directly to homes and businesses. The network serves the school districts, court system, executive branch offices, public universities and community and technical colleges.
In a Wednesday afternoon email, one of the board members appointed after the passage of HB 314 pushed back on the authority of the executive order to remake the board. 
Russ Hensley wrote the Kentucky Supreme Court decision that Beshear relies on in his executive order does not allow for “replacing KCNA’s statutory Board by executive order.” 
“I do not accept that this executive order lawfully ends my service, and I reserve my objections to its validity,” Hensley wrote. 
Shepherd during the Thursday morning court hearing also questioned the authority of Beshear’s executive order.
“I know he’s a very good lawyer. And I think I also know that he realizes he can’t declare statutes unconstitutional,” Shepherd said about the order. 
He said he believed HB 314 still had “full force and effect.” 
“If the governor disputes that, he’s welcome to come in here and file a motion to intervene and to raise the arguments that he’s made,” Shepherd said. 
He also said it was his belief the ongoing lawsuit has hampered the ability of the KentuckyWired network to benefit Kentuckians. 
“It is not a fully operational program now, and the longer it stays in litigation, the more the public interest is going to suffer,” Shepherd said. 
This story will be updated.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Senators decry ‘disastrous,’ ‘flabbergasting’ Census changes
text:
LAWMAKERS ARE TRYING to get their arms around possible changes to the US Census that they fear could dramatically alter congressional representation and cause funding for federal assistance to be slashed. 
The Massachusetts Senate Committee on the Census, which has been grappling with the looming 2030 decennial census, held a hearing Wednesday to examine proposed federal rules that would exclude non-citizens from the count and change the way residency is determined. The new residency requirements would count people based on where they are between January 3 and April 1, potentially decimating counts for university students and the “snowbird” population who spend the harsh winter months in warmer climes. 
During the hearing, experts testified that these changes would hit Massachusetts with particular force.  
The change, if implemented, would “dramatically and inaccurately favor southern states where many northern residents, sometimes called snowbirds, spend some or all of the months of December through March, despite spending a majority of their time voting in and paying taxes to northern states like Massachusetts,” Jessie Partride Guerrero, director of data services at the Metropolitan Area Planning Commission, testified. 
The new rules, if enacted, would mean census counts could not include many international students, international workers, those with Temporary Protected Status because their home countries are considered unsafe to live in, refugees, asylum seekers, and more. 
Some 1.3 million residents in the Bay State are foreign born — about a fifth of the state’s population, and over 641,000 of whom are noncitizens, said Susan Strate, senior program manager at the UMass Donahue Institute’s Population Estimates Program. That would be the rough equivalent of losing the entire city of Boston in the Census. 
“It’s flabbergasting to think of the impact that this could have,” said Sen. Becca Rausch of Needham. “It is disastrous in so many ways. Maybe it’s not sloppy. Maybe it’s deliberate. Maybe it is a deliberate attempt by the Trump administration to force counts out of northern states and into southern states. It’s certainly not beyond the pale or beyond comprehension that that could be a goal here. It’s disgusting.” 
The Census Bureau proposed these changes in September to the regulations governing the decennial census. Public comment on the regulations is open until November 2 — the day before the midterm elections. 
“These proposals are intended to ensure fidelity to the Constitution, improve and protect the core decennial census data, and promote efficiency,” the Census Bureau said in its explanation of the rule. Based on its reading of Founding-era documents, the bureau said “illegal aliens (among others) should not be included in the apportionment count, as they are not true inhabitants, members of the body politic, or persons with a ‘usual residence’ in the United States due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States.” 
Strate testified that inaccurate Census count impacts will ripple out into inaccurate employment rates, inaccurate health care statistics, and federal dollars per person.  
These counts are used to guide funding formulas for programs like the Community Development Block Grant program. Excluding non-citizens could mean a loss of $1.5 billion a year in federal funding, Strate said. The Census “is about data, money, and power,” she added. 
The state could also lose congressional representation, Strate said. Massachusetts once had 10 seats in Congress, but lost one after the 2010 census. New York lost a seat by just 89 people after the 2020 Census. 
These changes reflect a broader disruption in the US Census Bureau, said Beth Jarosz, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy. She estimated about 13 to 19 percent of staff had been lost since 2025, along with the elimination of scientific advisory committees, a year without staff attending conferences, and the termination of all data-user advisory groups. 
In June 2026, the Department of Commerce issued an order banning modern privacy protection methods from any statistical product, cutting in half the tools the bureau uses to publish detailed data on specific communities. Jarosz said that order is now being used to justify removing race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 questionnaire — the argument being that, without modern privacy tools, granular demographic data can’t be safely published.  
Race has appeared on every US Census since 1790, she said. 
The privacy “proposal feels like it’s being used as pretext for removing demographic questions in the decennial census,” Jarosz told lawmakers. 
Kristy Senatori, executive director of the Cape Cod Commission, described a stunning regional undercount risk: a combined undercount of more than 12 percent for Barnstable County if both the snowbird and non-citizen exclusions take effect.  
Cape Cod could potentially see an undercount of approximately 10,500 individuals in total from the non-citizen change. The three month “enumeration period” between January and April also has the potential to result in an undercount of approximately 18,000 individuals, Senatori said. 
“Along with the demographic changes, we’re also concerned about the utility of the data moving forward,” she said. “When parameters that have been collected for a very long time change, the data sets are no longer comparable. And if the census results in an undercount of our regional population … those effects will ripple throughout distribution of funds and services, certainly throughout regional and local planning and those services that we need to continue to provide to our residents throughout Cape Cod.” 
Committee members and experts said they expect litigation to challenge the rule if it is ultimately adopted.  
Committee chair Sen. William Brownsberger of Belmont said the proposal was “disastrous,” and though he said speculation was probably unwise, he is “almost certain the US Supreme Court won’t uphold this,” and he expects the attorney general’s office will get involved.  
“I personally fear that the ramifications and the impact of these kinds of changes, assuming they go through, are going to be felt long before we get a decision from SCOTUS,” Rausch said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Duke’s fixation on dirty energy is costing you
text:
A Duke Energy coal-fired power plant near Roxboro, NC. (Photo:  Southern Environmental Law Center) When an unusual heat wave hit North Carolina on September 18, millions of residents turned on the AC to escape the high temperatures. This unexpected demand strained the electric grid, jeopardizing the ability of homes and businesses to keep power on and stay safe. In a warming world with increasingly extreme weather, the lesson is clear: we need more affordable energy to ensure that everyone has year-round access to electricity.
But according to Duke Energy, the state’s largest utility, it’s ratepayers who have to fix this problem.
During the heat wave, Duke asked its 3.9 million North Carolina customers to reduce their electricity use from 2 – 8 p.m. to ease the strain on the electric grid. At the hottest point in the day, Duke wanted families to turn up the heat and limit oven use. Similarly, during Winter Storm Fern, Duke asked customers to set the thermostat to the coldest comfortable setting and avoid using appliances.
The point is not that we should never moderate our electricity use for the common good. The point is that this demand is coming from a monopoly utility that controls electricity for almost four million people. A utility that has abandoned renewable energy projects that would bring affordable, reliable power to our grid and prevent situations like these from happening. A utility that wants to raise electricity prices by 9.5%, lock North Carolina into decades of expensive, dirty energy projects, and shift your money into the pockets of its CEO and shareholders.
As it actively courts new power-hungry data centers, Duke is asking you to sacrifice your electricity needs, all while increasing your bills. And the reason you’re being asked to live with less is Duke’s commitment to dirty energy.
Last year, Duke slashed its planned solar capacity by over 50% (earlier this year, regulators froze the smaller plans entirely). In June, Duke accepted a $129 million buyout from the Trump administration to scrap an offshore wind project that could have powered 300,000 homes annually and sheltered customers from fossil fuel price volatility. Meanwhile, Duke is doubling down on dirty energy: Duke delayed three North Carolina coal plant retirements and has the second-most planned gas capacity nationally.
These decisions will make energy more expensive for North Carolina families and small businesses while Duke reaps the profits. A renewable-heavy energy portfolio would save North Carolinians between $4.5 and $8 billion. Solar and wind power are the cheapest ways to produce electricity and the quickest types of power to bring online, meaning they’re the best solutions to address rising energy needs. Coal and gas, meanwhile, are volatile fuel sources, subject to price shocks from external factors like geopolitical conflicts and extreme weather that send monthly bills soaring. Pipeline, storage, and processing infrastructure make gas plants particularly expensive. Conveniently for Duke, this allows them to raise rates for customers and reward their shareholders and executives due to state-sanctioned return on capital investments.
These costs aren’t an oversight: locking North Carolina into decades of expensive fossil fuel projects allows Duke to justify endless rate hikes, all while they make record profits. It’s why they are demanding a 9.5% rate increase despite posting billions of dollars in profits already this year, and paying their CEOs $22 million last year.
By prioritizing profits over affordability, Duke is jeopardizing the safety and wellbeing of its customers. The biggest threat to reliable electricity isn’t keeping the thermostat too low on a hot day: it’s Duke. Last year, Duke disconnected customers 187,000 times, a 37% increase from 2024. One in five Duke customers in North Carolina are indebted to the utility, a number that could grow if they raise rates even higher.
Thankfully, people are fighting back. Duke initially proposed raising electricity rates by 18%, only to reduce the proposal after intense backlash (Attorney General Jackson continues to fight the 9.5% proposed increase). On September 18, regulators rejected Duke’s proposal to build a new gas power plant over cost concerns. These decisions only happened because advocates and ratepayers sounded the alarm. For the sake of affordable, reliable electricity, we must continue holding Duke accountable for its dirty, expensive energy agenda.
Mikaela Curry is Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal Campaign Manager based in North Carolina. Tyson Slocum is the director of Public Citizen’s Energy Program.

name: Mississippi Today
title: These Yazoo City families overcome hurdles to own their homes
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
YAZOO CITY — Forty families in Yazoo City learned Wednesday they will soon become homeowners — without the burden of a mortgage — after overcoming obstacles that threatened to derail their dreams of owning homes.
The families began renting the houses in the Roberts Estates development as many as 19 years ago with the promise of the opportunity to purchase their homes after 15 years through a lease-to-own arrangement. But as they reached the end of the term, obstacles arose. 
The agreed-upon purchase price for the homes was $15,000 each, but the amount was so low that mortgage companies did not want to underwrite the purchase, said Alpresteon “Sabrina” Billings, the CEO of Yazoo City-based Gateway Community Development Corp., the community’s original developer. Roof damage from storms and limited reserves to make home repairs added to the hurdles. 
U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, fifth left, and other dignitaries and homeowners snip a ribbon to celebrate homeownership at the Roberts Estates, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2024, in Yazoo City. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Democratic U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi secured a $3 million grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to help shore up the gap.
“Words can’t explain how I feel,” Billings said Wednesday. “I’m just grateful to see the smiles on the families’ faces.” 
Of the community’s 40 homes, 38 are occupied by original residents and two by their descendants. The home sales are expected to begin closing Nov. 1, Billings said. 
Giving families outright ownership of the homes will immediately build their equity and strengthen their financial stability, said Bill Bynum, CEO of Jackson-based HOPE Enterprise Corp. HOPE stepped in as an intermediary, using the HUD grant to purchase the properties, make repairs and fulfill the conditions of the original agreements with residents. 
“Without a mortgage, the resources that they used for their rent can now go toward taxes, insurance and maintenance,” Bynum said. 
Entrance to the Roberts Estates neighborhood, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Yazoo City. A celebration was held to honor 40 families that now own their homes after renting them for more than 19 years. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Miranda Alexander, who serves as tax collector of Yazoo County, has rented her home in Roberts Estates for 19 years. She said becoming a homeowner will immediately boost her financial stability. 
“Liberated. Free. I feel renewed,” she said. 
It is common for developers to face challenges at the end of a lease-to-own agreement term, especially as the housing market changes over time, said Scott Spivey, executive director of the Mississippi Home Corp. These real estate agreements combine a standard rental lease with a future right or obligation to buy the property at the end of a term. 
Gateway’s agreement — to sell the homes for $15,000 each at the end of the leasing term — was bold, Spivey said. 
The end result, which eschews the need for a mortgage completely, is good for both families and for lenders, because managing small mortgages can be costly, he said. 
“There’s no surer way to build multigeneration wealth,” Spivey said.  
John Jackson, a Roberts Estates homeowner, shares his gratitude for his home during a home ownership celebration held in the neighborhood, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Yazoo City. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The project, fittingly located off of Haley Barbour Parkway, was funded in the wake of Hurricane Katrina through Mississippi’s Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program during the former governor’s administration. 
Through the program, developers receive the credits through a process managed by the state housing authority and sell them to investors. Developers then use the funds to build affordable housing. 
Building on previous success, Gateway Community Development Corporation has begun work to develop Roberts Estates II in Yazoo City, which will create a path to homeownership for 33 additional future homebuyers under a similar lease-to-own agreement. 
Bettie Reed rented her home for nearly two decades, and like the other residents of Roberts Estates, she faced uncertainty when the agreed upon term of 15 years of leasing her house expired with no clear path to homeownership. 
She said the home means everything to her. 
“I don’t owe anybody nothing,” Reed said. “Ain’t that a blessing?”
Editor’s note: Bill Bynum sits on Deep South Today’s Board of Directors.

name: Daily Montanan
title: One-party rule has cost Montana millions because of the Legislature’s love of unconstitutional bills
text:
Lawyer Kyle Gray, left, with Holland & Hart, argues on behalf of plaintiffs who allege Senate bill 458 is unconstitutional. Lawyer Alex Rate, with the ACLU of Montana, also represents plaintiffs. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)During the last several years anyone following the news has been made aware of the majority party in Montana pushing to reform the state judiciary.
Their complaints, including judicial activism, have been many – enough so to create a select committee for judicial review and oversight after the 2023 legislative session. From that select committee dozens of bills were created to reign in a supposedly malfeasant and reckless judicial branch. Does the judicial branch need reforming and oversight, or is there something else going on here?
Statistics don’t lie, yet as history shows, regardless of party affiliation, elected officials can and will if they can get away with it. Historical statistics show that in the state of Montana from 1900 to 2020 a total of 36 pieces of legislation passed and executed into law were deemed unconstitutional by state and federal courts, with 24 of those occurring between 1900 and 1989.
In 2021, everything changed to a historic level. In that legislative session alone, 16 pieces of legislation passed and executed into law were rule unconstitutional by the courts. That was followed by the 2023 legislative session with another eight pieces of legislation passed, executed, and ended up being unconstitutional, a total of 24 in two legislative sessions. Think about that: What took previous legislative sessions almost a century to accomplish, the current majority party managed to accomplish in two sessions.
Ask yourself what caused this flurry of bills to be ruled unconstitutional: Was it judicial activism, out-of-control courts, or legislative recklessness on a historic scale? For some citizens reading this, the idea of passing unconstitutional laws may be a nonstarter, and why bother even talking about it? That is because there is another aspect to this: Money—our money—being spent on legislating, then defending the legislation against constitutional legal challenges.
It doesn’t come cheap, as documented in this publication when Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen signed the check for $825,000 to pay the attorneys who represented the plaintiffs against the state in Senate Bill 266, passed in the 2021 legislative session. We taxpayers had other costs to bear by paying for the time and energy to multiple hearings in the legislature, Gov. Greg Gianforte’s speech about “woke overzealous regulators,” and paying attorneys in the Montana Department of Justice to defend the state. All told, more than $1 million of our tax money was spent, the bulk of which, for out-of-state attorneys who charged several hundred dollars an hour. One million of our tax dollars to settle unconstitutional law. Now multiply that times 24, and the majority party has decided millions in taxpayer money was an inexpensive price to pay for nothing more than grandiose political theater.
Again, is this blitzkrieg of unconstitutional bills from two legislative sessions the product of an out-of-control judicial branch, or constitutionally corrupt legislative and executive branches? With millions and counting, the readers of this publication might want to think that through. Is this an isolated issue, or the tip of the iceberg with the unchecked power of one-party rule? Your property taxes tell the tale.
It’s time then for a full line-item audit by the state auditor of the legislative and executive branches pertaining to all expenses related to these unconstitutional bills. Everyone listed above are our employees. It’s time for that their employers to keep them accountable to the true costs of this historic legislative assault on the rule of law.
Realize it’s not over.
Multiple pieces of legislation passed in 2025, like HB 719, recently ruled unconstitutional, are being contested. No doubt many others will be ruled unconstitutional. More millions down the drain with potentially more to come in the 2027 legislative session. In economically stressed times like these, can we afford our employees tossing our money around like “Monopoly” money? Obviously one-party rule is not as fiscally conservative as we’ve been promised.
Remember Montana, if those we elect to public office don’t have to follow the rule of law and the Constitution they took an oath to uphold, neither do we. Anarchy anybody?
Before answering, ask former Vice President Mike Pence about anarchy.
Marshall lives in Hot Springs, Montana.
